By His saying, "suddenly" (baghtah), He means: abruptly, without the one who is overtaken by it knowing the time of its onset.

* *

It is said from this: "baghattuhu, abghatuhu baghtah," meaning: when it seizes him in that manner.

* *

"They say, 'Oh, our regret over what we neglected concerning it!'" He, exalted is His mention, says: those who denied the meeting with God were cheated by selling their places in Paradise for the places of those in Paradise who bought them, to be in Hell. So when the Hour comes upon them suddenly, they say, when they witness what they sold and what they bought, and recognize the loss of the transaction of their sale that they made in the world, in remorse and anguish over the great deception they inflicted upon themselves and the tremendous loss, which has no greater loss than it: "Oh, our regret over what we neglected concerning it!" — meaning: Oh, our remorse over what we wasted in it, namely that transaction. [[See the explanation of "al-hasrah" (regret) in what has preceded, 3: 295 / 7: 335.]]

* *

The pronoun "hā" and "alif" in His saying "fīhā" refers to "the transaction," though it is not mentioned explicitly; the reference is sufficed by His saying "Those who denied the meeting with God have certainly lost," since it is known that loss occurs only in a trade transaction that has taken place. [[In the printed edition: "qad khasirat" (feminine), and I have retained what is in the manuscript, which is correct.]]

* *

The meaning of the speech is: those who denied the meeting with God were cheated by selling faith, through which they would deserve God's pleasure and Paradise, for disbelief, through which they would deserve His wrath and punishment, and they do not perceive the loss they incur in that, until the Hour arrives. When the Hour comes upon them suddenly and they see the loss they suffered in their trade, they will then say, in remorse: "Oh, our regret over what we neglected concerning it!"

* *

Those of the interpreters (ahl al-ta'wil) said things similar to what we have said on this.

Those who said that:

13185 — Muhammad ibn al-Husayn narrated to me, saying: Ahmad ibn al-Mufaddal narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, regarding His saying: "Oh, our regret over what we neglected concerning it!" As for "Oh, our regret," it is our remorse; "over what we neglected concerning it," meaning, what we wasted of the deeds of Paradise.

13186 — Muhammad ibn 'Umarah al-Asadi narrated to us, saying: Yazid ibn Mihran narrated to us, saying: Abu Bakr ibn 'Ayyash narrated to us, from al-A'mash, from Abu Salih, from Abu Sa'id, from the Prophet (ﷺ) regarding His saying: "Oh, our regret," he said: "The people of the Fire will see their places in Paradise, and they will say: Oh, our regret!" [[The narration 13186: Yazid ibn Mihran al-Asadi, the bread-seller, Abu Khalid. Truthful; Ibn Hibban mentioned him among the reliable narrators and said he "reports strange things." He is biographed in al-Tahdhib and Ibn Abi Hatim 4/2/290.

This report was cited by al-Suyuti in al-Durr al-Manthur 3: 9, who said: "Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Khatib narrated it with a sound chain, from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri," and mentioned the report.]]

* *

The interpretation of His saying: ﴿While they bear their burdens upon their backs. Unquestionably, evil is what they bear﴾

Abu Ja'far said: He, exalted is His mention, says: And these who denied the meeting with God "bear their burdens upon their backs." The "they" in His saying "they bear their burdens" refers to them, meaning: their sins and wrongdoings.

* *

Its singular is "wizr" (burden). It is said from it: "wazara al-rajul yazir" when he committed a sin. God says: "Unquestionably, evil is what they bear." [[In the printed edition, the phrase "God says: Unquestionably, evil is what they bear" is omitted.]] If it is meant that they were made sinful, [["uthimu" with a dammah on the hamzah and a shaddah on the kasrah-marked tha', in the passive voice, meaning: they were charged with sin.]] it is said: "The people were burdened (wuzira), so they are burdened, and they are burdened (mawzurun)."

* *

Some have claimed that "wizr" means weight and load. I do not know it to be so in any attested usage, nor from a trustworthy transmission from the Arabs.

* *

God, exalted is His mention, said "upon their backs," because a load may be carried on the head, the shoulder, or other places, so the specification of the place of their carrying clarifies what they carry.

* *

It is mentioned that their carrying their burdens on that Day will be upon their backs, similar to what was narrated:

13187 — Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: al-Hakam ibn Bashir ibn Salman narrated to us, saying: 'Amr ibn Qays al-Mala'i narrated to us, saying: When the believer rises from his grave, the most beautiful thing in form and the most fragrant in scent will meet him, [[In the printed edition: "his deed in the most beautiful form and most fragrant scent," which is a weak and incorrect statement; the manuscript reads "the most beautiful form and most fragrant scent," with "thing" (shay') dropped by the copyist, which I have restored and inferred from the later phrase "the most repulsive thing in form and most foul in scent will meet him."]] and he will say to him: "Do you know me?" He will say: "No, except that God has made your scent fragrant and your form beautiful!" He will say: "Thus you were in the world. I am your righteous deed; you rode me often in the world, so ride me today!" And he recited: "On the Day We gather the righteous to the Most Merciful as a delegation" [Surah Maryam: 85]. And the disbeliever will be met by the most repulsive thing in form and most foul in scent, and he will say: "Do you know me?" He will say: "No, except that God has made your form ugly and your scent foul!" He will say: "Thus you were in the world. I am your evil deed; you rode me in the world, so today I ride you." And he recited: "While they bear their burdens upon their backs. Unquestionably, evil is what they bear." [[Narration 13187: al-Hakam ibn Bashir ibn Salman al-Nahdi, trustworthy; he has passed several times. In the printed edition, it reads "Sulayman" here, which is an error; I have corrected it from the manuscript and the references. 

'Amr ibn Qays al-Mala'i has passed several times.

Al-Suyuti cited this report in al-Durr al-Manthur 3: 9 and attributed it additionally to Ibn Abi Hatim. Abu Hatim's chain, as narrated by Ibn Kathir in his tafsir 3: 303, is: "Abu Sa'id al-Ashaj narrated to us, saying: Abu Khalid al-Ahmar narrated to us, from 'Amr ibn Qays, from Abu Marzuq," and he related the report in abridged form with different wording.]]

13188 — Muhammad ibn al-Husayn narrated to me, saying: Ahmad ibn al-Mufaddal narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, regarding "While they bear their burdens upon their backs": there is no wrongdoing man who dies and enters his grave, except that there comes to him a man of ugly face, black in color, foul in scent, wearing dirty garments, until he enters the grave with him. When he sees him, he says: "How ugly is your face!" He says: "Thus your deed was ugly!" He says: "How foul is your scent!" He says: "Thus your deed was foul!" He says: "How dirty are your garments!" He says: "Your deed was indeed filthy." He says: "Who are you?" He says: "I am your deed!" So he remains with him in his grave. When he is raised on the Day of Resurrection, he will say to him: "I used to carry you in the world with pleasures and desires, and today you carry me." So he will ride on his back and drive him until he enters the Fire. That is His saying: "They bear their burdens upon their backs." [[In the printed edition: "He said: There is no wrongdoing man who dies," and I have retained the manuscript reading.]]

* *

As for His saying, exalted is His mention, "Unquestionably, evil is what they bear," it means: Unquestionably, evil is the burden they bear, that is, the sin they commit against their Lord. [[The printed edition read "the sin their disbelief against their Lord," adding "their disbelief," which corrupts the sentence. I have retained the manuscript, which is the pure correct reading. I have explained earlier the meaning of "athima fulan bi-rabbihi" (so-and-so sinned against his Lord) in 4: 530, footnote 3; 6: 92; 11: 180, footnote 3.]] As:

13189 — Al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah regarding His saying: "Unquestionably, evil is what they bear," he said: "Evil is what they do."

**The interpretation of His saying: ﴿And the life of this world is but play and amusement; and the Hereafter is better for those who fear Allah. Will you not then reason?﴾**

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: This is a rebuke from Allah, may He be remembered, against these disbelievers who deny resurrection after death, in their saying: ﴿There is nothing but our life of this world, and we will not be resurrected﴾ [Surat al-Ma'ida: 29].

He, may He be remembered, says, rebuking them for their claim: ﴿"The life of this world"﴾, O people, ﴿"is but play and amusement"﴾. He means: the one who seeks the pleasures of the life that has been brought near to you and made close to you in this abode of yours, and its delights and joys, ﴿in it﴾, [[The structure of the sentence is: "the one who seeks the pleasures of the life... and its delights and joys", joined by coordination, then his saying "in it", whose structure is: "the one who seeks the pleasures of the life... in it". And his later saying "and the one who takes pleasure in it" is in the nominative, coordinated with his saying "the one who seeks the pleasures of the life".]] and the one who takes pleasure in it and competes for it, is only engaged in play and amusement, because it will soon depart from the one who enjoys it and takes pleasure in its delights, or the days will bring it their calamities and vicissitudes, so that it turns bitter for him and becomes turbid, [[In the printed edition: "then it passes over him and becomes turbid" differs from what is in the manuscript, and I have adopted the manuscript's reading, which is correct. "Tamurru" (it passes bitter) comes from "al-marara" (bitterness), meaning it becomes bitter after its sweetness and turbid after its clarity.]] like the playful, amusement-seeking player whose play and amusement quickly vanish from him, and then leave him with regret and bring him sorrow. He says: Do not be deceived by it, O people, for the one deceived by it will soon regret. ﴿"And the Hereafter is better for those who fear Allah"﴾, He says: and obedience to Him, and preparation for the Hereafter through righteous deeds whose benefits remain for their doers and whose joy endures for their people in it, is better than the abode that perishes swiftly, [[In the printed edition, the word "washīkan" (swiftly) has been omitted, as if its reading were not well understood. "Washīkan" means quickly.]] so that its inhabitants have no joy left and no lasting bliss. ﴿"For those who fear Allah"﴾, He says: for those who fear Allah and guard themselves by obeying Him, avoiding His disobedience, and hastening to His pleasure. ﴿"Will you not then reason?"﴾, He says: Will these deniers of resurrection not reason about the truth of what We inform them, namely that the life of this world is play and amusement? They see those among them who are taken away, [["Ukhtuoima al-rajul" (in the passive) and "ukhtaramathu al-maniyyah min bayn ashabihi" mean: he was taken from among them and his place was left empty, as if his place had become a gap in their ranks.]] those who perish and die, and those on whom its calamities fall, whom its misfortunes strike and whose afflictions grieve them. In that there is a reminder and a deterrent for whoever has understanding, against inclining toward it and enslaving the soul to it, and it is a clear proof that it has a Governor and Disposer, to whom all creation must sincerely direct worship, without associating anything else with Him.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 6, verse 33:

The interpretation of His words: ﴿We know indeed that what they say grieves you, but it is not you they deny; rather, the wrongdoers deny the signs of Allah﴾ (33).

Abu Ja'far said: Exalted is He, says to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ): "We know," O Muhammad, "that what the polytheists say grieves you," that is, their saying to you that you are a liar, "for they do not deny you."

* *

The reciters differed regarding the reading of this.

A group of the people of Kufa recited it: ﴿fa-innahum la yukdhibunaka﴾ with lightening (takhfif). [[This addition between the brackets is omitted from the manuscript and the printed edition, but its inclusion is necessary, and I have inferred it from the attribution of this reading, for it is the reading of Ali, Nafi' and al-Kisa'i. See Ma'ani al-Qur'an of al-Farra' 1: 331, and Tafsir of Abu Hayyan 4: 111, and others.]] meaning: they do not call you a liar regarding what you have brought them from Allah's revelation, and they do not deny that it is true; rather they know its truth, but they reject its reality verbally, so they do not believe in it.

* *

Some scholars of the Arabic language used to report from the Arabs that they say: "akdhabtu al-rajul" (I attributed falsehood to the man) when you inform that he has brought falsehood and related it. He said: and they say: "kadhdhabtuhu" (I called him a liar) when you inform that he is a liar. [[See Ma'ani al-Qur'an of al-Farra' 1: 331.]]

* *

A group of the reciters of Madina, the Iraqis, Kufa and Basra recited it: ﴿fa-innahum la yukadhdhibunaka﴾, meaning: they do not call you a liar in knowledge, rather they know that you are truthful, = but they call you a liar verbally out of obstinacy and envy.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The correct view on this matter, in my opinion, is to say: both are two well-known readings, each of which has been recited by a group of reciters, and each has a comprehensible meaning in soundness.

That is because there is no doubt that among the polytheists there were people who denied the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and repudiated what Allah, exalted is He, had singled him out with of prophethood. Some of them would say, "He is a poet," some would say, "He is a soothsayer," some would say, "He is a madman," and all of them would deny verbally that what he brought them was a revelation from heaven and a revelation of the Lord of the worlds. Some of them had clearly understood his affair and knew the soundness of his prophethood, yet he was obstinate in that, denying his prophethood out of envy and rebellion.

* *

So the one who reads ﴿fa-innahum la yukdhibunaka﴾ means that those who knew the reality of your prophethood and the truth of what you say deny verbally that what you recite to them is a revelation from Allah and from the presence of Allah, while they know with certain knowledge that it is from Allah = he is correct, [[The context: "fa-al-qari'... musib" (so the reciter... is correct).]] for what we have mentioned, that there were among them those with this description.

In the saying of Allah, exalted is He, in this surah: ﴿Those to whom We gave the Book recognize it as they recognize their sons﴾ [Surah al-Ma'idah: 20], there is clear evidence that among them there were those obstinate in denying his prophethood (ﷺ), while knowing him and the soundness of his prophethood.

* *

Likewise the one who reads ﴿fa-innahum la yukadhdhibunaka﴾ = meaning: they do not deny the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) except out of obstinacy, not out of ignorance of his prophethood and the truthfulness of his speech = he is correct, [[The context: "wa-kadhalika al-qari'... musib" (likewise the reciter... is correct).]] for what we have mentioned, that there were among them those with this description.

Each of these two interpretations has been adopted by a group of the scholars of interpretation.

* *

Mention of those who said: the meaning of that is: they do not deny you, but they reject the truth while knowing that you are a prophet of Allah and truthful.

13190 - Hannad related to us, saying: Abu Mu'awiyah related to us, from Isma'il ibn Abi Khalid, from Abu Salih, regarding His words: "We know indeed that what they say grieves you, but it is not you they deny," he said: Jibril came to the Prophet (ﷺ) one day while he was sitting sad, and said to him: What grieves you? He said: These people have called me a liar! He said: Jibril said to him: They do not deny you; they know that you are truthful, "but the wrongdoers deny the signs of Allah."

13191 - Ibn WakI' related to us, saying: Abu Mu'awiyah related to us, from Isma'il, from Abu Salih, who said: Jibril came to the Prophet (ﷺ) while he was sitting sad, and said to him: What grieves you? He said: These people have called me a liar! Jibril said to him: They do not deny you, they indeed know that you are truthful, "but the wrongdoers deny the signs of Allah."

13192 - al-Hasan ibn Yahya related to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah regarding His words: "but the wrongdoers deny the signs of Allah," he said: They know that you are the Messenger of Allah and deny.

13193 - Muhammad ibn al-Husayn related to us, saying: Ahmad ibn al-Mufaddal related to us, saying: Asbat related to us, from al-Suddi regarding His words: "We know indeed that what they say grieves you, but it is not you they deny; rather the wrongdoers deny the signs of Allah." When the day of Badr came, al-Akhnas ibn Shariq said to the Banu Zuhrah: O Banu Zuhrah, Muhammad is the son of your sister, so you have the most right to hold back from him; if he is a prophet you will not fight him today, and if he is a liar, you have the most right to hold back from your sister's son! Stop here until I meet Abu al-Hakam; if Muhammad (ﷺ) is defeated you will return safe, and if Muhammad prevails, your people will not do anything to you. On that day he was named "al-Akhnas," and his name had been "Ubayy" [[He was named "al-Akhnas" because he is from "khanasa yakhnusu khunusan," meaning he withdrew from a thing, drew back and returned.]]. Al-Akhnas met Abu Jahl, and al-Akhnas went aside with Abu Jahl and said: O Abu al-Hakam, tell me about Muhammad: is he truthful or a liar? For there is no one of Quraysh here other than you and me hearing our words! Abu Jahl said: Woe to you! By Allah, Muhammad is truthful, and Muhammad has never lied, but when the sons of Qusayy take the banner, the custodianship of the Ka'bah, the watering of the pilgrims and the prophethood, what will remain for the rest of Quraysh? That is His saying: "they do not deny you, but the wrongdoers deny the signs of Allah," and "the signs of Allah" refers to Muhammad (ﷺ).

13194 - Al-Harith ibn Muhammad related to me, saying: 'Abd al-'Aziz related to us, saying: Qays related to us, from Salim al-Aftas, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr: "fa-innahum la yukadhdhibunaka," he said: They do not call Muhammad a liar, but they deny the signs of Allah.

* *

Mention of those who said: the meaning of that is: they do not deny you, but they deny what you have brought.

13195 - Muhammad ibn Bashshar related to us, saying: 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Mahdi related to us, saying: Sufyan related to us, from Abu Ishaq, from Najiyah, who said: Abu Jahl said to the Prophet (ﷺ): We do not accuse you, but we accuse what you have brought! So Allah, exalted is He, revealed: "They do not deny you, but the wrongdoers deny the signs of Allah."

13196 - Ibn WakI' related to us, saying: Yahya ibn Adam related to us, from Sufyan, from Abu Ishaq, from Najiyah ibn Ka'b: that Abu Jahl said to the Prophet (ﷺ): We do not deny you, but we deny what you have brought! So Allah, exalted is He, revealed: "They do not deny you, but the wrongdoers deny the signs of Allah."

* *

Others said: the meaning of that is: they do not nullify what you have brought them.

Mention of those who said that:

13197 - Ibn WakI' related to us, saying: Ishaq ibn Sulayman related to us, from Abu Ma'shar, from Muhammad ibn Ka'b: "fa-innahum la yukadhdhibunaka," he said: They do not nullify what is in your hands.

* *

As for His saying: "but the wrongdoers deny the signs of Allah," He means: but the polytheists deny, with the proofs of Allah and the verses of His Book and His Messenger, so they reject the soundness of all of that.

* *

al-Suddi used to say: "the signs" in this place refers to Muhammad (ﷺ). We have already mentioned the report to that effect from him earlier. [[See the end of the previous report, no. 13193.]]

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 6, verse 34:

The interpretation of His saying: ﴿And indeed messengers were denied before you, but they were patient over what they were denied and harmed until Our help came to them. There is none who can alter the words of Allah. And there has certainly come to you some of the news of the messengers.﴾

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: This is consolation from Allah, may His remembrance be exalted, to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ), and solace for him over the grief he suffered from his people's denial of what he had brought them of the truth from Allah.

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: Even if these polytheists among your people, O Muhammad, deny you, reject your prophethood, and deny that the signs of Allah are from Him, do not let that grieve you. Be patient over their denial of you and the hardship you encounter from them for the sake of Allah, until the help of Allah comes. [[In the manuscript: "until the help of Allah came to them", which is a scribal error; the correct reading is what appears in the printed edition.]] For messengers were denied before you, whom I sent to their nations, and they were harmed, yet they remained patient over their people's denial of them, and that did not turn them away from carrying out the command of Allah that He had given them, calling their people to Him, until Allah judged between them and their people. ﴿There is none who can alter the words of Allah﴾: that is, none who can change the words of Allah. "His words," may His remembrance be exalted, refer to what Allah revealed to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ), including His promise to him of help against those who oppose and contend with him, and of victory over those who turn away from him and retreat. ﴿And there has certainly come to you some of the news of the messengers﴾: that is, there has certainly come to you, O Muhammad, news of those messengers who came before you, and news of their nations, and what I did to them when they denied My signs and persisted in their error and misguidance. [[See the explanation of "naba'" (news) above, p. 262, note 3, and the references.]] The word "news" (anba') is omitted here, because "min" (some of) indicates it.

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: So await, you too, victory and triumph like that which was granted by Me to those messengers who came before you when their peoples denied them, and take them as an example in their patience over what they suffered from their people.

* *

Similar to this is what those among the people of interpretation have said regarding this verse.

Mention of those who said that:

13198 - Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, he said: Yazid ibn Zurai' narrated to us, he said: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His saying: ﴿And indeed messengers were denied before you, but they were patient over what they were denied﴾: He consoles His Prophet (ﷺ), as you hear, and informs him that messengers were denied before him, and they were patient over what they were denied, until Allah judged, and He is the best of judges.

13199 - Al-Muthanna narrated to me, he said: Ishaq narrated to us, he said: Abu Zuhayr narrated to us, from Juwaybir, from al-Dahhak: ﴿And indeed messengers were denied before you﴾, he said: He consoles His Prophet (ﷺ).

13200 - Al-Qasim narrated to us, he said: Al-Husayn narrated to us, he said: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Juraij: ﴿And indeed messengers were denied before you﴾, the verse, he said: He consoles His Prophet (ﷺ).

The commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 6, verse 35:

On the interpretation of His words: ﴿And if their turning away has been hard for you, then if you are able to seek a tunnel in the earth or a ladder into the sky to bring them a sign—﴾

Abu Ja'far said: May His remembrance be exalted, He says: If the turning away of these polytheists from you, O Muhammad, and their withdrawal from believing in what you have brought them of the truth with which I sent you, has been grievous to you, so that it distressed you and you did not endure the harm that reaches you from them [[See the explanation of "al-i'rad" (turning away) previously, p. 262, note 1, and the references there.]] — ﴿then if you are able to seek a tunnel in the earth﴾: that is, if you are able to make a passage in the earth like the burrow-entrance of the jerboa (nafaqa' al-yarbu'), which is one of its holes, and go into it [[See the explanation of "ibtaghā" previously, 10:394, note 1, and the references there.]] — ﴿or a ladder in the sky﴾: that is, an ascent by which you may climb, like a staircase and the like, as the poet said: [[He is Tamim ibn Ubayy ibn Muqbil.]]

*"The strongholds of the lands do not protect a man, nor are ladders built for him in the heavens."*

[[From a fine ode of his, transmitted from of old; the verse is in Majaz al-Qur'an by Abu 'Ubayda, 1:190, Sharh Shawahid al-Mughni: 227, and al-Lisan (s-l-m) (h-j-w), and elsewhere. Before the verse, and these are verses of Hassan: "If time diminishes me, the youth is a target for time, from its returns, both whole and wounded. And if that is a decree by which I was afflicted, the course of time is both crookedness and straightening. How pleasant is life, if only the youth were a stone that misfortunes glance off while it stays unbroken. Neither supporters nor a protecting hill prevent a man, which refuses humiliation when the noble lineages are counted. Neither protects a man..." And "ahjā' al-bilād": its regions and extremities. It is also narrated as "a'nā' al-bilād", which has the same meaning.]]

— ﴿then bring them a sign﴾: that is, a sign and proof of the truth of what you say, other than what I have brought you — ﴿then do it﴾. [[His words "then do it" mean: "if you are able to seek a tunnel... then do it."]]

* *

Some interpreters have said similarly to what we have said on this matter.

Those who said so:

13201 – Al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: 'Abd Allah ibn Salih narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiya ibn Salih narrated to me, from 'Ali ibn Abi Talha, from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words: "And if their turning away has been hard for you, then if you are able to seek a tunnel in the earth or a ladder in the sky," and "al-nafaq" is the burrow, so you go into it — ﴿then bring them a sign﴾, or He makes for you a ladder in the sky, [[In the manuscript: "makes for them a ladder," and the correct reading is that of the printed edition.]] so you climb upon it and bring them a sign better than what We brought them. So do it.

13202 – Al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatada regarding His words: "then if you are able to seek a tunnel in the earth," he said: a burrow — "or a ladder in the sky," he said: meaning the staircase.

13203 – Muhammad ibn al-Husayn narrated to me, saying: Ahmad ibn al-Mufaddal narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: "And if their turning away has been hard for you, then if you are able to seek a tunnel in the earth or a ladder in the sky." As for "al-nafaq," it is the burrow, and as for "al-sullam," it is the means of ascent.

13204 – Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from 'Ata' al-Khurasani, from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words: "a tunnel in the earth," he said: a burrow.

* *

The answer to the conditional is omitted and not mentioned, due to the sense of the speech indicating it and the hearers' knowledge of its meaning. The Arabs do this in matters whose meaning is understood by those addressed. A man of them says to another: "If you are able to rise with us in our need, if you are able to help us," and omits the answer, meaning: if you are able to help us, then do it. But when the addressee and hearer can only know the meaning of the speech by stating the answer, they do not omit it. One does not say, "If you rise," and stay silent omitting the answer, because the one addressed does not know its answer unless it is stated, so one says: "If you rise, you will gain good," or "If you rise, it is good," and the like. [[See al-Farra's Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1:331, 332.]] A parallel to what is in the verse, where the answer is omitted but intended, because the addressee understands the meaning, is the words of the poet: [[He is 'Ubayd ibn al-Abras.]]

*"So be content with a share of what we live, and let the vain trifles in dire matters not carry you away."*

[[The verse has passed with its takhrij previously, 3:284. In the manuscript the verse was as I have recorded it, though undotted. As for the printed edition, it read thus: "Then let him be eased of what he lives, and let not the trifles carry you off in terrors," which misread and distorted the manuscript.]]

And the meaning: "so with a share of what we live, my living." [[In the printed edition: "and the meaning: then he is eased of what he lives, and he lives," which is an error; its correct form is in the manuscript.]]

* *

On the interpretation of His words: ﴿And if Allah had willed, He would have gathered them upon guidance, so do not be among the ignorant﴾ (6:35)

Abu Ja'far said: May His remembrance be exalted, He says: Those of these disbelievers who deny you, O Muhammad, so that their denial grieves you — if I had willed to gather them upon uprightness of religion and correctness of the path of Islam, until your word and theirs were one, and your religion and theirs one, I would have gathered them upon that, and it would not have been far for Me, since I am able to do that by My kindness. But I did not do that because of My prior knowledge concerning My creatures and My executed decree concerning them, before I created them and shaped their bodies — ﴿so do not be, O Muhammad, among the ignorant﴾: that is, do not be among those who do not know that if Allah willed, He would gather all His creatures upon guidance by His kindness, and that whoever among His creatures disbelieves in Him disbelieves only because of Allah's prior knowledge concerning him and His executed decree that he will be among the disbelievers by choice, not compulsion. For when you know the truth of this, the turning away of those polytheists from the truth to which you call them, and the denial of those among them who denied you, will not be grievous to you.

* *

Some interpreters have said similarly to what we have said on this matter.

Those who said so:

13205 – Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: 'Abd Allah ibn Salih narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiya ibn Salih narrated to me, from ' Ali ibn Abi Talha, from Ibn 'Abbas: Allah, glorified is He, says: "If I willed, I would have gathered them upon guidance, all of them."

* *

Abu Ja'far said: In this report from Allah, may His remembrance be exalted, is clear evidence of the error of what the Tafwid-folk of the Qadariyya said, [[The "Ahl al-tafwid" are those who say that the affair has been delegated to the human being, so that his will alone suffices for the bringing about of his act, whether obedience or disobedience, and that he is the creator of his acts and that choice is in his hand. See what has passed, 1:162, note 1. As for "al-Qadariyya" and "Ahl al-qadar," they are those who deny divine decree. And those who affirm decree, who are the people of truth, are called "Ahl al-ithbat." See what has passed, 1:162, note 1.]] who deny that Allah has subtle graces for whomever He wills to grant success among His creatures, by which He kindly guides him until he is guided to the truth, submits to it, turns to right guidance, believes in it, and prefers it over error and disbelief in Allah. For He, may His remembrance be exalted, informed that if He willed to guide all who disbelieve in Him, until they gathered upon guidance, He would have done so. There is no doubt that had He done that with them, they would have been guided, not misguided. And if they had been guided, there is no doubt that their being guided would have been good for them. In His, may His remembrance be exalted, leaving them unassembled upon guidance is His leaving undone for them some of what would be good for them in their religion, though He is able to do it for them, and He has left doing it for them. And in His leaving that done for them is the clearest proof that He did not give them all the means by which they could reach guidance and through which they could be led to faith.

Discourse on the interpretation of His words: "Only those who listen will respond, and the dead—Allah will raise them, then to Him they will be returned" (6:36)

Abu Ja'far said: The Exalted says to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ): Let not the aversion of these who turn away from you grieve you, nor their refusal to respond to your call when you invite them to the Oneness of their Lord and to acknowledging your prophethood. For none responds to your call to what you summon them to in this matter [[See the explanation of "al-istijabah" (response) above, 3:483-484, and 7:486-488.]] except those whom Allah has opened their hearing to attend to the truth and has made easy for them to follow right guidance, unlike those upon whose hearing Allah has set a seal. So, from your calling them to Allah and to following the truth, they comprehend nothing except what cattle comprehend of the voices of their herders. They are, as the Exalted described them: "Deaf, dumb, blind; so they do not understand" (2:171). ="And the dead—Allah will raise them": that is, the disbelievers, Allah will raise them along with the dead. He, the Exalted, has placed them among the dead who hear no sound, comprehend no call, and understand no speech, since they do not reflect upon the proofs of Allah, do not take heed of His signs, and do not remember so as to desist from what they are upon of denying the messengers of Allah and opposing them. [[In the printed edition: "wa la yatadhakkarun fayanzajiru" and in the manuscript: "wa la yatadhakkaru fayanzajiru"; the correct reading is what I have adopted.]]

* *

What the commentators have said agrees with what we have said on this matter.

Those who said this:

13206 - Muhammad ibn Amr told me, he said: Abu Asim told us, he said: Isa told us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: "Only those who listen will respond" — the believers, to the Reminder — "and the dead" — the disbelievers — when Allah raises them along with the dead.

13207 - al-Muthanna told me, he said: Abu Hudhayfah told us, he said: Shibl told us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, the like of it.

13208 - Bishr ibn Mu'adh told me, he said: Yazid told us, he said: Sa'id told us, from Qatadah regarding His words: "Only those who listen will respond," he said: This is the parable of the believer, who heard the Book of Allah, benefited from it, acted upon it, and understood it. "And those who denied Our signs are deaf and dumb": this is the parable of the disbeliever, deaf and dumb, who sees no guidance and derives no benefit from it.

13209 - Ibn Wakf' told us, he said: Abu Usamah told us, from Sufyan al-Thawri, from Muhammad ibn Juhadah, from al-Hasan: "Only those who listen will respond," the believers, "and the dead," he said: the disbelievers.

13210 - Ibn Bashshar told me, he said: Abd al-Rahman told us, he said: Sufyan told us, from Muhammad ibn Juhadah, who said: I heard al-Hasan say regarding His words: "Only those who listen will respond, and the dead—Allah will raise them," he said: the disbelievers.

* *

As for His words: "then to Him they will be returned," the Exalted means: then to Allah will return the believers who responded to Allah and the Messenger, [[In the printed and manuscript editions: "then to Allah they will be returned, the believers," which is not right here; the correct reading is what I have adopted.]] and the disbelievers whom Allah has placed between them and understanding anything from you. He will reward this believer for the righteous deeds he performed in the world with the reward that Allah promised to the people of faith, and He will punish this disbeliever with the punishment that Allah threatened the people of disbelief with, not wronging any of them the weight of an atom.

The interpretation of His words: ﴿And they say, "Why has no sign been sent down to him from his Lord?" Say, "Indeed, Allah is able to send down a sign, but most of them do not know."﴾ (6:37)

Abu Ja'far said: The Exalted says: And those who ascribe equals to their Lord, who turn away from His signs, said: "Why has no sign been sent down to him from his Lord?" That is, they said: Why has a sign not been sent down upon Muhammad from his Lord? [See the explanation of "lawla" (why not / if only) earlier: 2:552, 553; 10:448; 11:262.] As the poet said: [This is Jarir.]

"You consider the slaughter of the barren she-camel your greatest glory, O sons of Dawtara, were it not for the armored horseman, veiled [in his armor]."

Meaning: "Why not the armored horseman?" [The verse was passed over earlier, along with its takhrij, its explanation, and the correct attribution, at 2:552, 553.]

* *

And "ayah" (āyah) means a sign, a clear indicator.
[See the explanation of "ayah" in the earlier linguistic indexes, under the root (ʾ-y).]

* *

This is because they said: "What is this Messenger that he eats food and walks in the markets? Why has an angel not been sent down to him to be a warner with him, or a treasure cast upon him, or a garden for him from which he may eat?" [Surat al-Furqan: 7–8.] Allah the Exalted said to His Prophet Muhammad ﷺ: Say, O Muhammad, to those who utter this statement to you: "Indeed, Allah is able to send down a sign," meaning: a proof for what they desire and ask for. "But most of them do not know," meaning: but most of those who say this and ask you for a sign do not know what would be upon them in the sign, if He sent it down, of affliction, and they do not know the reason for withholding its sending down to you. Had they known the cause for which I did not send it down to you, they would not have said that, nor asked you for it. But most of them do not know that.

The Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 6, verse 38:

The interpretation of His saying: ﴿There is no creature on the earth, nor a bird that flies with its two wings, but they are communities like you. We have not neglected anything in the Book. Then to their Lord they will be gathered.﴾ (6:38)

Abu Ja'far said: May He be exalted, says to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ): Say to these people who turn away from you and deny the signs of God: "O people, do not think that God is unaware of what you do, or that He will not requite you for what you earn!" How could He be unaware of your deeds, or leave off requiting you for them, when He is not unaware of the deed of any creature that crawls on the earth, small or great, [[See the explanation of "dabbah" (creature) above, 3:275.]] nor of the deed of any bird that flies with its wings in the air? Rather, He has made all of that into kinds classified and types sorted, [[See the explanation of "ummah" (community) above, 10:465, note 1, and the references there.]] that know as you know, and act within what they have been subjected to as you act, and whose deeds, good and bad, are preserved for them and against them, and all of their deeds are recorded in the Mother of the Book. Then He, may He be exalted, causes them to die, then raises them, and requites them on the Day of Resurrection for their deeds. He says: The Lord who did not waste the preservation of the deeds of the beasts and creatures on the earth, and the birds in the air, so that He preserved their movements and actions for them and recorded these in the Mother of the Book, and gathered them and then requited them for what they had done in the abode of trial, is more worthy not to waste your deeds, and not to neglect the preservation of your actions which you commit, O people, until He gathers you and requites you for all of them, good for good, and evil for evil. For He has singled you out with His favours, and extended over you His bounty in a way He has not extended it to others in this world, and you are more deserving of His thanks and more obliged to know what is due to Him, because of the intellect He gave you, by which you distinguish between things, and the understanding He did not give to the beasts and birds, by which you differentiate between your benefits and your harms.

* *

Those who interpret the Qur'an have said the like of what we have said in this matter.

Those who said that:

13211 - Muhammad ibn Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, saying: 'Isa narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His saying "communities like you": they are classified kinds known by their names.

13212 - al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, the like of it.

13213 - al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah regarding His saying "There is no creature on the earth, nor a bird that flies with its two wings, but they are communities like you": he said: the birds are a community, the humans are a community, and the jinn are a community.

13214 - Muhammad ibn al-Husayn narrated to me, saying: Ahmad ibn al-Mufaddal narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi regarding His saying "but they are communities like you": he said: but they are creations like you.

13215 - al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj regarding His saying "There is no creature on the earth, nor a bird that flies with its two wings, but they are communities like you": he said: the ant and what is above it, of the varieties of the creatures God created.

* *

As for His saying "We have not neglected anything in the Book," its meaning is: We have not failed to record any part of it, as in what was narrated:

13216 - al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: 'Abd Allah ibn Salih narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiyah ibn Salih narrated to me, from Ali ibn Abi Talhah, from Ibn 'Abbas regarding "We have not neglected anything in the Book": We have left nothing except that We have recorded it in the Mother of the Book.

13217 - Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said regarding His saying "We have not neglected anything in the Book," he said: We have not omitted the Book; there is nothing except that it is in the Book.

13218 - Yunus narrated it to me again, saying regarding His saying "We have not neglected anything in the Book": they are all written in the Mother of the Book.

* *

As for His saying "Then to their Lord they will be gathered," the interpreters differed regarding the meaning of "their being gathered" that God, may He be exalted, intended in this place. [[See the explanation of "hashr" (gathering) above, p. 297, note 1, and the references there.]]

Some of them said: "their gathering" is their death.

Those who said that:

13219 - Muhammad ibn 'Ammarah al-Asadi narrated to me, saying: 'Ubayd Allah ibn Musa narrated to us, from Isra'il, from Sa'id, from Masruq, from Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas regarding "There is no creature on the earth, nor a bird that flies with its two wings, but they are communities like you": Ibn 'Abbas said: the death of the beasts is their gathering. [[The report 13219: "'Ubayd Allah ibn Musa ibn Abi al-Mukhtar al-'Absi," mentioned shortly before as no. 13177. In both the printed edition and the manuscript it was here "'Abd Allah ibn Musa," which is an error; I have pointed it out previously.]]

13220 - Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, saying: my father narrated to me, saying: my paternal uncle narrated to me, saying: my father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas regarding "Then to their Lord they will be gathered": he said: by gathering is meant death.

13221 - It was narrated to us from al-Husayn ibn al-Faraj, saying: I heard Abu Mu'adh al-Fadl ibn Khalid say: 'Ubayd ibn Sulayman narrated to us, saying: I heard al-Dahhak say regarding His saying "Then to their Lord they will be gathered": by gathering is meant death.

* *

Others said: "the gathering" in this place is meant as the assembling for the raising of the Hour and the rising of the Resurrection.

Those who said that:

13222 - Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-A'la narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Thawr narrated to us, from Ma'mar; and al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us; from Ja'far ibn Burqan, from Yazid ibn al-Asamm, from Abu Hurayrah regarding "communities like you: We have not neglected anything in the Book. Then to their Lord they will be gathered": he said: God will gather all creation on the Day of Resurrection, the beasts, the creatures, the birds and everything. Of God's justice on that day is that He will take retribution for the hornless sheep from the horned one. Then He will say: "Be dust!" For this reason the disbeliever will say: "Would that I were dust!" [Surah al-Naba' 78:40]. [[The report 13222: "Ja'far ibn Burqan al-Kilabi," reliable, passed as no. 4577, 7836. "Yazid ibn al-Asamm ibn 'Ubayd al-Bakka'i," a reliable Successor, passed as no. 7836. This report was transmitted by al-Hakim in al-Mustadrak 2:316, through 'Abd al-Razzaq, from Ma'mar, from Ja'far al-Jizri, from Yazid ibn al-Asamm, and he said: "This Ja'far al-Jizri is Ibn Burqan; Muslim relied on him, and it is authentic according to his conditions, though they did not record it," and al-Dhahabi agreed with him.
Ibn Kathir recorded it in his tafsir 3:308-309, then said: "This has been related as a marfu' (traced to the Prophet) report in the hadith of the Trumpet." It was also recorded by al-Suyuti in al-Durr al-Manthur 3:11, and he added its attribution to Abu 'Ubayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim. "Al-jamma'" means a sheep without horns; "al-qarna'" means a sheep with large horns.]]

13223 - Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-A'la narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Thawr narrated to us, from Ma'mar; and al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us; from al-A'mash, from one whom he named, [[In the printed edition and manuscript: "from al-A'mash, dhakarahu," which is a scribal error; the correct reading is from Ibn Kathir's tafsir. The phrase "from one whom he named" appears to mean "Mundhir al-Thawri" or "al-Hudhayl ibn Shurahbil," as becomes clear from the takhrij.]] from Abu Dharr, who said: While I was with the Messenger of God (ﷺ), two she-goats butted each other. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Do you know why they butted?" They said: "We do not know!" He said: "But God knows, and He will judge between them."

13224 - al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq ibn Sulayman al-Razi narrated to us, saying: Fitr ibn Khalifah narrated to us, from Mundhir al-Thawri, from Abu Dharr, who said: Two sheep butted each other in the presence of the Prophet (ﷺ), and he said to me: "O Abu Dharr, do you know why they butted?" I said: "No!" He said: "But God knows, and He will judge between them!" Abu Dharr said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) left us, and no bird flapped its wings in the sky without his reminding us of knowledge of it.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The correct view in this matter, in my opinion, is to say: God, may He be exalted, has informed that every creature and bird will be gathered to Him. It is possible that by this is meant the gathering of the Resurrection; it is possible that by it is meant the gathering of death; and it is possible that both gatherings are meant. There is no indication in the apparent sense of the revelation, nor in a report from the Prophet (ﷺ), as to which of these is meant by His saying "Then to their Lord they will be gathered," since "hashr" (gathering) in the speech of the Arabs means assembling. [[See the explanation of "hashr" above, p. 346, note 2, and the references there.]] Among its examples is the saying of God, may He be exalted: ﴿And the birds gathered, each one returning to Him in repentance﴾ [Surah Sad 38:19], meaning: assembled. Since "hashr" is assembling, and God, may He be exalted, assembles His creation to Him on the Day of Resurrection, and assembles them by death, the more correct view is to generalise the meaning of the verse to what God has generalised in its apparent sense, and to say: every creature and every bird will be gathered to God after annihilation and after the raising of the Resurrection, since God, may He be exalted, has generalised by His saying "Then to their Lord they will be gathered," and has not restricted it to one gathering over another.

* *

If someone says: What is the purpose of His saying "nor a bird that flies with its two wings"? Does a bird fly except with its wings? What benefit is there in the report of its flying with the two wings?

It is said: We have already mentioned above that God, may He be exalted, sent down this Book in the tongue of a people, and in their dialects and what they know and use in their speech among themselves, He addressed them. Since it is part of their speech, when they wish to emphasise in speech, to say: "I spoke to so-and-so with my mouth," "I walked to him with my foot," "I struck him with my hand," He, may He be exalted, addressed them with the like of what they know in their speech and use in their address. Among this is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, this is my brother; he has ninety-nine ewes, and I have one ewe﴾ [Surah Sad 38:23]. [[In the printed edition the verse is cited as it is recited in our Mushaf, thus: "Indeed, this is my brother; he has ninety-nine ewes, and I have one ewe." This is not the place of Abu Ja'far's citation. The correct reading in the manuscript is as I have recorded it. It is the reading of 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, which Abu Ja'far mentioned in his tafsir after this (23:91, Bulaq), and then said: "That is by way of the Arabs' emphasis on the word, as in their saying: 'This is a male man.' They only do this with the feminine and the masculine whose masculinity and femininity are in themselves, like the woman, the man and the she-camel. They would not say: 'This is a feminine house,' or 'a feminine cloak,' because its femininity is in its name, not in its meaning."]]

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 6, verse 39:

The explanation of His saying: ﴿Those who deny Our signs are deaf and dumb, in darknesses. Whomever Allah wills, He leaves astray; and whomever He wills, He places on a straight path.﴾

Abu Ja'far said: Exalted is He, He says: Those who deny the proofs of Allah, His signs and His evidences [[See the explanation of "ayah" in the earlier lexical indexes (ayy).]] are "deaf," from hearing the truth, "dumb," from speaking it, "in the darknesses," meaning: in the darkness of disbelief, bewildered therein. [[He made the pronoun singular after the plural, saying "bewildered therein," meaning the disbeliever who denies the signs of Allah, and this is permissible in such a place of tafsir.]] He says: He is floundering in the darknesses of disbelief, not seeing the signs of Allah so that he may take heed from them and know that the One who created him and brought him into being, arranged him, perfected his arrangement, measured him in the best measure, gave him strength, and made sound for him the instruments of his body, did not create him in vain, nor leave him neglected, nor give him what He gave him of faculties except to use them in His obedience and in what pleases Him, rather than in His disobedience and what angers Him. So he, in his bewilderment in the darknesses of disbelief and his wavering in its depths, is heedless of what Allah has already written for him in the Mother of the Book, and of what He will do with him on the day he is gathered before Him along with the rest of the nations. Then Exalted is He, He informed that He is the One who leads astray whomever of His creation He wills to lead astray from faith to disbelief, and the One who guides to the straight path whomever of them He loves to guide, granting him success by His grace and bounty to believe in Him and to abandon disbelief in Him, His messengers, and what His prophets brought. And that none of His creation is guided except one for whom happiness was already decreed in the Mother of the Book, and none of them is led astray except one for whom wretchedness was decreed therein; and that all good is in His hand, all bounty is to Him, and to Him belong the creation and the command. [[See the explanation of "dalal" (misguidance) in the earlier lexical indexes (dalla). And the explanation of "al-sirat al-mustaqim" (the straight path) earlier, vol. 10: 429, note 4, and the references there.]]

* *

Qatadah said similarly to what we have said regarding this:

13225 - Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah: "Deaf and dumb," this is the likeness of the disbeliever, deaf and dumb, who does not see guidance and does not benefit from it. He is deaf to the truth in the darknesses, unable to find a way out of them, wandering blindly within them.

The commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 6, verse 40:

The explanation of His words: ﴿Say: Tell me, if the punishment of God comes upon you, or the Hour comes upon you, would you call upon other than God, if you are truthful?﴾

Abu Ja'far said: The grammarians (ahl al-'arabiyya, the scholars of Arabic grammar) differed concerning the meaning of His words "arayitakum" (أرأيتكم, "tell me" / "have you considered").

Some of the grammarians of Basra said: The "ka" (الكاف) that follows the "ta" (التاء) in "arayitakum" came only to address the audience, while the "ta" was left open, as it is for the singular. He said: It is like the "ka" in "ruwaydaka Zaydan" (رويدك زيدًا), when you say: "arud Zaydan." This "ka" has no grammatical position marked by a letter, neither nominative nor accusative; it is, in address, like the "ka" of "dhaka" (that). A similar usage of the Arabs is their saying "absarak Zaydan" [in the printed edition: "ansarak Zaydan" with an n, but the correct form is with a b, as will come], where they add the "ka" for address.

* *

Others among them said: The meaning of "arayitakum in atakum" is "arayitum." He said: This "ka" is added for address together with emphasis, and the "ta" alone is the noun, just as the "ka" that distinguishes the singular, dual and plural in address is added, as in their saying "hadha, wa dhaka, wa tilka, wa ulaika," so the "ka" is added for address and is not a noun, while the "ta" is the noun for the singular and the plural, left in one unchanged state. A similar usage is their saying "laysaka thamma illa Zayd" (meaning: "laysa"), and "la siyyaka Zayd" (meaning: "wa la sima Zayd"), and "balaka" (meaning "bala" in the sense of "na'am"), and "li-bi'saka rajulan wa lini'maka rajulan." They also said "unzurak Zaydan ma asna'u bihi" (meaning: "absirhu," look at him), and "absarak ma asna'u bihi" (in the sense of "absirhu"). Some have reported "absarukum ma asna'u bihi," meaning "absiru" (look), and "unzurukum Zaydan," that is "unzuru." It is reported from some of the Banu Kilab: "Atalamaka kana ahadun ash'ara min dhi al-Rumma?" and so they added the "ka."

Some grammarians of Kufa said: "Arayitaka 'Amran" — most of the speech in it omits the hamza. He said: The "ka" in "arayitaka" is in the accusative position, as if the original were: "Have you seen yourself in other than this state?" He said: This form is used for the dual, plural and feminine, so it is said "arayitumaka" and "arayitumuka." And "wa arayitunnakunna" [in the printed edition it is written "arayitan kunna," and I have kept what is in the manuscript, which matches what is in al-Farra's Ma'ani al-Qur'an], made its verb fall upon itself and asked about it. Then speech about it became common, until they left the "ta" in one form for the masculine, feminine, dual and plural, and said: "arayitakum Zaydan ma sana'a" and "arayitakunna ma sana'a," so they made the "ta" singular and the "ka" dual and plural, placing them in the position of the "ta." [See al-Farra, Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1:333, 334.] As He said: ﴿Here, read my book﴾ [Surah al-Haqqah: 19], and "ha' ya rajul" and "ha'uma," then they said "hakum," relying on the "ka" and the "mim" from what used to be dualized and pluralized. So the "ka" is in the nominative position, since it has become a substitute for the "ta." It may also be used in one form for dual, plural, masculine and feminine, like the speaker's saying "alayka Zaydan," where the "ka" is in the genitive position but the meaning is nominative. As for what is asked about, it most often falls on nouns, and then the interrogative is brought, so it is said: "arayitaka Zaydan hal qam," because it has come to mean "inform me about Zayd," then it clarifies what is being asked about. This is the most common usage, and the interrogative does not come directly after it. One does not say "arayitaka hal qumta," because they intended to first specify whom one asks about, and then specify the condition about which one asks. Sometimes the conditional is brought without a noun, so they say: "arayta in ataytu Zaydan hal ya'tina" — and "arayitaka" also — and "arayitu Zaydan in ataytuhu hal ya'tina," when it means "inform me," so it is said in all three forms.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The meaning of the speech is: Say, O Muhammad, to these who ascribe equals to God, the idols and the images: Tell me, if the punishment of God comes upon you, O people, as it came upon the nations before you, some of whom perished by the quake and some by the thunderbolt, or the Hour comes upon you, in which you will be raised from your graves and sent forth to the place of standing on the Day of Resurrection, would you call upon other than God there, to remove the calamity that has come down upon you, or would you cry out to one of your other gods to rescue you from the great calamity that has befallen you? "If you are truthful," that is: if you are right in your claim and your assertion that the gods you call upon besides God benefit or harm.

Discourse on the interpretation of His words: ﴿Nay, it is Him you call upon, and He removes that for which you call upon Him, if He wills, and you forget what you associate with Him﴾ (41).

Abu Ja'far said: Exalted is His remembrance, rebuking those who ascribe equals to Him, the idols: "You, O polytheists who associate with God gods and rivals, if the punishment of God comes upon you, or the Hour comes upon you, you will not seek refuge in anything other than God in the state of severe terror that descends upon you from gods, idols and images. Rather, there you will call upon your Lord, who created you, and to Him you will cry for help, and to Him you will turn in fear, to the exclusion of everything else besides Him." ﴿Then He removes that for which you call upon Him﴾: meaning, He relieves you, when you call upon Him for help and humble yourselves before Him, of the great affliction that has descended upon you, if He wills to relieve you of it, because He is capable of all things and is the Owner of all things, not what you call gods of idols and images. ﴿And you forget what you associate﴾: meaning, you forget, when the punishment of God comes upon you or the Hour comes upon you with its terrors, what you associate with God in your worship of Him, making for Him rivals of idols and images, and other things you worship besides Him and call gods.

The Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on Surah 6, Verse 42:

The explanation of His words: ﴿Indeed, We sent [messengers] to nations before you, then We seized them with adversity and hardship, so that they might humble themselves.﴾

Abu Ja'far said: He, may He be exalted and remembered, says: = warning those who associate idols with Him = and cautioning them that, if they persist in their misguidance, they may be treated in the way He treated the nations before them who followed the same path, by hastening His punishment upon them in this world = and informing His Prophet of His practice regarding those nations that passed before them, who followed the same course in denying the messengers =: "We sent," O Muhammad, "to nations," meaning: to groups and generations [[See the explanation of "ummah" (nation) above, p. 344, footnote 2, and the references there.]] "before you, then We seized them with adversity," meaning: We commanded them and forbade them, but they denied Our messengers and opposed Our command and prohibition, so We tested them through trial, "with adversity" (al-ba'sa'), which is severe poverty and straitened livelihood, "and hardship" (al-darra'), which is sickness and illnesses afflicting the body. [[See the explanation of "al-darra'" above, vol. 3: pp. 349–352; vol. 4: p. 288; vol. 7: p. 214.]]

* *

We have already explained this, with its evidence and its grammatical analysis, in "Surat al-Baqarah," in a way that makes repeating it here unnecessary. [[See all the references in the two footnotes above.]]

* *

As for His words: "so that they might humble themselves" (la'allahum yatada‘arru'), He means: We did that to them so that they would humble themselves before Me, make their worship sincerely for Me, and direct their desire to Me alone, with submission from them to Me in obedience and humility from them toward Me in turning back (to Him).

* *

In the speech there is an omitted element, which is dispensed with by what the apparent meaning indicates when it is stated, namely the words: [[In the printed edition: "by what the apparent meaning indicates from its statement, from His words," which differs from the manuscript. I have adopted the manuscript's wording as it stands, although I fear that some words may have dropped out from the copyist.]] "Indeed, We sent to nations before you, then We seized them." The cause of His seizing them was their denial of the messengers and their opposition to His command, not the sending of the messengers to them. Since this is so, it is evident that the meaning of the speech is: "Indeed, We sent to nations before you" messengers, "and they denied them, so We seized them with adversity."

* *

"Al-tadarru'" (humbling oneself) is the form "tafa''ul" from "al-di-rā'ah," which means abasement and humble submission.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 6, verse 43:

The interpretation of His saying: ﴿Why, when Our punishment came upon them, did they not humble themselves? But their hearts became hardened, and Satan made attractive to them what they were doing.﴾ (6:43)

Abu Ja'far said: This too is from the kind of speech in which something is omitted, the omitted part being dispensed with by the evident meaning. That is, He, may His remembrance be exalted, informed about the nations that denied their messengers that He seized them with misfortune and adversity so that they would humble themselves before Him, [[In the printed edition the word "lahu" (to Him) is omitted; it is present in the manuscript as "bihi" (by Him), and this is the correct reading.]] then He said: "Why, when Our punishment came upon them, did they not humble themselves?" He did not mention what they did when He seized them with misfortune and adversity. The meaning of the speech is: "And We certainly sent messengers to nations before you, and We seized them with misfortune and adversity so that they might humble themselves, but they did not humble themselves; so why, when Our punishment came upon them, did they not humble themselves?"

The meaning of "fa-lawla" (why) in this place is "fa-hallā" (why not). [[See the explanation of "lawla" earlier, p. 343, note 1, and the references there.]] When the Arabs place a nominal (noun) after "lawla" in the nominative, they make what follows it a predicate, and they follow it with a verb, as in "Fa-lawla akhūka la-zurtuka" ("If not for your brother, I would have visited you") and "Lawla abūka la-darabtuka" ("If not for your father, I would have struck you"). But when they place a verb after it, or do not place a noun, they make it an interrogative, saying "Lawla ji'tanā fa-nukrimuka" ("Why do you not come to us so that we may honor you?") and "Lawla zurta akhāka fa-nazūruka" ("Why do you not visit your brother so that we may visit you?"), meaning "hallā" (why not). As His saying, may His remembrance be exalted, shows: "Lawlā akhkhartanī ilā ajalin qarībin fa-aṣṣaddaqa" ("Why did You not delay me to a near term so that I might give charity") [Surah al-Munafiqun: 10]. The same applies to "lawmā" as to "lawlā". [[See al-Farra's Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1: 334, 335.]]

* *

So the interpretation of the speech is: "Why, when Our punishment came upon these nations that denied their messengers, did they not humble themselves when We seized them with misfortune and adversity, so that they humbled themselves, submitted to their Lord, and obeyed Him, whereupon their Lord would turn away from them His might, which is His punishment?"

* *

We have explained the meaning of "al-ba's" (might/severity) in another place, in a way that makes repeating it here unnecessary. [[See the explanation of "al-ba's" earlier, 3: 354, 355; 8: 580.]]

* *

"But their hearts became hardened": that is, He says: but they persisted in their denial of their messengers, insisted upon it, and were arrogant toward the command of their Lord, treating the punishment of God lightly and disdaining His torment, and their hearts were hardened. [[See the explanation of "qasā" earlier, 2: 233–237; 10: 126, 127.]] "And Satan made attractive to them what they were doing": that is, Satan made appealing to them the deeds they were doing, the deeds which God dislikes and abhors from them.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 6, verse 44:

The explanation of His saying: ﴿So when they forgot what they had been reminded of, We opened for them the gates of everything, until, when they rejoiced in what they had been given, We seized them suddenly, and then they were in despair﴾ (6:44).

Abu Ja'far said: By His saying, "So when they forgot what they had been reminded of," exalted is His remembrance, He means: when they abandoned acting upon what We had commanded them through the tongues of Our messengers [[See the explanation of "forgetting" (nisyan) earlier: 2:9, 473–480; 5:164; 6:132, 133–135; 10:129. And see the explanation of "reminding" (tadhkir) earlier: 10:130, footnote 2, and the references there.]] — like what was narrated:

13226 — Al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd Allah ibn Salih narrated to us, saying: Muʿawiya ibn Salih narrated to me, from ʿAli ibn Abi Talha, from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His saying, "So when they forgot what they had been reminded of," meaning: they abandoned what they had been reminded of.

13227 — Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: Al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj regarding His saying, "forgot what they had been reminded of," he said: what Allah and His messengers called them to, their fathers abandoned it and turned it back upon them.

* *

"We opened for them the gates of everything" — he says: We replaced hardship with ease and abundance of livelihood, and adversity with health and soundness of bodies, as a means of gradual enticement from Us toward them — like what was narrated:

13228 — Muhammad ibn ʿAmr narrated to me, saying: Abu ʿAsim narrated to us, saying: ʿIsa narrated to me — and Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfa narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us — from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid regarding the words of Allah, exalted is His remembrance, "We opened for them the gates of everything," he said: the ease and facility of this world, given to the earlier generations.

13229 — Al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Maʿmar informed us, from Qatada regarding His saying, "We opened for them the gates of everything," he said: it means ease and abundance of provision.

1323 0 — Muhammad ibn al-Husayn narrated to me, saying: Ahmad ibn Mufaddal narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi regarding His saying, "We opened for them the gates of everything," he says: from provision.

* *

If someone says to us: How is it said, "We opened for them the gates of everything," when you know that the gate of mercy and the gate of repentance were not opened for them, and many other gates besides them were not opened for them?

It is said: The meaning of that is other than the sense you have supposed. Rather the meaning is: We opened for them, as a means of gradual enticement from Us, the gates of everything We had closed to them when We seized them with hardship and adversity so that they would humble themselves; since they did not humble themselves and abandoned the command of Allah, exalted is His remembrance — because the end of this statement is referred back to its beginning. This is like what Allah, exalted is His remembrance, said in another place in His Book: "We did not send to any town a prophet except that We seized its people with hardship and adversity, so that they might humble themselves. Then We substituted for the evil the good, until they multiplied and said, 'Hardship and ease touched our fathers too,' so We seized them suddenly while they did not perceive" (7:94–95). So Allah's opening to the people mentioned in this verse [who forgot what] they had been reminded of, by His saying, "So when they forgot what they had been reminded of, We opened for them the gates of everything," is His substitution for them of the evil in which they were during the time of His testing them, from constriction of livelihood to ease and abundance, and from harm to bodies to health and well-being. This is "the opening of the gates of everything" that had been closed to them, which is what was mentioned before His saying "We opened for them the gates of everything," so His saying "We opened for them the gates of everything" is referred back to it.

* *

By His saying, "until, when they rejoiced in what they had been given," exalted is His remembrance, He means: until, when these deniers of their messengers rejoiced in Our opening for them the gates of abundance in livelihood and health in bodies — like what was narrated:

1323 1 — Muhammad ibn al-Husayn narrated to me, saying: Ahmad ibn al-Mufaddal narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: "until, when they rejoiced in what they had been given," from provision.

1323 2 — Al-Harith narrated to us, saying: Al-Qasim ibn Sallam narrated to us, saying: I heard ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Mahdi relating, from Hammad ibn Zayd, who said: A man used to say: May Allah have mercy on a man who recited this verse, then reflected on what was intended by it: "until, when they rejoiced in what they had been given, We seized them suddenly."

1323 3 — Al-Harith narrated to me, saying: Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi Raja, a man from the people of poetry, narrated to us, from ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Mubarak, from Muhammad ibn al-Nadr al-Harithi regarding His saying, "We seized them suddenly," he said: they were given respite for twenty years. [[Report 13233: "Ibn Abi Raja" — I do not know him. In the printed edition it read "from the people of the frontier" and omitted "man"; I have followed the manuscript. "Muhammad ibn al-Nadr al-Harithi," Abu ʿAbd al-Rahman al-ʿAbid, is biographied in al-Kabir 1/1/252, Ibn Abi Hatim 4/1/110, Hilyat al-Awliya 8:217, and Sifat al-Safwa 3:93. This report was transmitted by Abu Nuʿaym in al-Hilya 8:220 through Abu Bakr ibn Malik, from ʿAbd Allah ibn Ahmad ibn Hanbal, from Ahmad ibn Ibrahim, from Muhammad ibn Munabbih, the nephew of Ibn al-Mubarak, from ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Mubarak. I fear that "Ibn Abi Raja" is "Muhammad ibn Munabbih," the nephew of Ibn al-Mubarak. Perhaps his biography under "Muhammad ibn Munabbih" may be found, which would clarify what we do not know and correct what is in the manuscript — whether it is "a man from the people of poetry" or "from the people of the frontier," as in the printed edition.]]

* *

By His saying, "We seized them suddenly," exalted is His remembrance, He means: We came upon them with punishment unexpectedly, while they were deluded and did not perceive that it was about to happen or that it had come upon them — as: [[See the explanation of "suddenly" (baghta) earlier: p. 325.]]

1323 4 — Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: Al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj: "until, when they rejoiced in what they had been given, We seized them suddenly," he said: at the time it was most pleasing to them and most deceptive to them. [[In the printed edition: "wa-aʿazzahā lahum" (with ʿayn and zayn); the correct reading is "aghurrahā," from "ghurur" and "ghurra" (with ghayn and the unpointed rāʾ).]]

1323 5 — Muhammad ibn al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Ahmad ibn al-Mufaddal narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, "We seized them suddenly," he says: the punishment seized them suddenly.

1323 6 — Muhammad ibn ʿAmr narrated to me, saying: Abu ʿAsim narrated to us, saying: ʿIsa narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: "We seized them suddenly," he said: suddenly while they were secure.

* *

As for His saying, "then they were in despair," they are destroyed, their proofs cut off, regretting what had proceeded from them of denying their messengers — as: 

1323 7 — Muhammad ibn al-Husayn narrated to me, saying: Ahmad ibn al-Mufaddal narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: "then they were in despair," he said: then they were destroyed, their condition changed.

1323 8 — Al-Harith narrated to me, saying: ʿAbd al-ʿAziz narrated to us, saying: a shaykh narrated to us, from Mujahid: "then they were in despair," he said: dejection. [[In the printed edition: "then they were in despair, he said: then they were destroyed," which I do not know where he got. The manuscript reads as I have given, though undotted, so I preferred this reading. It will come that the meaning of "ibласs" is grief and remorse.]]

1323 9 — Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His saying, "then they were in despair," he said: the "mublis" is one upon whom an evil has descended that cannot be repelled. The "mublis" is more severe than the one who is humbled, and he recited: "Yet they did not humble themselves before their Lord, nor did they supplicate" (23:76). The first time there was reproach and a remnant of mercy [[In the printed edition: "reproach and taqiyya," which has no sense here; in the manuscript: "liqiya," the correct reading is what I have given. "Al-baqiyya" means sparing them.]]. He recited: "We seized them with hardship and adversity, so that they might humble themselves" — "Why, when Our might came upon them, did they not humble themselves?" — until "Satan made their deeds seem fair to them." Then a command came in which there was no remnant. He recited: "until, when they rejoiced in what they had been given, We seized them suddenly, and then they were in despair," so a command came in which there was no remnant. The first was such that if they had humbled themselves, the affliction would have been lifted from them.

1324 0 — Sa'id ibn ʿAmr al-Sakuni narrated to me, saying: Baqiyya ibn al-Walid narrated to us, from Abu Shurayh Dabara ibn Malik, from Abu al-Salt, from Harmala Abu ʿAbd al-Rahman, from ʿUqba ibn Muslim, from ʿUqba ibn ʿAmir, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: When you see Allah giving His servant in his worldly life, it is only a gradual enticement. Then he recited this verse: "So when they forgot what they had been reminded of," until His saying, "and praise belongs to Allah, Lord of the worlds." [[Reports 13240–13241: Sa'id ibn ʿAmr al-Sakuni appeared as no. 5563, 6521. Baqiyya ibn al-Walid al-Himsi appeared many times, the first being no. 152 and the last 9224; he is trustworthy, but critics faulted him for tadlis. Dabara ibn Malik is attributed to his grandfather, Dabara ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn Malik ibn Abi al-Sulayk al-Hadrami al-Alhani, Abu Shurayh al-Himsi, also called Dabara ibn Abi al-Sulayk; Ibn Hibban mentioned him in al-Thiqat and said his narrations are to be considered when transmitted by trustworthy narrators; Ibn ʿAdi mentioned him in al-Kamil and cited six disavowed narrations from him. Biographied in al-Tahdhib, al-Kabir 2/2/343, and Ibn Abi Hatim 2/1/471. Abu al-Salt is mentioned in Dabara's biography in al-Tahdhib and described as "al-Shami," but I have found no mention of him in the biographical works available to me. As for "Harmala, Abu ʿAbd al-Rahman," this is problematic, since Harmala ibn ʿImran ibn Qarad al-Tujibi al-Misri has the kunya Abu Hafs, and I have found no other kunya for him. I do not presume this to be a copyist's error; I fear that Abu ʿAbd al-Rahman may be another kunya of his. He is trustworthy and was among the people of intellect. Biographied in al-Tahdhib, al-Kabir 2/1/64, and Ibn Abi Hatim 1/2/273. ʿUqba ibn Muslim al-Tujibi al-Misri, imam of the ancient mosque, an Egyptian Successor, trustworthy; biographied in al-Tahdhib. ʿUqba ibn ʿAmir al-Juhani, early in migration, precedence and companionship; he was a learned jurist, eloquent, a poet, a writer, and one of those who collected the Qur'an. Abu Ja'far will narrate this report again below through Ibn Lahi'a, from ʿUqba ibn Muslim. Ahmad recorded it in his Musnad 4:145 through Yahya ibn Ghaylan, from Rishdin ibn Sa'd, from Harmala ibn ʿImran, from ʿUqba ibn Muslim, from ʿUqba ibn ʿAmir, similarly. Al-Haythami cited it in Majma' al-Zawa'id 7:20, attributing it to Ahmad and al-Tabarani, and mentioned nothing about its soundness or weakness in its chain. Ibn Kathir cited it in his tafsir 3:311 from Ahmad's narration, and pointed to the routes of Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim. Al-Suyuti cited it in al-Durr al-Manthur 3:12 and added attribution to Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn al-Mundhir, Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab.]]

1324 1 — And this report was narrated to me from Muhammad ibn Harb, from Ibn Lahi'a, from ʿUqba ibn Muslim, from ʿUqba ibn ʿAmir: that the Prophet ﷺ said: And when you see Allah, exalted is His remembrance, giving the servants what they ask for despite their disobedience to Him, it is only a gradual enticement from Him toward them! Then he recited, "So when they forgot what they had been reminded of, We opened for them the gates of everything," the verse.

* *

The root of "ibласs" in the speech of the Arabs, according to some: grief over a thing and remorse for it. According to others: the cutting off of proof and silence when proof is cut off. According to others: humility. They also said: it means one who is forsaken and abandoned, and from it is the verse of al-ʿAjjaj:

"O companion, do you recognize a worn-out traces?" ... "He said: Yes! I recognize it! And he was dismayed (wa-ablasa)."
