[[In the printed edition: "He means: you forgot, so you sit with them" — which has no meaning; in the manuscript: "Our prohibition, so you sit with them" — which is confused. I have deduced its correct form from the earlier interpretation of the verse. His words "Our prohibition" are the object of His words in the verse: "And if Satan causes you to forget," and this is the habit of the early people of ta'wil in abbreviation.]] Then, when you remember, rise.

13390. Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: "Engage in vain talk concerning Our signs," he said: they deny Our signs.

13391. Yahya ibn Talhah al-Yarbu'i narrated to me, saying: Fudayl ibn Iyad narrated to us, from Layth, from Abu Ja'far, who said: Do not sit with the people of disputes, for they are those who engage in vain talk concerning the signs of God.

13392. Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Salih narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiyah ibn Salih narrated to us, from Ali ibn Abi Talhah, from Ibn Abbas, concerning His words: "And when you see those who engage in vain talk concerning Our signs," and His words: ﴿Those who divided their religion and became sects﴾ [6:159]; and His words: ﴿And do not be like those who became divided and disputed after clear proofs had come to them﴾ [3:105]; and His words: ﴿Establish the religion and do not become divided therein﴾ [42:13], and similar things in the Qur'an, he said: God commanded the believers to unity, and forbade them disagreement and division, and informed them that those before them were destroyed only through disputation and quarrels concerning the religion of God.

13393. Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: Al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Juraij, from Mujahid, concerning His words: "And when you see those who engage in vain talk concerning Our signs," he said: they mock them. He said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) was forbidden to sit with them unless he forgot; if he remembered, he should rise. That is His words: "And when you see those who engage in vain talk concerning Our signs, turn away from them until they engage in another discourse. And if Satan causes you to forget, do not sit, after the remembrance, with the wrongdoing folk." = Ibn Juraij said: The polytheists would sit before the Prophet (ﷺ), wishing to hear from him; when they heard, they mocked, so it was revealed: "And when you see those who engage in vain talk concerning Our signs, turn away from them," the verse. [[The report 13393 will come later; Ibn Juraij's tafsir in full appears later as no. 13396.]]

13394. Ibn WakI' narrated to us, saying: My father narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from Mansur, from Mujahid: "And when you see those who engage in vain talk concerning Our signs," he said: they deny.

13395. Ibn WakI' narrated to us, saying: Abdullah narrated to us, from Isra'il, from al-Suddi, from Abu Malik, concerning His words: "And when you see those who engage in vain talk concerning Our signs, turn away from them until they engage in another discourse," meaning the polytheists. "And if Satan causes you to forget, do not sit, after the remembrance, with the wrongdoing folk," if you forget and then remember, do not sit with them.

**The discussion on the interpretation (ta'wil) of His words:** ﴿Nor is there anything upon those who fear God for their reckoning, but it is a reminder, that perhaps they may fear God.﴾ (6:69)

Abu Ja'far said: Exalted is His remembrance, says: Whoever fears God, dreading Him, obeying Him in what He has commanded him and avoiding what He has forbidden him, then there is no burden upon him, in what lies between him and God, for not turning away from these people who are immersed in the verses of God while they are immersed in them, if his not turning away from them is not an approval of what they are engaged in, and he is God-fearing with regard to His rights, [[This is also the wording in the manuscript, "بحقوقه متقيًا" (God-fearing with regard to His rights). I think the more likely reading is "بخوفه متقيًا" (God-fearing in His dread), but I have not changed it, because the other reading is nearly acceptable.]] and there is no sin upon him for that, but that they should turn away from them at that time as a reminder of God's command, ﴿that perhaps they may fear God﴾, meaning: that they may fear God.

* *

The meaning of "dhikra" (reminder) is "dhikr" (remembrance). "Dhikr" and "dhikra" have the same meaning.

* *

It is also possible that "dhikra" is in the accusative or the nominative position:

As for the accusative, it is according to the interpretation I have described: "But that they should turn away from them as a reminder."

As for the nominative, it is according to the interpretation: "Nor is there anything upon those who fear God for their reckoning by not turning away, but their turning away is a reminder of God's command, that perhaps they may fear God." [[See Ma'ani al-Qur'an by al-Farra' 1:339.]]

* *

It has been mentioned that the Prophet (ﷺ) was only commanded to rise and leave the polytheists when they immersed themselves in the verses of God, because his rising from them was something they disliked. So God said to him: When they immerse themselves in the verses of God, then rise from them, so that they may avoid immersing themselves in them and abandon that.

Those who said this:

13396: Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: Al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: The polytheists used to sit with the Prophet (ﷺ), wishing to hear from him. When they heard, they mocked, so this was revealed: ﴿And when you see those who immerse themselves in Our verses, turn away from them until they immerse themselves in another discourse﴾ (6:68). He said: So whenever they mocked, he would rise, and they became wary and said: Do not mock, or he will rise! That is His saying: ﴿that perhaps they may fear God﴾, that they might immerse themselves and he would rise. And it was revealed: ﴿Nor is there anything upon those who fear God for their reckoning﴾, if they sit with them, but you should not sit with them. Then that ruling was abrogated (naskh) by His saying at Medina: ﴿And He has already sent down to you in the Book that when you hear the verses of God being disbelieved in and mocked, do not sit with them until they immerse themselves in another discourse; indeed, you would then be like them﴾ (4:140). So it abrogated His saying: ﴿Nor is there anything upon those who fear God for their reckoning﴾, the verse.

13397: Muhammad ibn al-Husayn narrated to me, saying: Ahmad ibn al-Mufaddal narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, regarding His saying: ﴿Nor is there anything upon those who fear God for their reckoning﴾, meaning: nothing of the reckoning of the disbelievers. ﴿But it is a reminder﴾, meaning: if you remember, then rise. ﴿That perhaps they may fear God﴾, your displeasure; when they see you not sitting with them, they will be ashamed before you and refrain from you. Then God later abrogated it and forbade them to ever sit with them. He said: ﴿And He has already sent down to you in the Book that when you hear the verses of God being disbelieved in﴾, the verse.

13398: Muhammad ibn Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu Asim narrated to us, saying: Isa narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: ﴿Nor is there anything upon those who fear God for their reckoning﴾, if they sit, but you should not sit.

13399: Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfa narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, the same.

13400: Ibn Waki' narrated to us, saying: Ubayd Allah narrated to us, from Israil, from al-Suddi, from Abu Malik: ﴿Nor is there anything upon those who fear God for their reckoning, but it is a reminder﴾. He said: What is it upon you if they immerse themselves in the verses of God, when you have done that?

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 6, verse 70 (part 1 of 2):

The discussion of His saying: ﴿And leave those who have taken their religion as amusement and diversion, and whom the worldly life has deceived. And remind [them] by it, lest a soul be delivered to destruction for what it has earned. It will have, besides Allah, no protector and no intercessor﴾

Abu Ja'far said: Allah, may His remembrance be exalted, says to His Prophet Muhammad ﷺ: Leave these people who have taken the religion of Allah and their obedience to Him as amusement and diversion [[See the explanation of "dhar" (leave) earlier: 6:22 / 7:424.]], so they have made their portion of obedience to Him into playing with His verses [[See the explanation of "al-la'b" (play) earlier: 10:429, 432.]], and diversion and mockery of them whenever they hear them and they are recited to them. So turn away from them, for I am watching them closely (al-mirsad), and I am behind them with retribution against them and punishment for them for what they do, and for their being deceived by the adornment of the worldly life, and their forgetting the return to Allah, may His remembrance be exalted, and their arrival to Him after death, like what was narrated:

1340[1] - Muhammad ibn Amr related to me, saying: Abu Asim related to us, saying: Isa related to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding the words of Allah: ﴿Leave those who have taken their religion as amusement and diversion﴾, he said: It is like His saying: ﴿Leave Me with whom I created alone﴾ [Surah al-Muddaththir: 11].

1340[2] - al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah related to us, saying: Shibl related to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, the like of it.

* *

Allah, may His remembrance be exalted, has abrogated this verse with His saying: ﴿Then kill the polytheists wherever you find them﴾ [Surah al-Tawbah: 5]. Likewise a number of the people of interpretation have said.

Those who said that:

1340[3] - al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Hajjaj ibn al-Minhal related to us, saying: Hammam ibn Yahya related to us, from Qatadah: "Leave those who have taken their religion as amusement and diversion", then He revealed in "Surah Bara'ah" and commanded fighting them.

1340[4] - Ibn Waki' related to us, saying: Abdah ibn Sulayman related to us, saying: I read to Ibn Abi Arubah, and he said: Thus I heard it from Qatadah: "Leave those who have taken their religion as amusement and diversion", then Allah, may His remembrance be exalted, revealed "Bara'ah" and commanded fighting them, saying: ﴿Then kill the polytheists wherever you find them﴾ [Surah al-Tawbah: 5].

* *

As for His saying: "And remind [them] by it, lest a soul be delivered to destruction for what it has earned," its meaning is: And remind, O Muhammad, by this Qur'an those who turn away from you and from it [[See the explanation of "al-tadhkir" (reminding) earlier: 6:63, 64, 66; 10:211 / 11:130; 11:357]], "lest a soul be delivered to destruction," meaning: lest it not be delivered, as He said: ﴿Allah makes clear to you, lest you go astray﴾ [Surah al-Nisa: 176], meaning: lest you not go astray [[See what preceded: 9:445, 446.]]. The meaning of the speech is: Remind them by it so that they believe and follow what has come to them from Allah of the truth, so that their souls are not delivered to destruction for the sins they have earned. But "la" (not) was omitted, because the speech indicates it.

* *

The people of interpretation differed regarding the interpretation of His saying: "lest a soul be delivered to destruction."

Some of them said: its meaning is: to be handed over (to be surrendered).

Those who said that:

1340[5] - Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Yahya ibn Wadih related to us, saying: al-Husayn ibn Waqid related to us, from Yazid al-Nahwi, from Ikrimah regarding His saying: "lest a soul be delivered to destruction for what it has earned", he said: to be surrendered.

1340[6] - Muhammad ibn Abd al-A'la related to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Thawr related to us, from Ma'mar, from al-Hasan: "lest a soul be delivered to destruction," he said: to be surrendered.

1340[7] - al-Hasan ibn Yahya related to us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from al-Hasan, the like of it.

1340[8] - Muhammad ibn Amr related to me, saying: Abu Asim related to us, saying: Isa related to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid regarding the words of Allah, may His remembrance be exalted: "lest [it be] delivered", he said: to be surrendered.

1340[9] - al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah related to us, saying: Shibl related to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: "lest a soul be delivered to destruction," he said: to be surrendered.

1340[10] - Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Hakkam related to us, from Anbasah, from Layth, from Mujahid: "Those are they who have been delivered [to destruction]" — they surrendered.

* *

Others said: rather, its meaning is: to be imprisoned.

Those who said that:

1340[11] - Muhammad ibn Abd al-A'la related to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Thawr related to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatadah: "lest a soul be delivered to destruction," he said: it is seized and imprisoned.

1340[12] - al-Hasan ibn Yahya related to us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah, the like of it.

1340[13] - Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said regarding His saying: "lest a soul be delivered to destruction for what it has earned," that a soul be seized for what it has earned.

* *

Others said: its meaning is: to be disgraced.

Those who said that:

1340[14] - al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Abd Allah ibn Salih related to us, from Ali ibn Abi Talhah, from Ibn Abbas: "And remind [them] by it, lest a soul be delivered to destruction for what it has earned," he says: to be disgraced.

* *

Others said: its meaning is: to be recompensed.

Those who said that:

1340[15] - Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Yahya ibn Wadih related to us, saying: al-Husayn ibn Waqid related to us, saying: al-Kalbi said: "lest [it be] delivered," meaning: to be recompensed.

* *

The root of "al-ibsal" is prohibition. It is said from it: "absalt al-makan" when you forbid it so that none approaches it. From it is the saying of the poet [[He is Damrah ibn Damrah al-Nahthali.]]:

"She rose early blaming you after weakness in generosity; (may) my blame and my reproach be forbidden (basl) to you."

[[The Diwan of Abu Zayd (Nawadir): 2; al-Amali 2: 279; al-Shi'r wa'l-shu'ara': 250; al-Wahshiyyat no. 424; al-Azmina wa'l-amkina 1: 160; al-Lisan (b-s-l) and others. After this verse are verses of Hassan, which he said to his wife when she reproached him for slaughtering his camels for his guests and family and loving stinginess, and forbidding him to spend wealth in drought and famine: "Shall I withhold them while my paternal cousins are hungry? So let your shame and blame of me suffice you! And indeed I know — so do not suppose otherwise — that the path of my companions will surely draw me on. Do you see, if my head should cry out at night and I leave it naked of my garments? Will my camels scratch their faces for me, or will you bind their heads with black mourning-bands?" "Bakarat" means she hastened at the beginning of the pre-dawn. "After weakness" means after rising from the depth of the night. What kept her awake was what he gave to his paternal cousins from his wealth, and she did not wait to blame him until the morning, but began reproaching him at dawn. Then he began reminding her of manliness, saying: "Ash-simma-ha" — meaning the she-camels — tying the sirar (a cord tied over the udder) on them lest they be milked, or lest their young suckle them. He says: I will not do that, while my paternal cousins are hungry until I quench them; "sighb" is hunger, for that is baseness. "Ibah" is disgrace one is ashamed of, and "'ab" is defect. He says: this deed suffices you as baseness that disgraces its doer. Then he argued against her with the grief his paternal cousins and guests would feel for him if he died, and that camels do not do that. He said to her: death is the path of every living being, and I am taking the path of my companions who went and left me behind, and this path draws me (i.e., pulls and snatches me) as it drew them before. His saying "sarakhat bi-layl hamati" belongs to the pre-Islamic beliefs, which Allah nullified with Islam: they claimed that the spirit of the slain becomes a bird like an owl that cries at his grave, saying: give me drink, give me drink! His saying "aryan athwabi" means naked of my garments with which I enjoyed wearing in the world. It is also narrated as "baliyan athwabi," meaning then his shrouds that decay in the dust. "Hal takhmish ibili" means: will the camels slap their faces so that the slapping scratches and wounds them, as my paternal cousins and paternal aunts do when I die. "Al-sillab" are black head-bands worn in mourning. He says: this is the grief of my paternal cousins over me; will the camels do as they do, so that I grieve over their slaughter and destruction in feeding and watering them in a time of drought while they are hungry?]] i.e., forbidden: [your blame and reproach of me is forbidden]. From it comes the saying "asad basil" (a brave lion), meaning that nothing approaches it, as if it has forbidden itself; then this becomes an attribute of every fierce one who is avoided for his fierceness. It is said: "a'ti al-raqi bus'latahu" [[In the printed edition: "busaylatahu," an obvious error; the correct reading is in the manuscript. See Ma'ani al-Qur'an by al-Farra' 1: 339.]], meaning: his fee (ujrah). "Shara bail" means abandoned drink. Likewise "al-mubsal bi'l-jarirah," who is held as a pledge for it; he was called "mubsal" because he is forbidden from everything except that for which he is pledged and surrendered. From it is the saying of Awf ibn al-Ahwas al-Kilabi:

"And my delivering my sons without any crime — we committed no offense and shed no blood..." [[Diwan..., with the rest of the poem: "We met from your assault upon us and killing our nobles..."]]

And al-Shanfara said: [[Also attributed to Ta'abbata Sharran.]]

"There, I do not hope for a life that pleases me, companion of the nights, delivered (mubsalan) to crimes..."

Abu Ja'far said: The meaning of the speech, then, is: And remind by the Qur'an those who plunge into Our verses and others who have followed their path among the polytheists, lest a soul be delivered to destruction by its sins and its disbelief in its Lord, and be held in pledge, and be shut up by what it has earned of its crimes in the punishment of Allah ["the explanation of 'kasb' (earning) above..."]. "It will have, besides Allah," meaning: it will have, when it is surrendered with its sins and held in pledge for what it has earned of its wrongs, no one who helps it and rescues it from Allah, who repays it for its sins with their due recompense. "Nor any intercessor," who might intercede for it, having any means with Him.

* *

The discussion of His saying: ﴿And if it should offer every ransom, it would not be accepted from it﴾

Abu Ja'far said: Allah, may His remembrance be exalted, says: And if it should ransom the soul that was delivered to destruction for what it has earned, meaning: "and if it offers every equivalent," meaning: every ransom.

* *

It is said from it: "'adala yu'dilu" when he ransoms, "'adlan," and from it the saying of Allah, may His remembrance be exalted: ﴿or its equivalent in fasting﴾ [Surah al-Ma'idah: 95], which is what equals it of another kind.

* *

Those who said the like of what we have said in this were the people of interpretation.

Those who said that:

1341[16] - Muhammad ibn Abd al-A'la related to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Thawr related to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatadah: "And if it should offer every ransom, it would not be accepted from it," he said: even if it came with the earth filled with gold, it would not be accepted from it.

1341[17] - Muhammad ibn al-Husayn related to us, saying: Ahmad ibn al-Mufaddal related to us, saying: Asbat related to us, from al-Suddi regarding His saying: "And if it should offer every ransom, it would not be accepted from it," so nothing equals it: even if it came with the earth filled with gold to ransom itself with it, it would not be accepted from it.

1341[18] - Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said regarding His saying: "And if it should offer every ransom, it would not be accepted from it," he said: "And if it should offer," even if it ransoms itself, it would have the world and all that is in it to ransom itself with — "it would not be accepted from it," as an equivalent for itself; it would not be accepted from it.

* *

Some people of Arabic linguistic knowledge interpreted it as: "And if it should dispense every justice, it would not be accepted from it," and said: it refers to repentance in life. [[This is the view of Abu Ubaydah in Majaz al-Qur'an 1: 195.]]

But there is no meaning to what he said, because every penitent in this world — Allah, may His remembrance be exalted, accepts his repentance.

* *

The discussion of His saying: ﴿Those are they who have been delivered to destruction for what they earned. For them is a drink of boiling water and a painful punishment for what they used to disbelieve﴾ (70)

Abu Ja'far said: Allah, may His remembrance be exalted, says: And these are the ones who, even if they ransomed themselves from the punishment of Allah on the Day of Resurrection with every ransom, it would not be taken from them — they are "those who have been delivered to destruction for what they earned," meaning: they have been surrendered to the punishment of Allah, held in pledge for their earned sins and burdens in the world [[See the explanation of "absala" above shortly, and of "kasaba" p. 446 n.3 and the references there.]], "for them is a drink of boiling water."

* *

"Al-hamim" in the speech of the Arabs is the hot; it is originally "mahmum" transferred to the pattern "fa'il," and from it the bath (hammam) is so called for heating the body. From it is the saying of Murraqqash:

"In every evening there is for her a censer, in which is incense prepared, and boiling water [hamim]..." [[From his ode about the daughter of Ajlan... "al-miqtarah" is the brazier; "al-kiba'" a kind of aloes-wood.]]

It means by it hot water. From it is the saying of Abu Dhu'ayb al-Hudhali describing a horse:

"She refuses, with her flow, when she is provoked, except boiling water (hamim); for it trickles..." [[Diwan 17; al-Mufaddaliyyat 879; al-Lisan... Variants exist; "istudghibat" (provoked) is explained as "frightened," etc.]]

It means by "hamim": the sweat of the horse.

* *

Allah, may His remembrance be exalted, made the drink of those whose description He gave in this verse "a drink of boiling water," because hot water does not quench thirst. He informed that when they are thirsty in Hell, they will not be given water that quenches them, but what increases their thirst beyond what they already have. "And a painful punishment," meaning: and for them, in addition to the boiling drink, from Allah is the painful punishment and enduring humiliation. "For what they used to disbelieve," meaning: for their disbelief in Allah in the world, their denial of His oneness, and their worship of others besides Him.

* *

1341[19] - Muhammad ibn al-Husayn related to me, saying: Ahmad ibn al-Mufaddal related to us, saying: Asbat related to us, from al-Suddi: "Those are they who have been delivered to destruction for what they earned," he said: it is said: they surrendered.

[13420] Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abdullah ibn Salih narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiyah ibn Salih narrated to me, from Ali ibn Abi Talhah, from Ibn Abbas, regarding "Those are the ones who were given over to ruin (ubsilu)," he said: they were disgraced.

[13421] Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His words, ﴿Those are the ones who have been given over to destruction for what they earned﴾, he said: they were seized for what they had earned.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 6, verse 71:

The interpretation of His words: ﴿Say: Shall we call upon, besides Allah, that which can neither benefit us nor harm us, and be turned back on our heels after Allah has guided us, like one whom the devils have lured in the earth, bewildered, who has companions calling him to guidance, "Come to us"?﴾

Abu Ja'far said: This is an admonition from Allah, may His remembrance be exalted, to His Prophet ﷺ concerning His proof against the polytheists of his people, the worshippers of idols. Allah, may His remembrance be exalted, says to him: Say, O Muhammad, to these who equate others with their Lord, the idols and rivals, and who command you to follow their religion and worship the idols along with them: Shall we call upon, besides Allah, a stone or a piece of wood that has no power to benefit us or harm us, so that we single it out for worship instead of Allah, and abandon the worship of the One in whose hand is harm and benefit, life and death, if you are people who reason and distinguish between good and evil? There is no doubt that you know that serving that whose benefit is hoped for and whose harm is feared is more worthy and more fitting than serving that whose benefit is not hoped for and whose harm is not feared!

* *

"And be turned back on our heels" means: and be returned to our backs, going backward behind us, not having attained our need.

* *

We have already explained the meaning of "turning back on the heel," and that the Arabs say of everyone seeking a need who does not attain it: "He turned back on his heels," earlier, in a way that makes repeating it here unnecessary. [See the explanation of "turning back on the heels" above, 3:163, and Majaz al-Qur'an by Abu 'Ubaydah, 1:196.]

* *

What is meant here is: that we would turn back from Islam to unbelief "after Allah has guided us, granted us success in it," so our case would be like that of the man whom the devil has enticed, wandering bewildered in the earth.

* *

As for His words "istahwathu" (lured), it is "istaf'alahu," from the saying of the speaker: "Fulan hawa ila kadha yahwi ilayhi" (so-and-so inclined toward such-and-such), and from the words of Allah, may His remembrance be exalted: ﴿So make hearts of people incline toward them﴾ [Surah Ibrahim: 37], meaning: incline toward them and desire them.

* *

As for "hayran" (bewildered), it is "fa'lan," from the saying: "Fulan has wandered (haara) in the road; he wanders in it, bewilderment (hayra), hayaran, and hayrura," ["Hayrura" is a verbal noun like "sayrura," which the lexicographers did not mention; this is something to be gleaned from Abu Ja'far and added to the dictionaries.] and that is when he goes astray and is not guided to the right path.

"He has companions calling him to guidance": means: for this bewildered one whom the devils have lured in the earth, there are companions upon the right path and the straightness of the way, calling him to the right road of guidance that they are upon, saying to him: "Come to us."

* *

"Hayran" is not declined because it is "fa'lan," and every noun on the pattern "fa'lan" whose feminine is "fa'la" is not declined in Arabic speech, whether definite or indefinite.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: This is a parable which Allah, may His remembrance be exalted, gives for one who disbelieves in Allah after his faith and follows the devils, from among the people of polytheism toward Allah; and his companions were his companions in the state of his Islam, who remain upon the true religion, calling him to the guidance in which they abide and the right course to which they cling, and he has parted from it and departed from it. They say to him: "Come to us, so be with us in straightness and guidance!" But he refuses that and follows the promptings of the devil and worships gods and idols.

* *

Similar to what we have said on this was stated by a group of the people of interpretation, and a group differed on this.

Mention of those who said the same as what we have said:

13422 – Muhammad ibn al-Husayn related to me, saying: Ahmad ibn al-Mufaddal related to us, saying: Asbat related to us, from al-Suddi: "Say: Shall we call upon, besides Allah, that which neither benefits us nor harms us, and be turned back on our heels after Allah has guided us, like one whom the devils have lured in the earth, bewildered, who has companions calling him to guidance, 'Come to us'," he said: The polytheists said to the believers: Follow our way and leave the religion of Muhammad ﷺ. So Allah, may His remembrance be exalted, said: "Say: Shall we call upon, besides Allah, that which neither benefits us nor harms us?" These are the gods. "And be turned back on our heels after Allah has guided us," so our case would be like that of the one whom the devils have lured in the earth. He means: your likeness, if you disbelieve after faith, is like the likeness of a man who was with a people on the road, then lost the road, and the devils bewildered him and lured him in the earth, while his companions were on the road, and they began calling him to them, saying: "Come to us, for we are on the road," but he refused to come to them. That is the likeness of one who follows you after knowing Muhammad, and Muhammad is the one who calls to the road, and the road is Islam.

13423 – Al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Abu Salih related to us, saying: Mu'awiyah related to me, from Ali ibn Abi Talhah, from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His words: "Shall we call upon, besides Allah, that which neither benefits us nor harms us, and be turned back on our heels," he said: This is a parable which Allah struck for the idols and for those who call to them, and for the callers who call to Allah: it is like a man who has strayed from the road, lost and astray, when a caller calls out to him: "O so-and-so son of so-and-so, come to the road!" and his companions call him: "O so-and-so, come to the road!" If he follows the first caller, he sets off with him until he casts him into destruction, and if he answers the one calling him to guidance, he is guided to the road. This is the calling that is heard in the wilderness from the ghouls. He means: the likeness of one who worships these gods besides Allah, for he thinks he is in something until death comes to him, and he meets destruction and regret. And His words: "like one whom the devils have lured in the earth," are the ghouls, who call him by his name and his father's name and his grandfather's name, so he follows them, thinking he is in something, and in the morning they have cast him into destruction, and perhaps devoured him, or cast him into a desert wasteland where he perishes of thirst. This is the likeness of one who answers the idols that are worshipped besides Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

13424 – Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-A'la related to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Thawr related to us, saying: Ma'mar related to us, from Qatadah: "the devils have lured him in the earth," he said: they led him astray in the earth, bewildered.

13425 – Muhammad ibn 'Amr related to me, saying: Abu 'Asim related to us, saying: 'Isa related to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid concerning His words: "that which neither benefits us nor harms us," he said: the idols.

13426 – Muhammad ibn 'Amr related to me, saying: Abu 'Asim related to us, saying: 'Isa related to us; and al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah related to us, saying: Shibl related to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid concerning the words of Allah, may His remembrance be exalted: "the devils have lured him in the earth, bewildered," he said: a bewildered man whose companions call him to the road; that is the likeness of one who strays after being guided. [In the printed edition: "kadhalika mathal," and in the manuscript: "lidhalika mathal...," and the correct reading is what is recorded.]

13427 – Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-A'la related to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Thawr related to us, from Ma'mar, saying: a man related to us, from Mujahid, who said: "hayran": this is a parable which Allah struck for the disbeliever; he means: the disbeliever is bewildered, and a Muslim calls him to guidance, but he does not answer.

13428 – Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah concerning His words: "Say: Shall we call upon, besides Allah, that which neither benefits us nor harms us," until "that we may submit to the Lord of the worlds": Allah taught them to Muhammad and his companions, that they might dispute with them against the people of error.

* *

Others said concerning the interpretation of this, what follows:

13429 – Muhammad ibn Sa'd related it to me, saying: My father related to me, saying: My paternal uncle related to me, saying: My father related to me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His words: "like one whom the devils have lured in the earth, bewildered, who has companions calling him to guidance," he is the man who does not respond to the guidance of Allah; he is a man who obeyed the devil and acted in the earth with disobedience, and turned bewildered from the truth and strayed from it, and has companions calling him to guidance, and they claim that what they command him is guidance. Allah says that to their allies among mankind: The guidance is the guidance of Allah, and error is what the jinn call to.

* *

So it appears that Ibn 'Abbas, according to this narration, held that the companions of this bewildered one who call him are calling him only to error, and claim that this is guidance, and that Allah refuted them by His words: "Say: Indeed, the guidance of Allah is the guidance," not what his companions call him to.

This interpretation has a basis, were it not that Allah named the thing to which the companions called the bewildered one "guidance," and the report of that concerns his companions who call him to what they called him to: that they are the ones who named it. But Allah named it "guidance" and informed that the companions of the bewildered one call him to it. It is not permissible that Allah call "error" guidance, for that would be a lie, and it is not permissible to describe Allah as lying, for that would ascribe to Him what is not among His attributes. This could only be directed toward correctness if that were a report from Allah about the bewildered caller, that they said to him: "Come to the guidance." But since He says "they call him to guidance," it is not permissible that this be so, when they were calling him to error.

* *

As for His words "Come to us" (ait-na), the meaning is: they say: "Come to us, hurry to us," so the verb "say" is omitted, because the context indicates it.

* *

It is related from Ibn Mas'ud that he used to recite it: ﴿yad'unahu ila al-huda bayyinan﴾ (calling him to the clear guidance).

13430 – Ibn WakI' related this to us, saying: Ghundar related to us, from Shu'bah, from Abu Ishaq, who said: In the recitation of 'Abdullah: ﴿yad'unahu ila al-huda bayyinan﴾.

13431 – Al-Qasim related to us, saying: Al-Husayn related to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: 'Abd Allah ibn Kathir informed me that he heard Mujahid say: In the recitation of Ibn Mas'ud: ﴿lahu ashabun yad'unahu ila al-huda bayyinan﴾, he said: "al-huda" is the road, that it is clear.

* *

When it is recited thus, "al-bayyin" (clear) is an attribute of "al-huda," and the accusative of "al-bayyin" is by way of "qat'" (detachment) from "al-huda," [See the explanation of "qat'" in the index of technical terms above; this is a clear statement that "qat'" is the indefinite when it becomes an attribute of a definite.] as if it were said: calling him to the clear guidance, then "al-bayyin" was put in the accusative when the definite article was removed, and it became an indefinite qualifying a definite.

* *

This recitation attributed to Ibn Mas'ud supports the view of those who said that "al-huda" in this place is guidance in its true sense.

* *

The interpretation of His words: ﴿Say: Indeed, the guidance of Allah is the guidance, and we have been commanded to submit to the Lord of the worlds﴾ (71)

Abu Ja'far said: Allah, may His remembrance be exalted, says to His Prophet Muhammad ﷺ: Say, O Muhammad, to these who equate others with their Lord, the idols, who say to your companions: "Follow our way, and we will bear your sins, for we are upon guidance": the matter is not as you claim. "Indeed, the guidance of Allah is the guidance": that is, the path of Allah which He has made clear to us and shown us, and our way which He commanded us to hold to, and His religion which He legislated for us and explained, is the guidance and the straightness about which there is no doubt, not the worship of idols and images which neither harm nor benefit, so that we would abandon the truth and follow falsehood. "And we have been commanded to submit to the Lord of the worlds": that is, our Lord, the Lord of all things, may His face be exalted, has commanded us to submit to Him, to humble ourselves before Him with lowliness, obedience and servitude, so that we single that out for Him apart from any rivals and gods besides Him.

* *

We have already explained the meaning of "Islam" with its evidences earlier in our book, in a way that makes repeating it unnecessary.

* *

It has also been said that "wa-umirna li-nuslima" means: "and we have been commanded that we submit," and that we submit to the Lord of the worlds, because the Arabs place "kay" (in order that) and the "lam" that means "kay" in place of "an" (that), and "an" in its place.

**The interpretation (ta'wil) of His saying:** ﴿And that you establish the prayer and fear Him. It is He to whom you will be gathered﴾ (6:72)

Abu Ja'far says: He, exalted is His remembrance, says: "And we were commanded to establish the prayer."

* *

The phrase "wa-an aqimu al-salah" (and that you establish the prayer) is conjoined with "an" to the "lam" in "linuslima" (that we may submit), because "linuslima" means "an nuslima" (that we submit). So "wa-an aqimu" is returned to the meaning of "linuslima," since the "lam" in "linuslima" is a lam that only precedes verbs in the future tense, and "an" is one of the particles that indicate the future in the same way that the "lam" in "linuslima" does. Therefore it is conjoined to it, because their meanings agree in what I have mentioned.

So "an" is in the accusative position, as a return to the "lam" [1].

* *

Some of the grammarians of Basra (nahwiyyi al-Basra) used to say: It may be that the meaning is: "We were commanded to submit to the Lord of the worlds, and that we establish the prayer." That is, "We were commanded in order that we submit," as He says: ﴿And I was commanded to be among the believers﴾ (10:104), meaning: "I was only commanded to that." [2] Then He says, "And that you establish the prayer and fear Him," meaning: "We were commanded that we establish the prayer." Or the verb is connected with the "lam," and the meaning is: "I was commanded that I be," just as the verb is connected with the "lam" in His saying: ﴿Those who fear their Lord﴾ (7:154).

* *

The meaning of the speech, then, is: "We were commanded to establish the prayer," and that is performing it within the limits that were prescribed for us [3]. "And fear Him": that is, fear the Lord of the worlds, to whom we were commanded to submit, and beware of His wrath by performing the prayer that is obligatory upon you, and by submitting to Him in obedience and sincerely worshipping Him. "And it is He to whom you will be gathered": that is, your Lord, the Lord of the worlds, is the One to whom you will be gathered and assembled on the Day of Resurrection [4], and He will recompense each doer among you for his deeds, and every soul will be paid in full for what it earned.

[1] See Ma'ani al-Quran by al-Farra', 1:339.
[2] In the printed edition and the manuscript: "wa-umirtu li-an akuna min al-mu'minin." This is not a verse in the Book of God; the verse is the one mentioned, and it is the correct proof in this context.
[3] In the printed edition and the manuscript: "innama umirtu lidhalika," which is an error; the correct reading is what has been established here.
[4] On the meaning of "hashr" (gathering), see the earlier discussion at p. 373, note 2, and the references given there.

The interpretation of His saying, "And it is He who created the heavens and the earth in truth. And the day He says, 'Be,' and it is, His word is the truth. And His is the dominion, the day the Horn is blown. Knower of the unseen and the witnessed. And He is the Wise, the Acquainted" (6:73).

Abu Ja'far said: Exalted is He, says to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ): Say, O Muhammad, to these who ascribe equals to their Lord, who invite you to worship idols: "We are commanded to submit to the Lord of the worlds, who created the heavens and the earth in truth, not to one who neither benefits nor harms, neither hears nor sees."

* *

The commentators differed concerning the interpretation of His saying, "in truth" (bil-haqq).

Some of them said: The meaning is: He it is who created the heavens and the earth rightly and correctly, not in vanity and error, as He, exalted is He, says: "We did not create the heaven and the earth and what is between them in vain" (38:27). They said: The "bi" (in) and the "al" (the definite article) have been added to it, as the Arabs do in similar cases, saying, "So-and-so speaks in truth," meaning: he speaks the truth. They said: There is nothing in "His saying in truth" except that he hit upon the correct thing in it, not that "truth" is a meaning other than "saying"; rather it is a description of the saying: when the saying is accompanied by it, the speaker is described as speaking in truth and speaking the truth. They said: Likewise the creation of the heavens and the earth is a wisdom of God's wisdoms, so God is described as wise in creating them and in creating whatever else of His creation, not that this truth is other than the act of creating them by which He created them. [[In the printed edition: "other than their creation by it", which is an error, omits, substitutes and corrupts the sentence, then vocalized "other" as a verb with doubled waw, and made "creating them by it" a verbal noun in the accusative. This is corruption and nonsense.

The correct reading is what is in the manuscript: "sawā" (with kasra on the sīn) meaning "other than," and the first "khalqihimā" is a genitive verbal noun, and "khalaqahumā bihi" is a past verb. This is the true meaning and its correct sense. This is from the tampering of editors and correctors; one should seek refuge from the like of it, for it contradicts first the trust, and then the meanings of reason and understanding.]]

* *

Others said: The meaning is: He created the heavens and the earth by His speech and His saying to them: "Come willingly or unwillingly" (41:11). They said: Thus "the truth" in this place is intended to mean His speech. They cited in support of their view His saying: "And the day He says, 'Be,' and it is, His word is the truth," where "the truth" is His word and His speech. [[In the manuscript this phrase has omission and repetition; what is in the printed edition is closer to correct.]] They said: God created things by His speech and word, so what He created by it is other than the created things. [[This sentence in the printed edition read: "as He created by it the uncreated things", which is wholly defective, corrupt in meaning, indeed extremely far from the meaning. What is in the manuscript: "mimmā khalaqa bihi al-ashyā' bi-ghayr al-ashyā' al-makhlūqah", is distorted; its correct reading is what I have adopted, as the following sentence shows. It means that that by which He created things is other than the created things, and if it is other than them, it is uncreated.]] They said: Since that is so, it must be that God's speech by which He created creation is uncreated.

* *

As for His saying, "And the day He says, 'Be,' and it is," the grammarians differed concerning the governing element of "the day He says," and concerning the meaning of that.

Some Basran grammarians said: "al-yawm" (the day) is in apposition to "yaqūlu kun fa-yakūn" (He says, "Be," and it is). [[In the manuscript: "is in apposition to kun fa-yakūn," and the printed edition is correct.]] He said: It is in the accusative, and it has no apparent predicate, and God knows best; it is as I have explained to you. It is as if he means by this that its accusative is: "Remember the day He says, 'Be,' and it is." He said: Likewise "the day the Horn is blown." He said: Some of them said: "the day the Horn is blown, Knower of the unseen and the witnessed." [[I have not known the placement of this last sentence here, but I left it as it stands. It is clearly disconnected from what follows, for what follows is the view of al-Farrā' from the Kufans. I fear that something of the speech has fallen out.]]

* *

Some said: "He says, 'Be,' and it is" refers specifically to the Horn. [[This is the view of al-Farrā' in Ma'ānī al-Qur'ān, 1:340.]] So the meaning of the speech according to their interpretation is: the day He says to the Horn, "Be," and it is—His word is the truth—the day it is blown into, Knower of the unseen and the witnessed. Then "the saying" is in the nominative governed by "the truth," and "the truth" governed by "the saying," while "the day He says, 'Be,' and it is" and "the day the Horn is blown" are a relative clause of "the truth."

* *

Others said: Rather, "Be, and it is" refers to everything God restores in the Hereafter after its annihilation and originates after its non-existence. So according to their view the speech ends at "Be, and it is," and "His word is the truth" is the predicate of a subject. Its interpretation is: "He it is who created the heavens and the earth in truth, and the day He says to things, 'Be,' and it is, He created them in truth after their annihilation." Then He began to inform of His word and His promise to create that He would restore them after their annihilation, that it is truth, saying: "His word, this, is the truth beyond doubt." He informed that His is the dominion the day the Horn is blown; so "the day the Horn is blown" according to this interpretation is a relative clause of "the dominion."

It may also be permitted under this interpretation that "the day the Horn is blown" be a relative clause of "the truth."

* *

Others said: Rather, the meaning of the speech is: "And the day He says to what has perished, 'Be,' and it is; His word is the truth," making "the saying" nominative by "and the day He says, 'Be, and it is,'" and making "Be, and it is" a place for the saying, and "the day the Horn is blown" a relative clause of "the truth." It is as if he directed the interpretation to: "And on that day His word is the truth, the day the Horn is blown." If, according to this interpretation, "the day the Horn is blown" is taken as an explanation of the first day, it is a sound view. If "His word is the truth" is taken as nominative by "the day the Horn is blown," and "the day the Horn is blown" as a place, and "And the day He says, 'Be, and it is'" as its relative clause, it is permissible.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The correct view in this matter, in my judgment, is to say: God, exalted is He, informed that He alone created the heavens and the earth, to the exclusion of everything else, making known to those among His creatures who associate others with Him their ignorance in worshipping idols and images, and the error of what they persist in—worshipping what neither harms nor benefits, and cannot bring benefit to itself nor ward off harm from itself. And He argued against them in their denial of resurrection after death and of reward and punishment, by His power to originate that from the beginning, and that He who originated it is not incapable of annihilating it and then restoring it after its annihilation. So He said: "And it is He who created"—O you who ascribe equals to your Lord things that neither benefit nor harm and have power over nothing—"the heavens and the earth in truth," as a proof against His creatures, that they may know their Creator through them, and derive from them evidence of His great power and dominion, and thus devote worship to Him alone. "And the day He says, 'Be,' and it is" means: and the day He says, when the earth is changed into other than the earth and the heavens likewise, "Be," and it is, as God, exalted is He, wills, so the earth becomes other than the earth. And the speech ends at "Be, and it is." [[In the printed edition: "so the earth becomes other than the earth at His saying 'Be, and it is,' ending," which is a sickly sentence. The manuscript omitted "and it is" ("wa-yakūn"), which is present there, but the copyist dropped what I placed between the brackets, and by that the phrase is set right. This is clear from the context.]]

If the meaning is as such, there must be an omitted element in the speech indicated by the apparent wording, and the meaning of the speech is: "And the day He says thus, 'Be, and it is,' [the heavens and the earth are changed] into other than the heavens and the earth." [[What is between the brackets is an addition that is indispensable. In the manuscript it reads "tubadilahu" in place of "tubaddilu," and the printed edition is correct. The copyist at this point dropped and corrupted the speech.]] This is indicated by His saying: "And it is He who created the heavens and the earth in truth." Then He began to inform about the word, saying: "His word is the truth," meaning this His promise, which He, exalted is He, promised: that He will change the heavens and the earth into other than the earth and the heavens, is the truth beyond doubt. "And His is the dominion the day the Horn is blown," so "the day the Horn is blown" is a relative clause of "the dominion." The meaning of the speech is: "And to God belongs the dominion on that day, because the second blast on the Horn occurs while God is changing the heavens and the earth into other than them."

It is also permissible that "the saying," namely "His word is the truth," be nominative by "And the day He says, 'Be, and it is,'" and that "Be, and it is" be a place for the saying, nominative. The meaning of the speech then is: "He it is who created the heavens and the earth in truth, and the day He changes them into other than the heavens and the earth, and says to that, 'Be, and it is'—'His word is the truth.'"

* *

As for His saying, "And His is the dominion the day the Horn is blown," it was specified as a report about His dominion on that day, although the dominion is His alone at every time, in this world and the Hereafter, because He, exalted is He, meant that there is no contender with Him for it that day, nor any claimant to it, and that He alone possesses it, to the exclusion of every tyrant who used to dispute it with Him in this world. All of them will submit to Him in it that day, and they will know that their claims in this world were false.

* *

They differed concerning the meaning of "the Horn" (al-ṣūr) in this place.

Some said: It is a horn into which two blasts are blown: one for the annihilation of whoever is alive on the earth, and the second for the raising of every dead person. They argued for their view with His saying: "And the Horn is blown, and whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth swoons, except whom God wills. Then it is blown again, and behold, they are standing, looking" (39:68), and with the report transmitted from the Messenger of God (ﷺ), who, when asked about the Horn, said: it is a horn which is blown into. [[Narrated by Aḥmad in Musnad 'Abd Allāh ibn 'Amr, no. 6507, and see the note of my brother al-Sayyid Aḥmad on it.

Also narrated by Abū Dāwūd in his Sunan, 4:326, no. 326, from the hadith of 'Abd Allāh ibn 'Amr ibn al-'Āṣ, and by al-Tirmidhī in the chapter "What has come concerning the Horn," where he said: "This is a hasan ṣaḥīḥ hadith." Al-Ḥākim narrated it in al-Mustadrak, 4:560, and said: "A ṣaḥīḥ hadith in its chain, though they did not record it," and al-Dhahabī agreed with him. "Al-qarn" is a trumpet made from horns, blown into.]]

* *

Others said: "The Horn" in this place is the plural of "ṣūrah" (form), into which its spirit is blown so that it comes alive, like their saying "sūr" for the walls of a city, which is the plural of "sūrah," as Jarīr said:

"The walls of the city and the humbled mountains." [[Its takhrij and full text were given earlier, 2:17, 242.]]

* *

The Arabs say: "nafakha fī al-ṣūr" (he blew into the Horn) and "nafakha al-ṣūr" (he blew the Horn), and from their saying "nafakha al-ṣūr" is the verse of a poet: [[I have not known who said it.]]

Had it not been for Ibn Ja'dah, Quhunduzukum would not have been conquered, nor Khurasan, until the Horn is blown.

[[Ma'ānī al-Qur'ān of al-Farrā' 1:340; Nasab Quraysh 345; al-Mu'arrab of al-Jawāliqī 267; Lisān (ṣ-w-r). "Ibn Ja'dah" is 'Abd Allāh ibn Ja'dah ibn Hubayrah al-Makhzūmī, whose father Ja'dah ibn Hubayrah was over Khurasan, appointed by 'Alī ibn Abī Ṭālib. "Quhundudh" (with a damma on the qāf and hā', and sukūn on the nūn, damma on the dāl) is from the dialect of the people of Khurasan, meaning: a fortress or citadel.]]

Abu Ja'far said: The correct view in this matter, according to us, is what the reports from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) agree upon, that he said: "Indeed Isrāfīl has taken the Horn to his mouth and bowed his forehead, awaiting when he will be commanded and will blow." [[Narrated by al-Tirmidhī in the chapter "What has come concerning the Horn," and at the beginning of the tafsir of Surah al-Zumar; Ibn Kathīr mentioned it in his tafsir, 3:337, then said: "Narrated by Muslim in his Ṣaḥīḥ," but I was unable to locate it in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim.]] And that he said: "The Horn is a trumpet blown into." [[See the earlier note, p. 462, note 1.]]

* *

It is reported from Ibn 'Abbās that he used to say concerning His saying, "the day the Horn is blown, Knower of the unseen and the witnessed," that it means: the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed is the one who blows into the Horn.

13432 — Al-Muthannā narrated to me, saying: 'Abd Allāh ibn Ṣāliḥ narrated to us, saying: Mu'āwiyah narrated to us, from 'Alī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah, from Ibn 'Abbās concerning His saying, "Knower of the unseen and the witnessed," meaning: that the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed is the one who blows into the Horn.

* *

= So Ibn 'Abbās interpreted that His saying "Knower of the unseen and the witnessed" is the agent noun whose doer is unnamed in His saying "the day the Horn is blown," and that the meaning of the speech is: "the day God blows into the Horn, Knower of the unseen and the witnessed." Just as the Arabs say, "Your food was eaten, 'Abd Allāh," bringing out the name of the eater after the report has been given without naming its eater. And this, though it is a view that cannot be rejected, the better of it is that "Knower of the unseen and the witnessed" be nominative as an adjective of "the One" in His saying, "And it is He who created the heavens and the earth in truth."

* *

It is also reported from him that he used to say that "the Horn" in this place is the first blast.

13433 — Muḥammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, saying: my father narrated to me, saying: my uncle narrated to me, saying: my father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbās, concerning His saying, "the day the Horn is blown, Knower of the unseen and the witnessed," meaning by the Horn: the first blast. Do you not hear that He says: "And the Horn is blown, and whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth swoons, except whom God wills. Then it is blown again"—meaning the second—"and behold, they are standing, looking" (39:68).

* *

By His saying "Knower of the unseen and the witnessed" is meant: the Knower of what you witness, O people, so you see it, and of what is hidden from your senses and sight, so you neither perceive it nor see it. "And He is the Wise" in His management and direction of His creatures from the state of existence to non-existence, then from the state of non-existence and annihilation to existence, and then in recompensing them with what He recompenses them with, of reward or punishment. "The Acquainted" with everything they do and earn, good or evil, preserving it for them so He may recompense them for all of it. Exalted is He says: Beware, O you who ascribe equals to your Lord, of His punishment, for He is Knowing of everything you do and leave undone, and He is behind you in recompense for what you do.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 6, verse 74:

The interpretation of His saying: ﴿And when Abraham said to his father Azar﴾

Abu Ja'far said: Exalted is He, says to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ): Remember, O Muhammad, the argument you use against your people, your disputing with them over their gods, and your debating them about these, with the proof and evidence that We send down to you and teach you, showing the falsehood of what your people adhere to, and the soundness of the religion you adhere to, and the truth by which you argue against them, = the argument of Abraham, the close friend (khalil) of God, against his people, and his debating them about the falsehood of their worship of idols, and his turning to God, being pleased with Him as Protector and Helper instead of the idols. So take him as your leader and follow him, and make his conduct among your people an example for yourself = when he said to his father, separating himself from his religion and rebuking his worship of idols instead of their Creator and Originator: "O Azar."

* *

Then the scholars differed concerning the one meant by "Azar," and what it is: is it a name or a description? And if it is a name, who is it the name of? Some of them said: it is the name of his father.

Those who said so mentioned:

13434 - Muhammad ibn al-Husayn narrated to me, saying: Ahmad ibn al-Mufaddal narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: "And when Abraham said to his father Azar," he said: the name of his father was "Azar."

13435 - Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salamah ibn al-Fadl narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ishaq narrated to me: "Azar" was the father of Abraham. And he was, as was related to us, and God knows best, a man from the people of Kutha, from a village in al-Sawad, the Sawad of Kufa.

13436 - Ibn al-Barqi narrated to me, saying: Amr ibn Abi Salamah narrated to us, saying: I heard Sa'id ibn Abd al-Aziz mention: he is "Azar," and he is "Tarih," like "Isra'il" and "Ya'qub."

* *

Others said: he is not the father of Abraham.

Those who said so mentioned:

13437 - Muhammad ibn Humayd and Sufyan ibn Waki' narrated to us, both saying: Jarir narrated to us, from Layth, from Mujahid, who said: "Azar" is not the father of Abraham.

13438 - Al-Harith narrated to me, saying: Abd al-Aziz narrated to me, saying: al-Thawri narrated to us, saying: a man informed me, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: "And when Abraham said to his father Azar," he said: "Azar" was not his father; rather, it is an idol.

13439 - Ibn Waki' narrated to us, saying: Yahya ibn Yaman narrated to us, from Sufyan, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, who said: "Azar" is a name, an idol.

13440 - Muhammad ibn al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Ahmad ibn al-Mufaddal narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, who said: "And when Abraham said to his father Azar," he said: the name of his father; it is also said: no, rather his name was "Tarih," and the name of the idol was "Azar." He means: Do you take Azar's idols as gods? [In the manuscript: "Do you take idols as gods," without "Azar," and what is in the printed edition is close to correct, God willing, as will come in Abu Ja'far's criticism of al-Suddi's view shortly.]

* *

Others said: it is an insult and a reproach in their speech, and its meaning is "crooked." It is as if they interpreted it as meaning that he reproached him for his deviation and crookedness from the truth. [See al-Farra's Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1: 340.]

* *

The reciters differed regarding the reading of this.

The majority of the reciters of the cities read it: ﴿And when Abraham said to his father Azar﴾ with a fatha on "Azar," following the case of "al-Ab" in the genitive; but because it is a non-Arabic name, they gave it a fatha, since they did not inflect it, even though it stands in the genitive position.

* *

It is related from Abu Zayd al-Madini and al-Hasan al-Basri that they read it: ﴿Azaru﴾ with a damma as a vocative, meaning: O Azar.

* *

As for what is reported from al-Suddi, that "Azar" is the name of an idol, and that he put it in the accusative meaning: Do you take Azar as idols, gods? — this is a view that is far from correct from the standpoint of Arabic grammar. The Arabs do not put a noun in the accusative by a verb after the interrogative particle; one does not say: "Your brother, did you speak to?" meaning: Did you speak to your brother?

Abu Ja'far said: The correct reading in this matter, in my view, is the reading of the one who reads "Azar" with a fatha on the "ra'", following the grammatical case of "al-Ab," and that it stands in the genitive position and is given a fatha, since it is not inflected, because it is a non-Arabic name. I have chosen this reading only because the consensus of the authoritative reciters agrees upon it.

Since this is the correct reading, and it is impossible for it to be in the accusative governed by the verb after the interrogative particle, it is valid for you to read it with a fatha on one of two grounds:

Either it is the name of the father of Abraham, peace be upon him and upon all his prophets and messengers, and so it stands in the genitive as an apposition to "al-Ab," but it has a fatha because, as you have mentioned, it is a non-Arabic name and so is not inflected, just as the Arabs do with non-Arabic names.

= Or it is a descriptive epithet of him, and so it is also in the genitive, by way of repeating the preposition on it, but since it follows the pattern of "ahmar" and "aswad," it is not inflected, and it is treated as its like is treated. The meaning of the sentence then would be: And when Abraham said to his father, the crooked one: Do you take idols as gods?

Since there is no valid direction for the correct reading except one of these two, the more preferable of the two views in my opinion is the view of the one who said: "He is the name of his father," because God, exalted is He, informed that he was his father, and this is the transmitted position of the scholars, rather than the other view whose proponent claimed it to be a descriptive epithet.

* *

If someone says: The genealogists only trace Abraham to "Tarih," so how can "Azar" be his name, when the name known for him is "Tarih"? It is said to him: It is not impossible that he had two names, as many people have in our time, and as was the case for many of them in the past. It is also possible that it is a title by which he was called.

* *

The interpretation of His saying: ﴿Do you take idols as gods? Indeed I see you and your people in clear error﴾ (74)

Abu Ja'far said: This is a report from God, exalted is He, about what Abraham said to his father Azar: "Do you take idols as gods, worshipping them and taking them as lords besides God, who created you, fashioned you, and provided for you?"

"Al-asnam" is the plural of "sanam," and "sanam" is a statue of stone, wood, or other material in the form of a human, and it is also called "wathan." The image depicted in the form of a human on a wall or elsewhere may also be called "sanam" and "wathan."

* *

"Indeed I see you and your people in clear error": he says: "Indeed I see you," O Azar, "and your people" who worship idols with you and take them as gods, "in error," meaning: in deviation from the path of truth, and turning away from the way of right = "clear," meaning: it becomes evident to whoever sees it that it is a deviation from the intended way and a departure from the straight path. He means by this that he and they had strayed from the Oneness of God and His worship, which was obligatory for them to sincerely direct to Him by His bounties upon them, rather than to other gods and idols. [See the explanation of "dalal" (error) and "mubin" (clear) in the earlier language indexes (d-l-l) (b-y-n).]

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 6, verse 75 (part 1 of 2):

The interpretation of His words: ﴿And thus We showed Abraham the dominion (malakut) of the heavens and the earth, that he might be among the certain (in faith)﴾ (6:75).

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: By His words "wa-kadhalika" (and thus), God, may His remembrance be exalted, means: just as We granted him insight into His religion and the truth, in opposition to the error in which his people were (([[In the printed edition: "في خلاف ما كانوا عليه من الضلال". In the manuscript: "في خلافه بما كانوا عليه من الضلال", with a blank space between them. In the margin there is the letter (ط) indicating an error. My opinion is that the copyist found the sentence confusing and left the blank, and the sentence is connected and sound in meaning.]])), We showed him the dominion of the heavens and the earth, meaning His kingdom (mulk). [[In the manuscript: "يعني ملكوت وزيدت فيه", with a blank space also between them, and what is in the printed edition is sound in meaning.]]

* *

The letter "ta'" (ت) was added to it (malakut), just as it was added to "al-jabarut" from "al-jabr" (([[In the manuscript: "من الجبروة", and the correct reading is what is in the printed edition.]])), and as it has been said: "rahabut khayrun min rahamut", meaning: awe is better than mercy. [[See Majaz al-Qur'an by Abu 'Ubaydah, 1:197-198.]] It is also related from the Arabs by transmission: "lahu malakut al-Yaman wa-al-'Iraq", meaning: he has the dominion of that (region).

* *

The people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) differed in their interpretation of His words: "We showed Abraham the dominion of the heavens and the earth."

Some of them said: the meaning of that is: We showed him the creation of the heavens and the earth.

Those who said this:

13441. Al-Muthanna related to me, saying: 'Abd Allah ibn Salih related to us, saying: Mu'awiyah ibn Salih related to us, from 'Ali ibn Abi Talhah, from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words: "We showed Abraham the dominion of the heavens and the earth," meaning: the creation of the heavens and the earth.

13442. Bishr ibn Mu'adh related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah: "And thus We showed Abraham the dominion of the heavens and the earth," meaning: the creation of the heavens and the earth, "and that he might be among the certain."

13443. Muhammad ibn Sa'd related to me, saying: my father related to me, saying: my paternal uncle related to me, saying: my father related to me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas: "And thus We showed Abraham the dominion of the heavens and the earth." By "the dominion of the heavens and the earth" he means: the creation of the heavens and the earth.

* *

Others said: the meaning of "malakut" is kingship (al-mulk), in a manner similar to the interpretation we have given. [[In the manuscript: "وبنحو الذي تأولناه", and in the margin "التأويل", and above it is the mark "صح", and on the other side of the line (كذا) in red ink. What is in the printed edition is more similar to the correct reading, except that it wrote "الذي أولناه", and the correct reading is what is in the manuscript.]]

Those who said this:

13444. Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Yahya ibn Wadih related to us, saying: 'Umar ibn Abi Za'idah related to us, saying: I heard 'Ikrimah, and a man asked him about His words: "And thus We showed Abraham the dominion of the heavens and the earth." He said: It is the kingship (al-mulk), except that in the language of the Nabateans it is "malakuta". [[The report: 13444 and 13445. 'Umar ibn Abi Za'idah al-Hamdani al-Wada'i, who is "Ibn Abi Za'idah" in the second chain, is the brother of Zakariya ibn Abi Za'idah, and he is the elder. Zakariya is much higher than him. He is trustworthy (thiqah), but he held the doctrine of qadar (divine decree), and he is upright in narration. He is biographed in al-Tahdhib.]]

13445. Ibn Wakf' related to us, saying: my father related to us, from Ibn Abi Za'idah, from 'Ikrimah, who said: It is in Nabatean: "malakuta".

* *

Others said: the meaning of that is: the signs (ayat) of the heavens and the earth.

Those who said this:

13446. Hannad ibn al-Sarri related to us, saying: Waki' related to us, from Sufyan, from Mansur, from Mujahid: "We showed Abraham the dominion of the heavens and the earth," he said: the signs of the heavens and the earth.

13447. Muhammad ibn 'Amr related to me, saying: Abu 'Asim related to us, saying: 'Isa related to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid regarding the saying of God, may His remembrance be exalted: "And thus We showed Abraham the dominion of the heavens and the earth," he said: signs.

13448. Al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah related to us, saying: Shibl related to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: "And thus We showed Abraham the dominion of the heavens and the earth," he said: The seven heavens were opened (tafarrajat) for Abraham, up to the Throne, so he looked into them, and the seven earths were opened for him, so he looked into them.

13449. Muhammad ibn al-Husayn related to me, saying: Ahmad ibn al-Mufaddal related to us, saying: Asbat related to us, from al-Suddi: "And thus We showed Abraham the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and that he might be among the certain," he said: He was made to stand on a rock, and the heavens were opened for him, so he looked at the kingdom of God in them, until he looked at his place in Paradise. And the earths were opened for him until he looked at the bottom of the earth. This is His saying: ﴿And We gave him his reward in this world﴾ (29:27), meaning: We gave him his place in Paradise. And it is said that "ajr" (reward) means a good reputation.

13450. Al-Qasim related to us, saying: al-Husayn related to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from al-Qasim ibn Abi Bazzah, from Mujahid regarding His words: "And thus We showed Abraham the dominion of the heavens and the earth," he said: The heavens were opened for him, so he looked at what is in them, until his sight reached the Throne, and the seven earths were opened for him, so he looked at what is in them.

13451. Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Hakkam related to us, from 'Anbasah, from Salim, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr: "And thus We showed Abraham the dominion of the heavens and the earth," he said: The covering (adim) of the heavens and the earth was removed for him, until he looked at them: on a rock, and the rock on a fish, and the fish on the seal of the Lord of Might, there is no god but Allah. [[What we have already said regarding this kind of report, which carries no proof from the truthful one (ﷺ), has passed.]]

13452. Hannad and Ibn Wakf' related to us, both saying: Abu Mu'awiyah related to us, from 'Asim, from Abu 'Uthman, from Salman, who said: When Abraham saw the dominion of the heavens and the earth, he saw a servant committing a grave sin, so he invoked a curse upon him, and he perished. Then he saw another committing a grave sin, so he invoked a curse upon him, and he perished. Then he saw another committing a grave sin, so he invoked a curse upon him, and he perished. Then it was said: Bring down My servant! He will not destroy My servants!

13453. Hannad related to us, saying: Qabisah related to us, from Sufyan, from Talhah ibn 'Amr, from 'Ata', who said: When God raised Abraham into the dominion (malakut) in the heavens, he looked down and saw a servant committing adultery, so he invoked a curse upon him, and he perished. Then he was raised and looked down, and saw a servant committing adultery, so he invoked a curse upon him, and he perished. Then he was raised and looked down, and saw a servant committing adultery, so he invoked a curse upon him, and then it was called out: "Gently, O Abraham! You are a servant whose supplication is answered. As for My servant, there are three possibilities regarding him: either he repents to Me and I accept his repentance, or I bring forth from him a good offspring, or he persists in what he is in, and I am behind him."

13454. Ibn Bashshar related to us, saying: Ibn Abi 'Adi, Muhammad ibn Ja'far and 'Abd al-Wahhab related to us, from 'Awf, from Usamah: that Abraham, the Friend of the Most Merciful, thought within himself that he was the most merciful of creation, and that God raised him until he looked down upon the people of the earth, and he saw their deeds. When he saw them doing acts of disobedience he said: O God, destroy them! His Lord said to him: I am more merciful to My servants than you. Descend, for perhaps they will repent to Me and return. [[In the printed edition: "ويرجعوا", and the correct and good reading is from the manuscript.]]

* *

Others said: rather, the meaning of that is what He, may He be exalted, informed that He showed him of the stars, the moon and the sun.

Those who said this:

13455. Ibn Waki' related to us, saying: Abu Khalid al-Ahmar related to us, from Juwaybir, from al-Dahhak: "And thus We showed Abraham the dominion of the heavens and the earth," he said: the sun, the moon and the stars.

13456. Ibn Bashshar related to us, saying: 'Abd al-Rahman related to us, saying: Sufyan related to us, from Mansur, from Mujahid: "And thus We showed Abraham the dominion of the heavens and the earth," he said: the sun and the moon.

13457. Al-Muthanna related to us, saying: 'Abd Allah ibn Salih related to us, saying: Mu'awiyah related to me, from 'Ali ibn Abi Talhah, from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words: "And thus We showed Abraham the dominion of the heavens and the earth," he meant by it: the sun, the moon and the stars. [[In the printed edition: "يعني به: نريه الشمس", and it added "نريه", which is not in the manuscript.]]

13458. Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-A'la related to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Thawr related to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatadah, who said: Abraham (ﷺ) was hidden from one of the tyrants, and his provision was placed in his fingers, so whenever he sucked one of his fingers he found in it provision. When he came out, God showed him the dominion of the heavens and the earth. The dominion of the heavens was: the sun, the moon and the stars, and the dominion of the earth: the mountains, the trees and the seas.

13459. Bishr ibn Mu'adh related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying [[In the printed edition, "قال حدثنا يزيد" is omitted.]] he related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah: It has been mentioned to us that the Prophet of God Abraham (ﷺ) was taken away from an affluent tyrant, and he was placed in a hidden tunnel, and his provision was placed in his fingers, so he did not suck a finger of his except that he found provision in it. When he came out of that tunnel, God showed him the dominion of the heavens: He showed him the sun, the moon, the stars, the clouds and a great creation, and He showed him the dominion of the earth: He showed him mountains, seas, rivers, trees, every kind of animal and a great creation. [[In the manuscript: "قربه جبار مترف", and as for what is in the printed edition, it is the exact text of what is in al-Durr al-Manthur, 3:25.]] [["al-Sarab" (with two fatha vowels): a pit in the ground, like a cellar.]]

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The most correct of the sayings regarding the interpretation of that is the saying of the one who said: God, may His remembrance be exalted, meant by His words: "And thus We showed Abraham the dominion of the heavens and the earth," that He showed him the kingdom of the heavens and the earth, and that is what He created in them of the sun, the moon, the stars, the trees, the animals and other things, and of His great authority in them, and He made clear to him the inner and outer aspects of matters, because of what we mentioned before concerning the meaning of "malakut" in the language of the Arabs, in what has passed before. [[See what has preceded, p. 470 and following.]]

* *

As for His words, "and that he might be among the certain," it means that He showed him the dominion of the heavens and the earth so that he would be among those who confess the oneness of God, [[In the printed edition and the manuscript: "ممن يتوحد بتوحيد الله", which is a statement with no meaning; its correct form is what I have written. It is only an error from the copyist's haste, and I deduced it from the meaning of "yuqin" in what has passed, 10:394.]] and know the reality of what He guided him to and gave him insight into, [[In the printed edition: "ويعلم حقية ما هداه له", which was treated as its companions were treated, as has passed shortly before: p. 465, note 2, and the references there.]] namely the knowledge of His unity, and the error in which his people were, from worshipping idols and taking them as gods besides God, may He be exalted. [[See the explanation of "ayqana" in what has passed, 10:394-395.]]

* *

Ibn 'Abbas used to say, regarding the interpretation of that, the following:

13460. Muhammad ibn Sa'd related to me, with it, saying: my father related to me, saying: my paternal uncle related to me, saying: my father related to me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words: "And that he might be among the certain": that the matter was made clear to him, its secret and its open aspects, so nothing of the deeds of creatures was hidden from him. When he began to curse the people of sins, God said: Indeed, you cannot bear this! So God returned him to what he was before that.

* *

The interpretation of that according to this interpretation: We showed him the dominion of the heavens and the earth so that he would be among those who are certain of the knowledge of everything by direct sensory perception, not by report.

13461. Al-'Abbas ibn al-Walid related to me, saying: my father informed me, saying: Ibn Jabir related to us, saying: and al-Awza'i also related to us, saying: Khalid ibn al-Lajlaj related to me, saying: I heard 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'A'ish al-Hadrami say: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) led us in prayer one morning, and someone said to him: I have never seen your face brighter than it is this morning! [[In the printed edition and the manuscript: "ما رأيت أسعد منك اليوم", which is an error; its correct form is from Muntakhab Dhayl al-Dhayl by Abu Ja'far al-Tabari, his history 13:59, where he related the report in full there. His saying "asfara wajhan minka al-ghadat" means: more radiant and illuminated. It is said: "safara wajhuhu husnan wa-asfara", when it became radiant and shining, and from it in the Mighty Revelation: "Faces that day shall be radiant (musfirah)."]] He said: What is with me? My Lord has appeared to me in the most beautiful form, [[In the printed edition: "ما لي قد أتاني ربي", and in the manuscript: "ومالي وقد ستاني ربي", unpointed and distorted; its correct form is from the Dhayl al-Dhayl of Abu Ja'far.]] and He said: About what do the Exalted Assembly dispute, O Muhammad? I said: You know best [O Lord]!
