[[The addition between the parentheses is from the narration of Abu Ja'far in Dhayl al-Dhayl.]] Then He placed His hand between my shoulders, and I found its coolness between my breasts, [[His saying: "fa-wajadtu bardaha bayna thadyayya"; the publisher of the printed edition omitted it, because in the manuscript it was thus: "فوضع يده بين كتفي، ثديي", the copyist dropped what was between the two statements, and its correct form is to add it from Abu Ja'far's narration in Dhayl al-Dhayl.]] so I knew what is in the heavens and the earth. [[In Dhayl al-Dhayl: "ما في السماء والأرض".]] Then he recited this verse: "And thus We showed Abraham the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and that he might be among the certain." [[The report: 13461. This is a very difficult report, as you will see later, and it was in the manuscript and the printed edition distorted to a very great degree, and its chain of narration was even more distorted, but I have corrected it, by the help of God, may His remembrance be exalted, from the narration of Abu Ja'far in Dhayl al-Dhayl (Tarikh al-Tabari 13:59-60).

"Al-'Abbas ibn al-Walid ibn Mazid al-'Udhri al-Amili al-Bayruti," the teacher of al-Tabari, is trustworthy; he related much from him that has passed under numbers 891, 11014, 11821. And his father: "al-Walid ibn Mazid al-'Udhri al-Bayruti," is trustworthy; passed under number 11821. Al-Awza'i, his teacher, said: "His books are sound." Al-Nasa'i said: "He is more beloved to us in al-Awza'i than al-Walid ibn Muslim; he does not err, nor does he commit tadlis (concealment of defects in chains)." And "Ibn Jabir" is: "'Abd al-Rahman ibn Yazid ibn Jabir al-Azdi, trustworthy; the group (of compilers) related from him; al-Awza'i related from him, and al-Walid ibn Mazid al-Bayruti, and others. He passed under number 6655. In the printed edition and the manuscript it was "Abu Jabir", which is an error; its correct form is from Dhayl al-Dhayl and elsewhere.]]

Khalid ibn al-Lajlaj al-Amiri was advanced in years and righteous, bold of tongue before the kings, and harsh with them. Al-Bukhari said: "He heard from Umar ibn al-Khattab and his father." Ibn Abi Hatim said: "He narrated from Umar, mursal, and from his father; and his father had the companionship (suhbah). He also narrated from Abd al-Rahman ibn A'idh al-Hadrami." Ibn Hibban mentioned him among the trustworthy Successors (thiqat al-tabi'in). He is biographed in al-Tahdhib, al-Kabir 2/1/156, and Ibn Abi Hatim 1/2/349. In the printed edition and the manuscript it reads "Khalid al-Hallaj," which is a pure error. As for "Abd al-Rahman ibn A'idh al-Hadrami," his status and the question of his companionship has been problematic from long ago, and mention of that will come later. In the printed edition and the manuscript it reads "Abd al-Rahman ibn Ayyash," and the editor of the printed edition dropped "al-Hadrami," though it is present in the manuscript. The correct form comes from the narration of Abu Ja'far in Dhayl al-Mudhayyal. But the greatest wonder is that it likewise appears in the Musnad (5:243) as "Abd al-Rahman ibn Ayyash al-Hadrami," although I have not found anyone who, in his biography, mentioned a disagreement about the name of his father, "A'idh." It is a remarkable coincidence, and a rare one of its kind, that it should appear the same way in the manuscript of al-Tabari and in the Musnad alike, which is a remarkable agreement upon an error in two different books. What is in the Musnad is also undoubtedly an error, because I found Ibn Kathir in his tafsir (7:220), who transmitted the report from this place in Musnad Ahmad, and there it reads "Abd al-Rahman ibn A'idh," which is correct. The change of "A'idh" to "Ayyash" is a plausible and close one, owing to the fame of "Ayyash" and the many who bear it, and the obscurity of "A'idh" and the rarity of those named with it. "Abd al-Rahman ibn A'idh al-Hadrami" is biographed in al-Tahdhib, in Ibn Sa'd 7/2/150 under the Companions, in Dhayl al-Mudhayyal of al-Tabari (13:59, 60), in al-Istay'ab of Ibn Abd al-Barr: 399, Ibn Abi Hatim 2/2/262, Usd al-Ghabah 3:303, 304, in al-Isabah, and in Mizan al-I'tidal 2:108. The question of "Abd al-Rahman ibn A'idh"'s companionship is disputed. Among those who explicitly affirmed his companionship are Ibn Sa'd, Ibn Jarir in Dhayl al-Mudhayyal, and Ibn Hibban. As for Ibn Abd al-Barr in al-Istay'ab and Ibn al-Athir in Usd al-Ghabah, they mention that his companionship is not sound, because his narration is erratic (mudtarib). As for Abu Hatim, he said: "Whoever said he had companionship erred; in my view he is a Successor." As for Abu Zur'ah, he said: "Abd al-Rahman ibn A'idh is not well known." The Hafiz Ibn Hajar, in al-Isabah, counted among those who listed him as a Companion, saying: "Mentioned among the Companions by Muhammad ibn Sa'd, al-Bukhari, Abu Zur'ah al-Dimashqi, Abu al-Hasan ibn Sumay', Abu al-Qasim, al-Baghawi, Abu Zur'ah al-Harrani, and others." He fully treated the discussion of his biography in al-Isabah. Al-Bukhari said: "He has one hadith only, but they are erratic concerning it," meaning this hadith. The Hafiz Ibn Hajar said in al-Isabah: "I say: I have found for him another hadith, marfu', and another, mawquf." This report was narrated by Abu Ja'far in Dhayl al-Mudhayyal (his history 13:59, 60) through this isnad, and al-Tirmidhi pointed to it in the tafsir of "Surah Sad" in his Sunan (12:116, 117, with the commentary of Ibn al-Arabi), after mentioning the hadith of Mu'adh ibn Jabal, through the route of Zayd ibn Sallam, from Abu Sallam, from Abd al-Rahman ibn A'idh al-Hadrami, that he narrated to him from Malik ibn Yukhamir al-Sakuni, from Mu'adh ibn Jabal, and mentioned the hadith. He said: "Abu Isa said: this is a hasan sahih hadith. I asked Muhammad ibn Isma'il (al-Bukhari) about this hadith and he said: this is more sound than the hadith of al-Walid ibn Muslim, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Yazid ibn Jabir, who said: Khalid ibn al-Lajlaj narrated to us, Abd al-Rahman ibn A'idh al-Hadrami narrated to me, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he mentioned the hadith. This is not preserved; thus al-Walid stated in his hadith from Abd al-Rahman ibn A'idh, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Bishr ibn Bakr narrated this hadith from Abd al-Rahman ibn Yazid ibn Jabir with this isnad, from Abd al-Rahman ibn A'idh, from the Prophet (ﷺ) — and this is more sound, and Abd al-Rahman ibn A'idh did not hear from the Prophet (ﷺ)." The Hafiz Ibn Hajar fully treated, in al-Isabah, in the biography of "Abd al-Rahman ibn A'idh," the aspects of difference and erratic narration in this report, and what they said in the books I mentioned, that in his hadith he did not say "I heard the Prophet (ﷺ)" except al-Walid ibn Muslim. He mentioned that al-Walid ibn Muslim was not alone in narrating that, but that a trustworthy and firm narrator, sound in narration from al-Awza'i, namely "al-Walid ibn Mazid al-Bayruti," narrated the same as al-Walid ibn Muslim's narration. Accordingly, the irregularity in it did not come through al-Walid ibn Muslim. The Hafiz mentioned all the corroborating routes that support al-Walid ibn Muslim's narration. As for the report by other than this isnad, it was narrated by Ahmad in his Musnad (5:243), and by al-Tirmidhi, as I indicated above. Then Ahmad narrated it from the hadith of Ibn Abbas in his Musnad, number 3484, in the same form. Al-Suyuti cited it in al-Durr al-Manthur (5:319–321) from the hadith of a group of Companions: Ibn Abbas, Mu'adh ibn Jabal, Abu Hurayrah, Anas ibn Malik, Abu Umamah al-Bahili, Tariq ibn Shihab, Adi ibn Hatim, Abu Ubaydah ibn al-Jarrah, and Thawban. This is a sufficient extent in the takhrij of this erratic report; refer to all the books I have mentioned. Written by Mahmud Muhammad Shakir.

**Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 6, verse 76:**

The explanation of His saying: ﴿So when the night covered him, he saw a star. He said, "This is my lord." But when it set, he said, "I do not love those that set."﴾ (6:76)

Abu Ja'far said: He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: when the night concealed him and hid him. [[In the printed edition: "daraha al-layl wa-jannahu" (it hid him from view and covered him). The correct reading, from the manuscript, is as given.]]

* *

It is said of this: *janna 'alayhi al-layl* and *jannahu al-layl* and *ajannahu* and *ajanna 'alayhi*. When you omit *'ala*, the form with the *alif* (*ajannahu al-layl*) is more eloquent than the form without it, and *janna 'alayhi al-layl* is more eloquent than *jannahu*. All of these are accepted and heard from the Arabs. [[This is a clarification that you will not find in the lexicon books, so note it there; see also al-Farra', Ma'ani al-Qur'an, 1:341.]] *Jannahu al-layl* is in the dialect of Asad, while *ajannahu* and *junnahu* are in the dialect of Tamim. [[That is, the first is more common in the dialect of the Banu Asad, and the second is more common in the dialect of the Banu Tamim.]] The verbal noun of *janna 'alayhi* is *jannan*, *junuban* and *janánan*, and of *ajanna* is *ijnánan*. It is said: "So-and-so came in the darkness of the night" (*fi jinn al-layl*). [[*Jinn al-layl* (with a kasra on the jim) means the mingling of its darkness.]] The *jinn* derive from this, because they are concealed from the eyes of the children of Adam and are not seen. Everything that is hidden from the sight of people, the Arabs say of it, "it has been concealed" (*qad jann*). From this is the saying of the Hudhali poet: [[He is al-Buraiq al-Hudhali, whose name is 'Iyad ibn Khuwailid al-Khana'i. Al-Asma'i related that the author of the poem is 'Amir ibn Sadus al-Khana'i.]]

*And water I reached before the sleep, while the dark night had concealed it.*

[[Diwan al-Hudhaliyyin 3:56; Ma Baqiya min Ash'ar al-Hudhaliyyin no. 31; Lisan al-'Arab (sadf) (jann). It is from verses in which he glorifies himself. After the verse: *"With me is a companion like the blade of a spear, fierce against his opponent, violent."* It is also related as: "*wa-ma wardtu 'alayya khifa*" and as "*qubayl al-sabah*"; all of it is good. *Al-sadaf* is the darkness at the beginning or end of the night, where light mingles with it. *Al-adham* is that which inclines toward blackness.]]

And 'Ubayd said:

*And a desolate wasteland in which the owls screech along with the echo, fearsome when the night has covered it, dreaded.*

[[His Diwan: 33. He mentions himself in this verse and then says after it: *"I crossed with a grey-white she-camel of the highland, slipping the saddles off the sides of the one who is afflicted."* He concluded it with the wise verse: *"You see the man longing for life and its length, and in the length of a man's life is the greatest torment."* He spoke the ultimate truth! In the printed edition it reads "al-layl murhib," and the correct reading is from the manuscript. *Al-kharq* (with a fatha and then a sukun) is the wide desert. The version in the Diwan is "tasih al-hamm," and *al-hamm* is the male owl; Abu Ja'far's version is better, because *al-sada* is also the male owl.]]

From this is *ajannat al-mayyit*, when I buried the dead person in the grave, and *jannatuhu*, which is similar to *junun al-layl* in the meaning of covering. From this the shield is called *mijann*, because it conceals the one who takes cover behind it, covering and hiding him.

* *

As for His saying, "He saw a star," it means: he saw a star when it rose. "He said, 'This is my lord.'" It is related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning this:

13462 – Al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Abu Salih related to us, saying: Mu'awiyah ibn Salih related to me, from 'Ali ibn Abi Talhah, from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: *"And thus We showed Abraham the dominion of the heavens and the earth, that he might be among the certain ones,"* meaning by it the sun, the moon and the stars. *"So when the night covered him, he saw a star and said, 'This is my lord.'"* He worshipped it until it set, and when it set he said: *"I do not love those that set."* *"Then when he saw the moon rising, he said, 'This is my lord.'"* He worshipped it until it set, and when it set he said: *"Unless my lord guides me, I will surely be among the misguided people."* *"Then when he saw the sun rising, he said, 'This is my lord; this is greater.'"* He worshipped it until it set, and when it set he said: *"O my people, indeed I am free from what you associate."*

13463 – Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah: *"So when the night covered him, he saw a star and said, 'This is my lord.' But when it set, he said, 'I do not love those that set.'"* He knew that his Lord is enduring and does not cease. Then he recited until he reached: *"This is my lord; this is greater,"* and he saw a creation greater than the first two and brighter. [[In the printed edition: "wa-ayy khalq" (and what creation), which is corrupt in meaning; in the manuscript: "wa-ayy khalqan," and the correct reading of it is what I have established.]]

The cause of Abraham's saying that was as follows:

13464 – Muhammad ibn Humayd related to me, saying: Salamah ibn al-Fadl related to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ishaq related to me, as was mentioned to us – and God knows best – that Azar was a man from the people of Kuthy, a village in the countryside of al-Sawad, the countryside of Kufa. At that time the king of the East was Nimrod. [[In the printed edition: "li-Namrud ibn Kan'an," which is not in the manuscript, nor in the History of al-Tabari 1:119. What is there is: "li-Namrud al-Khati'," and he was called "al-Hasir." His kingdom, they claim, encompassed the eastern and western parts of the earth, and he was in Babylon..." Abu Ja'far abridged the report as is his custom. It is a report he divided in his history: he related its opening here, then detailed it, then returned to the narration of Ibn Ishaq.]] When God willed to send Abraham, the Friend of the Merciful, as a proof against his people and as a messenger to His servants – and there was no prophet between Noah and Abraham except Hud and Salih – when the time of Abraham drew near, the time in which God willed what He willed, the astrologers came to Nimrod and said to him: "Know that we find in our knowledge that a boy will be born in this your town who will be called 'Abraham'; he will part from your religion and break your idols, in such-and-such a month of such-and-such a year." [["Ta'allam" (with a fatha on the ta and ayn and a shadda on the lam) is an imperative meaning "know." It often occurs in the Sirah of Ibn Ishaq, and many people err in its vocalization due to their lack of knowledge of the language.]] When the year that the astrologers described to Nimrod arrived, Nimrod sent to every pregnant woman in his town and detained her with him, except for the mother of Abraham, the wife of Azar, for he did not know of her pregnancy. That was because she was, it is said, a young woman who did not recognize the pregnancy within her. [["Imra'a hadatha" (with fatha vowels) means young in years, a clearly young woman. The masculine is "rajul hadath," a young man. In the printed edition it was "hadabah" with a ba, which is a clear error; in the manuscript it is undotted, and the correct reading is in the History of al-Tabari.]] And because God willed to bring her son to term – [[In the printed edition: "wa-lamma arada Allah an yuballigha bi-waladiha arada an yaqtula..." differs from what is in the manuscript, because the editor did not understand the context of the statement and put "arada" in place of "yurid." The context of the statement is: "...Nimrod sent to every pregnant woman in his town and detained her with him... he wants to kill every boy..." The dividing phrase concerning her son was placed between two dashes for that reason. His saying "wa-lamma arada Allah" means "and for what God willed." This sentence is not in the History of Abu Ja'far; he abridged the account there as is his custom.]] – he wanted to kill every boy born in that month of that year, out of caution for his kingdom. So no woman gave birth to a boy in that month of that year without his ordering it to be slaughtered. When the mother of Abraham felt the pains of labor, she went out at night to a cave near her and gave birth to Abraham in it, and she prepared for him what is done for a newborn. Then she sealed the cave over him, and returned to her house. Then she would visit him in the cave to see what had become of him, and she found him alive, sucking his thumb. They claim – and God knows best – that God placed Abraham's sustenance in it and what came to him from his sucking. Azar, it is claimed, asked the mother of Abraham about the outcome of her pregnancy, and she said: "I bore a boy, and he died!" So he believed her and remained silent about her. The day, it is said, for Abraham in youth was like a month, and a month like a year. Abraham did not remain in the cave more than fifteen months until he said to his mother: "Take me out so that I may see!" So she took him out at nightfall, and he looked, and reflected upon the creation of the heavens and the earth, and said: *"Indeed, He who created me and provided for me and fed me and gave me drink is my Lord; I have no god other than Him!"* Then he looked at the sky and saw a star and said: *"This is my lord."* Then he followed it with his sight until it set, and when it set he said: *"I do not love those that set."* Then the moon rose and he saw it rising and said: *"This is my lord."* Then he followed it with his sight until it set, and when it set he said: *"Unless my Lord guides me, I will surely be among the misguided people!"* When the day came upon him and the sun rose, he regarded the sun as great [[so in the printed edition and manuscript: "a'zam al-shams," as if he means: he considered it great and found it mighty. This is correct in meaning. But in the History there is: "ra'a 'azm al-shams" (he saw the greatness of the sun), which is also correct.]] and saw something greater in light than anything he had seen before. He said: *"This is my lord; this is greater!"* But when it set, he said: *"O my people, indeed I am free from what you associate. Indeed I have turned my face toward He who originated the heavens and the earth, as a hanif, and I am not of the polytheists."* Then Abraham returned to his father Azar, and his direction had been set straight; he knew his Lord and was free from the religion of his people, except that he did not begin to confront them with this. He informed him that he was his son, and the mother of Abraham informed him that he was his son, and informed him of what she had done concerning his affair. Azar was delighted by this and rejoiced with great joy. Azar used to make the idols of his people, which they worshipped, and then give them to Abraham to sell. Abraham would go with them, it is claimed, and say: *"Who will buy what harms him and does not benefit him?"* and no one would buy them from him. When they became unsaleable to him, he would take them to a river, turn their heads downward into it, [[In the printed edition and manuscript: "fadaraba fihi ru'usaha" (he struck their heads in it), and the correct reading is from the History. "Sawwaba ru'usaha" means he inverted them.]] and say: *"Drink!"* – mocking his people and what they were upon of misguidance – until his reproach of them and his mockery of them spread among his people and the people of his town, without that reaching Nimrod the king. [[The report: 13464 – This report Abu Ja'far related in his history at length, 1:119–120.]]

* *

Abu Ja'far said: Some people, not from the people of transmission, rejected this account which is related from Ibn 'Abbas and from those from whom he related, that Abraham said to the star or to the moon, "This is my lord." They said: It is not permissible that a prophet whom God sent with a message should, at any time while he was adult, be other than one who affirms the oneness of God, knows Him, and is free from everything worshipped besides Him. They said: If it were permissible that some time had passed over him while he was an unbeliever, it would not be permissible for Him to single him out with prophethood, because there is no meaning in him that does not also exist in others among the people of disbelief in Him; and there is no kinship between God and any of His creatures, such that He would favour him by singling him out with honour. They said: He honoured whoever He honoured among them only for his excellence in himself, and He rewarded him because he deserved the reward, by what He rewarded him with of honour. They claimed that God's report of the saying of Abraham when he saw the star or the moon or the sun, "This is my lord," was not because of his ignorance that it was impermissible for it to be his lord; rather he said that in the manner of denial on his part that it could be his lord, and as a rebuke to his people for their worship of idols, since the star, the moon and the sun were brighter, more beautiful and more radiant than the idols, and yet they were not worshipped; and they were setting, passing away and not enduring, whereas the idols which are inferior to them in beauty and smaller than them in body are more deserving of not being worshipped and not being gods. [[In the printed edition and manuscript: "wa-l-asnam allati dunaha fi al-husn," and in the manuscript: "fa-ahaqq," and I saw that the context requires what I have established, with the addition of [*hiya*] between the brackets.]] They said: He only said that to them as a counter-argument, as one of two debaters says to his companion, countering him in a false statement he made with falsehood, in the manner of demanding from him a distinction between the two corrupt statements in his view, of which his opponent affirms one and claims the corruption of the other.

* *

Others among them said: Rather, that was from him in his childhood, [[In the printed edition: "tufuliyyatihi" (his childhood), and I have established what is in the manuscript.]] and before the proof was established against him. That is a state in which there is neither disbelief nor belief.

* *

Others among them said: The meaning of the statement is: "Is this my lord?" in the manner of denial and reproach, meaning: this is not my lord. They said: The Arabs may do the like, omitting the *alif* that indicates the meaning of interrogation. They claimed that among that is the saying of the poet: [[He is Abu Khurash al-Hudhali.]]

*"They soothed me and said: 'O Khuwailid, do not be frightened!' – I said, denying the faces: 'Are they them? Are they them?'"*

[[Diwan al-Hudhaliyyin 2:144; al-Khizanah 1:211; Lisan al-'Arab (rafa') (rafw), and many others. It is the opening of a poem of his concerning a wild ass that he drove on its legs; he described that and praised its running. His saying "rafawni" means they calmed me, as if his heart had flown off in fragments, so they gathered some of it together to others. It is said: "rafawtuhu min al-ru'b" and "rafa'tuhu."]]

That is: "Are they them?" They said: Among that also is the saying of Aws: [[It is also attributed to al-Aswad ibn Ya'fur al-Nahshali and to al-La'in al-Minqari.]]

*"By your life, I do not know – though I am knowing – whether it is Shu'ayth ibn Sahm or Shu'ayth ibn Minqar."*

[[Sibawayh 1:485; al-Bayan wa-l-Tabyin 4:40–41; al-Kamil 1:384, 2:115; al-Khizanah 4:450; Sharh Shawahid al-Mughni: 51; and many others. Al-Jahiz said: "They mentioned that Hazn ibn al-Harith, one of the Banu al-'Anbar, fathered 'Mihjan,' and Mihjan fathered 'Shu'ayb ibn Sahm,' and his camels were raided, so he came to Aws ibn Hajar seeking help. Aws said to him: 'Or something better than that: I will urge Qays ibn 'Asim for you!' It was said that 'Hazn ibn al-Harith' was 'Hazn ibn Minqar,' so Aws said: 'Ask your patron Qays ibn 'Asim through them, for your patron is a patron of evil unless he changes...' ..." Qays then went after the camels until he returned them all. The verse in al-Jahiz's version contains no witness. In the printed edition throughout, it reads "Shu'ayb" with a ba, which is an error. In the printed edition: "aw Shu'ayb," and the correct reading is "am," as in the manuscript and all the other transmissions.]]

meaning: "Is it Shu'ayth ibn Sahm?" So the *alif* was omitted, and similar cases. As for the masculine form of "this" in His saying, "So when he saw the sun rising, he said, 'This is my lord,'" it is only according to the meaning: "This rising thing is my lord."

* *

Abu Ja'far said: In God's report of the saying of Abraham when the moon set – "Unless my Lord guides me, I will surely be among the misguided people" – there is evidence of the error of these statements which those people made, and that the correct view in this matter is to affirm God's report which He related concerning him, and to turn away from whatever else there is. [[See also al-Farra', Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1:341.]]

As for His saying, "When it set," its meaning is: when it disappeared and went away, as:

13465 – Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Salamah ibn al-Fadl related to us, saying: Ibn Ishaq said: "*al-Uful*" means going away.

It is said of this: "*afala al-najm yafulu wa-yafilu ufulan wa-fulan*," when it set, and from it is the saying of Dhu al-Rummah:

*"Lamps which are not led by the stars, nor by the setting, circling ones."*

[[His Diwan: 425; Majaz al-Qur'an of Abu 'Ubaydah 1:199; al-Azminah 2:49; Kitab al-Qirtain 1:261; Lisan al-'Arab (dalk), from a long qasidah in which he described camels; this verse is a description of camels. "Masabih" is the plural of "misbah," and "al-misbah" is the one that is awake in its resting place and does not graze until the day rises, which is a praised quality in camels, due to their strength and fatness. He says: they are not stars that set, but camels.]]

It is said: "*Ayna afalta 'anna*," meaning: where have you gone from us? [[This is a metaphor that you will hardly find in any other book.]]

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 6, verse 77–78:

On the words of Him, exalted is He: ﴿So when he saw the moon rising, he said, "This is my lord." But when it set, he said, "Unless my lord guides me, I will surely be among the misguided people."﴾ (77)

Abu Ja'far said: He, exalted is His remembrance, says: When the moon rose and Abraham saw it rising, and this is its "buzugh" (rising).

* *

It is said of it: "bazaghat al-shams tabzughu buzugh (the sun rose, rising)", meaning it rose, and likewise the moon.

* *

"He said, 'This is my lord,' then when it set," meaning: when it disappeared, "he said," Abraham, "Unless my lord guides me," and grants me success in reaching the truth in His oneness, "I will surely be among the misguided people," i.e., among the people who erred from the truth in this matter, so they did not attain guidance, and worshipped other than God.

* *

We have already explained the meaning of "misguidance" (al-dalal) in another place, in a way that makes repeating it here unnecessary. [[See the explanation of "al-dalal" in the earlier lexical indexes: (ḍ-l-l).]]

* *

On the words of Him, exalted is He: ﴿So when he saw the sun rising, he said, "This is my lord; this is greater." But when it set, he said, "O my people, indeed I am free from what you associate."﴾ (78)

Abu Ja'far said: He, exalted is His remembrance, means by His words [the word "bi-qawlihi" ("by His words") is absent from the manuscript and the printed edition, and it is indeed the correct continuation of the discourse] "So when he saw the sun rising": when Abraham saw the sun rising, he said: This rising one is my lord. "This is greater," meaning: this is greater than the star and the moon. The object was omitted because the context indicates it. "But when it set," meaning: when it disappeared, Abraham said to his people, "O my people, indeed I am free from what you associate," i.e., from worshipping the gods and idols and calling upon anything as a god alongside God, exalted is His remembrance. [[See the explanation of "bari'" earlier, p. 293.]]

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 6, verse 77–78:

On the words of Him, exalted is He: ﴿So when he saw the moon rising, he said, "This is my lord." But when it set, he said, "Unless my lord guides me, I will surely be among the misguided people."﴾ (77)

Abu Ja'far said: He, exalted is His remembrance, says: When the moon rose and Abraham saw it rising, and this is its "buzugh" (rising).

* *

It is said of it: "bazaghat al-shams tabzughu buzugh (the sun rose, rising)", meaning it rose, and likewise the moon.

* *

"He said, 'This is my lord,' then when it set," meaning: when it disappeared, "he said," Abraham, "Unless my lord guides me," and grants me success in reaching the truth in His oneness, "I will surely be among the misguided people," i.e., among the people who erred from the truth in this matter, so they did not attain guidance, and worshipped other than God.

* *

We have already explained the meaning of "misguidance" (al-dalal) in another place, in a way that makes repeating it here unnecessary. [[See the explanation of "al-dalal" in the earlier lexical indexes: (ḍ-l-l).]]

* *

On the words of Him, exalted is He: ﴿So when he saw the sun rising, he said, "This is my lord; this is greater." But when it set, he said, "O my people, indeed I am free from what you associate."﴾ (78)

Abu Ja'far said: He, exalted is His remembrance, means by His words [the word "bi-qawlihi" ("by His words") is absent from the manuscript and the printed edition, and it is indeed the correct continuation of the discourse] "So when he saw the sun rising": when Abraham saw the sun rising, he said: This rising one is my lord. "This is greater," meaning: this is greater than the star and the moon. The object was omitted because the context indicates it. "But when it set," meaning: when it disappeared, Abraham said to his people, "O my people, indeed I am free from what you associate," i.e., from worshipping the gods and idols and calling upon anything as a god alongside God, exalted is His remembrance. [[See the explanation of "bari'" earlier, p. 293.]]

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 6, verse 79:

The interpretation of His saying: ﴿Indeed, I have turned my face toward He who created the heavens and the earth, inclining toward truth, and I am not of those who associate others with Allah﴾ (6:79).

Abu Ja'far said: This is a report from Allah, may He be remembered, about His friend Ibrahim, peace be upon him: that when the truth became clear to him and he recognized it, he bore witness to the testimony of truth and openly opposed his people, the people of falsehood and the people of association with Allah. He was not deterred by the blame of any blamer, nor did he feel lonely in speaking the truth and holding firm to it, despite the opposition of all his people to his words and their rejection of him. He said to them: "O my people, indeed I am free of what you associate" with Allah, who created me and created you, in worship of your gods and idols. [See the explanation of "fatara" in what has preceded, pp. 283, 284.] "Indeed, I have turned my face in my worship toward He who created the heavens and the earth, the Eternal who remains and does not perish, who gives life and causes death, not toward one who perishes and does not remain, who passes away and does not endure, and who neither harms nor benefits."

Then Allah, may He be remembered, informed them that his turning of his face to worship Him was by sincerely devoting worship to Him and being upright in that toward his Lord according to what He loves of monotheism, not in the manner of one who turns his face toward something without being hanif, rather being a associator. [See the explanation of "hanif" in what has preceded, 3:104-108, 6:494, 9:250.] For turning the face without hanifiyyah is not beneficial to the one who turns toward it, but rather harmful and destructive to him. "And I am not of the associators" means: I am not one who follows your religion or adopts your creed, O polytheists.

* *

And Ibn Zayd used to say something similar to what we have said regarding this:

13465 - Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, regarding the words of Ibrahim's people to Ibrahim, "Have you abandoned the worship of these?" He said: "Indeed, I have turned my face toward He who created the heavens and the earth." They said: "You have brought nothing! We worship Him and turn toward Him!" He said: "Not hanifan!" He said: sincerely, not associating Him as you associate.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 6, verse 80:

Discourse on the interpretation of His saying: ﴿And his people argued with him. He said: "Do you argue with me concerning God when He has already guided me? I do not fear what you associate with Him, unless my Lord wills something. My Lord encompasses all things in knowledge. Will you not then take heed?"﴾ (6:80)

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: May His remembrance be exalted, He says: Ibrahim argued with his people concerning the oneness of God and His freedom from idols [see the explanation of "al-muhajjah" (disputation) in earlier volumes: 3:121, 5:429, 430, 6:280, 473, 492]. Their argument with him was their saying that their gods, which they worshipped, were better than his God. Ibrahim said: "Do you argue with me concerning God," meaning: Do you dispute with me about my affirming the oneness of God and my sincerity in worship toward Him alone, without anything else that is worshipped besides Him? "When He has already guided me," meaning: My Lord has already granted me success in knowing His oneness and has shown me the path of truth, until I became certain that nothing deserves to be worshipped besides Him [in the printed edition and the manuscript it reads "until I came to know that nothing deserves to be worshipped besides Him," which makes no sense; the correct reading is what has been given here]. "And I do not fear what you associate with Him," meaning: I do not dread your gods that you invoke besides Him, nor any harm of theirs that might reach me in myself by way of evil or injury. [In the printed edition it reads "reaches me in myself" without "with it" (bihi), which is present in the manuscript; the editor, having misread "yanalni," deleted it.] That is because they said to him: "We fear that our gods will touch you with evil, such as leprosy or madness, because of your speaking ill of them!" So Ibrahim said to them: I do not fear those gods you associate with God, that they might reach me with harm or injury, because they neither benefit nor harm. "Unless my Lord wills something," meaning: But my fear is of God, who created me and created the heavens and the earth; if He wills to reach me in myself or my property with whatever He wills, whether death or life, increase or decrease, or otherwise, He will reach me with it, for He is capable of that.

* *

Ibn Juraij used to say in accordance with what we have said:

13466 - Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Juraij: "His people argued with him. He said: Do you argue with me concerning God when He has already guided me?" He said: His people invoked other gods alongside God and threatened him with their gods, that some madness would befall him from them. Ibrahim said: "Do you argue with me concerning God when He has already guided me?" He said: I have come to know my Lord; I do not fear what you associate with Him.

* *

"My Lord encompasses all things in knowledge," meaning: My Lord knows every thing, so nothing is hidden from Him [see the explanation of "al-si'ah" (encompassing) in earlier volumes: 10:423, note 4, and the references there], because He is the Creator of all things, unlike the gods, which neither harm nor benefit, nor understand anything; they are merely carved wood and a fashioned image. "Will you not then take heed?" meaning: Will you not reflect, O ignorant ones, so that you understand the error in which you persist, [see the explanation of "al-tadhakkur" (taking heed) in earlier volumes, p. 442, note 1, and the references there], in worshipping an image that is formed and carved wood, which can neither harm nor benefit, nor comprehend or understand anything, and in abandoning the worship of Him who created you and created all things, in whose hand is good, who has power over all things, and who knows all things.

**The interpretation (ta'wil) of His words:** ﴿And how should I fear what you have associated, while you do not fear that you have associated with God that for which He has sent down to you no authority? So which of the two parties is more deserving of security, if you know?﴾ (6:81)

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: This is Abraham's reply to his people when they frightened him about their gods, that they might harm him because he had spoken ill of them and mentioned them with disparagement. He said to them: "How should I fear and be afraid of what you have associated in your worship with your Lord, and worshipped besides Him, when it neither harms nor benefits? If they could benefit or harm, they would have defended themselves against my breaking them and my striking them with the axe!" "And you do not fear God, who created you and provided for you, and who is able to benefit and harm you, for associating with Him in worship what He has not sent down to you any authority for": that is, He has not given you any proof for associating others with Him in worship, nor set for you any evidence concerning it, nor given you any excuse for it. [[See the explanation of "authority" (sultan) in what has preceded: 7:279; 9:336, 337, 360.]] "So which of the two parties is more deserving of security": he means: I am more deserving of security from the consequence of worshipping my Lord, sincerely devoted to Him in worship, upright in my religion, free from the worship of idols and images, or are you, who worship besides God idols for which God has given you no proof or argument for your worship of them? [[See the explanation of "security" (al-amn) in what has preceded: 3:29; 4:87.]] "If you know": he says: if you know the truth of what I say and the reality of what I argue against you, then say and inform me: which of the two parties is more deserving of security?

* *

And in a manner similar to what we have said concerning this, Muhammad ibn Ishaq used to say:

13467 – Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Salama related to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ishaq said concerning His words: "And how should I fear what you have associated, while you do not fear that you have associated with God..." He says: How should I fear an idol that you worship besides God, which neither harms nor benefits, while you do not fear Him who harms and benefits, when you have set up with Him partners that neither harm nor benefit? "So which of the two parties is more deserving of security, if you know?" That is: security from the punishment of God in this world and the Hereafter: the one who worships He in whose hand is harm and benefit, or the one who worships what neither harms nor benefits? He sets forth for them examples and explains to them lessons, so that they may know that God is more deserving to be feared and worshipped than what they worship besides Him.

13468 – Al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Ishaq related to us, saying: Abdullah ibn Abi Ja'far related to us, from his father, from al-Rabi', who said: God gave Abraham ﷺ victory (aflaja) when he argued with them. [["I aflaja you over your opponent" means I overcame him; and "God aflaja him over it" means He gave him victory, success and triumph.]] So he said: "And how should I fear what you have associated, while you do not fear that you have associated with God that for which He has sent down to you no authority. So which of the two parties is more deserving of security, if you know?" Then He said: "And that was Our argument, which We gave to Abraham against his people." [Qur'an 6:83]

13469 – Al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfa related to us, saying: Shibl related to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, concerning the words of Abraham when he asked them: "Which of the two parties is more deserving of security?" – it is the argument of Abraham ﷺ.

13470 – Muhammad ibn Amr related to me, saying: Abu Asim related to us, saying: Isa related to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, concerning the words of God, may He be remembered, He said: Abraham, when he asked them: "So which of the two parties is more deserving of security?" He said: And it is the argument of Abraham, peace be upon him.

13471 – Al-Qasim related to us, saying: Al-Husayn related to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, from Ibn Juraij, who said: "So which of the two parties is more deserving of security, if you know?" – Who worships one Lord, or who worships many lords? His people say: Those who believe in one Lord. [[Report 13471: see the following report no. 13475, and that this is the statement of the people of Abraham.]]

13472 – Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said concerning His words: "So which of the two parties is more deserving of security, if you know?" – Who fears other than God and does not fear Him, or who fears God and does not fear other than Him? Then God, may He be remembered, said: "Those who believed and did not mix their belief with wrongdoing," [Qur'an 6:82] – the verse.

The commentary of Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) on Surah 6, verse 82 (part 1 of 2):

The explanation of His saying, ﴿Those who believe and do not mix their belief with wrongdoing: for them is security, and they are rightly guided﴾ (6:82).

Abu Ja'far said: The people of ta'wil (interpretation, the explanation of meaning) differed about the one whom God, may He be remembered, reported as having said this statement, namely, "Those who believe and do not mix their belief with wrongdoing," and the verse.

Some of them said: This is God's decisive judgment between Abraham, His friend (ﷺ), and those among his people who argued with him, from among the people of polytheism toward God. When Abraham said to them, ﴿How should I fear what you associate, when you do not fear that you associate with God that for which He has sent down to you no authority? So which of the two parties is more deserving of security, if you know?﴾ (6:81), God, may He be remembered, said, making a separation between him and them: "Those who affirmed God and sincerely devoted worship to Him, and did not mix their worship of Him and their affirmation of Him with wrongdoing" [see the explanation of "mixing" (labs) above, p. 419, note 1, and the references there] — that is, with polytheism [see the explanation of "wrongdoing" (zulm) in the earlier linguistic indexes, root ẓ-l-m] — "and did not associate anything with Him in His worship, and then made their worship exclusively for God, are more deserving of security from His punishment, [the dispraised] (makruh) manner of worshipping their Lord," [in the printed edition, the phrase "their Lord" (rabbahum) is omitted], "[compared] to those who associate in their worship of Him idols and statues. For they are the ones who fear His punishment, [for] the dispraised manner of their worship." As for the immediate world, they are anxious about the descent of God's wrath upon them; and as for the Hereafter, they are certain of the painful punishment of God.

Those who said this:

13473 — Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salama ibn al-Fadl narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ishaq narrated to us, saying: God, may He be remembered, says: "Those who believe and do not mix their belief with wrongdoing," that is: those who were sincere as Abraham (ﷺ) was sincere in the worship of God and in His oneness; "and did not mix their oaths with wrongdoing," that is, with polytheism; "for them is security, and they are rightly guided": the security is from punishment, and the guidance is in the proof, through knowledge and steadfastness. God, may He be remembered, says: ﴿And that was Our argument, which We gave to Abraham against his people. We raise in degrees whom We will; indeed your Lord is Wise and Knowing﴾ (6:83).

13474 — Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, concerning His saying, ﴿So which of the two parties is more deserving of security, if you know?﴾ (6:81): He said, "God said, and judged between them: ﴿Those who believe and do not mix their belief with wrongdoing﴾," He said: "with polytheism." He said: ﴿for them is security, and they are rightly guided﴾. As for sins, no one is free of them.

* * *

Others said: This is the answer of Abraham's people to Abraham when he said to them: "Which of the two parties is more deserving of security?" So they said to him: Those who believed in God and affirmed His oneness are more deserving of security, if they did not mix their belief with wrongdoing.

Those who said this:

13475 — Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: Al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, concerning ﴿So which of the two parties is more deserving of security, if you know?﴾ (6:81): "Who worships one Lord, or who worships many lords?" His people say: ﴿Those who believe and do not mix their belief with wrongdoing﴾ — by worshipping idols — and this is the argument of Abraham: ﴿for them is security, and they are rightly guided﴾. [Editor's note on the report: see the earlier report no. 13471.]

* * *

Abu Ja'far said: The more correct of the two views in my judgment is the view of the one who said: This is a report from God, may He be remembered, about the party more deserving of security, and a decisive judgment from Him between Abraham (ﷺ) and his people. This is because if it were the statement of Abraham's people, who worshipped idols and associated them with the worship of God, they would have acknowledged the oneness of God and followed Abraham in what they had opposed him about regarding monotheism. But it is, as I have mentioned, its interpretation at the outset (badiyyan). [In the printed edition: "bad'an" (at the beginning); I have kept what is in the manuscript, which is entirely correct, meaning: first.]

* * *

The people of ta'wil differed about the meaning God intended by His saying, ﴿and did not mix their belief with wrongdoing﴾.

Some said: with polytheism.

Those who said this:

13476 — Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Ibn Idris narrated to us, saying: al-A'mash narrated to us, from Ibrahim, from Alqama, from Abdullah (Ibn Mas'ud), who said: When this verse was revealed, "Those who believe and do not mix their belief with wrongdoing," it weighed heavily on the companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). He said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Do you not look at the saying of Luqman: ﴿Indeed, polytheism is a great wrongdoing﴾ (31:13)?" [Editor's note: this is a hadith of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, transmitted through al-A'mash. Al-Tabari transmits it by many routes in nos. 13476–13480, 13483, and see no. 13507. It is also reported by al-Bukhari in his Sahih (al-Fath 1:81, 8:220) in similar wording; by Muslim in his Sahih (2:143, 144) through Abdullah ibn Idris, Abu Mu'awiya, and Waki', all from al-A'mash; by al-Tirmidhi in the Book of Tafsir through Isa ibn Yunus from al-A'mash; and by Ahmad through several routes in his Musnad, nos. 3589, 4031, 4240, which I will indicate later in their takhrij.]

13477 — Abu Kurayb said, Ibn Idris said: he narrated it to me first from my father, from Aban ibn Taghlib, from al-A'mash; then I heard it [again], and it was said to him: "From al-A'mash?" He said: "Yes!" [Editor's note: Muslim also recorded this in his Sahih, 2:144, through Abu Kurayb, in a similar statement to this one. Aban ibn Taghlib al-Rab'i is trustworthy. Ibn Adi said: "He has copies, most of which are sound when a trustworthy narrator transmits from him; he is among the people of truthfulness in transmission, though his creed is Shi'ism, and in transmission he is reliable and acceptable." (Benefit: al-Hafiz (Ibn Hajar) said in al-Tahdhib: "Tashayyu' ('Shi'ism') in the terminology of the earlier scholars means the belief in preferring Ali over Uthman, that Ali was correct in his wars, and that his opponent was mistaken, together with placing the two shaykhs (Abu Bakr and Umar) first and preferring them. Some of them believed that Ali was the best of creation after the Messenger of God (ﷺ). If one holds that belief, while being pious, religious, truthful, and diligent, his narration is not rejected on this account, especially if he was not a propagandist. As for Shi'ism in the terminology of later scholars, it is pure rafd (rejection), so the narration of an extremist rafidi is not accepted, nor is he honored." The reason for mentioning this second report after the first is that Abdullah ibn Idris transmitted it directly from al-A'mash earlier, and had transmitted it earlier from his father, from Aban ibn Taghlib, from al-A'mash, to draw attention to the elevated (high) chain of its transmission.]

13478 — Isa ibn Uthman ibn Isa al-Ramli narrated to me, saying: My paternal uncle Yahya ibn Isa narrated to me, from al-A'mash, from Ibrahim, from Alqama, from Abdullah, who said: When it was revealed, "Those who believe and do not mix their belief with wrongdoing," it weighed heavily on the Muslims. They said: "O Messenger of God, is there not one of us who wrongs himself?" The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "It is not that. Do you not hear the saying of Luqman to his son: ﴿Indeed, polytheism is a great wrongdoing﴾?" [Editor's note: Isa ibn Uthman ibn Isa ibn Abd al-Rahman al-Tamimi al-Ramli is trustworthy; he has passed as no. 300. His uncle Yahya ibn Isa ibn Abd al-Rahman al-Tamimi al-Ramli is trustworthy; he has passed as nos. 300, 6317, 9035.]

13479 — Hannad narrated to us, saying: Waki' narrated to us, from al-A'mash, from Ibrahim, from Alqama, from Abdullah, who said: When this verse was revealed, "Those who believe and do not mix their belief with wrongdoing," it weighed heavily on the companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and they said: "Which of us has not wronged himself?" He said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "It is not as you think; it is only what Luqman said to his son: ﴿Do not associate anything with God; indeed, polytheism is a great wrongdoing﴾." [Editor's note: Ahmad also recorded it in his Musnad, no. 4240, through Waki' as well, with a similar wording.]

13480 — Hannad narrated to us, saying: Abu Mu'awiya narrated to us, from al-A'mash, from Ibrahim, from Alqama, from Abdullah, who said: When this verse was revealed, "Those who believe and do not mix their belief with wrongdoing," it weighed heavily on the people, and they said: "O Messenger of God, and which of us does not wrong himself?" He said: "It is not as you mean. Did you not hear what the righteous servant said: ﴿O my son, do not associate anything with God; indeed polytheism is a great wrongdoing﴾? It is only polytheism." [Editor's note: Ahmad also recorded it in his Musnad, no. 3589, through Abu Mu'awiya, with a similar wording.]

13481 — Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Rahman narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from al-A'mash, from Ibrahim, from Alqama, concerning His saying, ﴿Those who believe and do not mix their belief with wrongdoing﴾, he said: "With polytheism."

13482 — Yahya ibn Talha al-Yarbu'i narrated to me, saying: Fudayl narrated to us, from Mansur, from Ibrahim, concerning His saying, ﴿Those who believe and do not mix their belief with wrongdoing﴾, he said: "With polytheism."

13483 — Ibn Waki' narrated to us, saying: Jarir narrated to us, from al-A'mash, from Ibrahim, from Alqama, from Abdullah, who said: When this verse was revealed, "Those who believe and do not mix their belief with wrongdoing," it weighed heavily on the companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and they said: "Which of us has not mixed his belief with wrongdoing?" The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "It is not that. Did you not hear the saying of Luqman: ﴿Indeed, polytheism is a great wrongdoing﴾?"

13484 — Ibn Waki' narrated to us, saying: Jarir and Ibn Idris narrated to us, from al-Shaybani, from Abu Bakr ibn Abi Musa, from al-Aswad ibn Hilal, from Abu Bakr, concerning ﴿Those who believe and do not mix their belief with wrongdoing﴾, he said: "With polytheism." [Editor's note: "al-Shaybani" is Abu Ishaq al-Shaybani, Sulayman ibn Abi Sulayman, who has passed many times, the last at no. 8869. "Abu Bakr ibn Abi Musa al-Ash'ari" is trustworthy; the group (of compilers) narrated from him; he is the subject of an entry in al-Tahdhib. "Al-Aswad ibn Hilal al-Maharibi," Abu Salam, had some encounter (with the Prophet), emigrated in the time of Umar, and did not meet Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him). He is the subject of an entry in al-Tahdhib, al-Kabir (1/1, 449) and Ibn Abi Hatim (1/1, 292), and has passed as nos. 10331, 10333. This report is mentioned by al-Suyuti in al-Durr al-Manthur (3:27) and attributed to al-Firyabi, Ibn Abi Shayba, al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi in al-Usul, Ibn al-Mundhir, Abu al-Shaykh, and Ibn Mardawayh.]

13485 — Hannad narrated to us, saying: Qabisa narrated to us, from Yunus ibn Abi Ishaq, from Abu Ishaq, from Abu Bakr, concerning ﴿Those who believe and do not mix their belief with wrongdoing﴾, he said: "With polytheism." [Editor's note: the printed edition omitted the words "from Abu Ishaq," and this is a mursal report (one missing a companion in its chain).]

13486 — Hannad narrated to us, saying: Waki' narrated to us, from Sa'id ibn Ubayd al-Ta'i, from Abu al-Ash'ar al-Abdi, from his father, that Zayd ibn Suhan asked Salman, saying: "O Abu Abdullah, a verse from the Book of God has reached me to every extent: ﴿Those who believe and do not mix their belief with wrongdoing﴾!" Salman said: "It is polytheism with God, may He be remembered." Zayd said: "It does not delight me that I had not heard it from you, and that I had in its place everything I possess." [Editor's note on nos. 13486–13487: "Sa'id ibn Ubayd al-Ta'i," Abu al-Hudhayl, was declared trustworthy by Ahmad and Ibn Ma'in; Abu Hatim said: "his hadith is written." He is the subject of an entry in al-Tahdhib, al-Kabir (2/1/455), and Ibn Abi Hatim (2/1/46). "Abu al-Ash'ar al-Abdi" is mentioned by al-Bukhari in al-Kuna (p. 8), who said: "Khalifa ibn Khalaf narrated from him." Abu Nu'aym said, from Isma'il ibn Ubayd, from Abu al-Ash'ar al-Abdi, who heard his father from Salman: ﴿and did not mix their belief with wrongdoing﴾, he said: "with polytheism." Thus "Isma'il ibn Ubayd" appears in this form, and I fear the correct reading is "Sa'id ibn Ubayd," as in al-Tabari, and as in the next report (no. 13487). I do not know who the "father" of Abu al-Ash'ar al-Abdi is. "Zayd ibn Suhan ibn Hijr al-Abdi," brother of "Sa'sa'a ibn Suhan," met the Prophet (ﷺ), is mentioned among the Companions, and had strong love for Salman al-Farisi. He was killed on the Day of the Camel with Ali (may Allah be pleased with both of them). He is the subject of an entry in Ibn Sa'd (6:84), who said "trustworthy, few narrations," in Ta'jil al-Manfa'a (142), in al-Kabir (2/1/363), and in Ibn Abi Hatim (1/2/565). Before the report no. 13486 ends, a section of the old division ends, from which our copy was taken; and in it is the following text: "Followed by: Hannad ibn Waki' narrated to us, saying: My father narrated to us, from Sa'id ibn Ubayd." And may God bless Muhammad the Prophet, his family, and grant them abundant peace. Then after it begins what follows: "In the name of God, the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful. My Lord, help, O Generous One."]

13487 — Ibn Waki' narrated to us, saying: My father narrated to us, from Sa'id ibn Ubayd, from Abu al-Ash'ar, from his father, from Salman, who said: "With polytheism." [Editor's note: see the preceding note.]

13488 — Ibn Bashshar and Ibn Waki' narrated to us, both saying: Abd al-Rahman ibn Mahdi narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, saying: Nusayr ibn Dhu'luq narrated to us, from Kurdus, from Hudhayfa, concerning His saying, ﴿and did not mix their belief with wrongdoing﴾, he said: "With polytheism." [Editor's note: "Nusayr ibn Dhu'luq al-Thawri" is trustworthy; he has passed as no. 5491. "Kurdus" is Kurdus ibn al-Abbas al-Tha'labi, who narrates from Hudhayfa, passed as nos. 13255–13257. In the printed edition it reads "Dirsab," which differs from the manuscript; in the manuscript it reads "Dadus," and this is, God willing, the correct reading. This report is cited by al-Suyuti in al-Durr al-Manthur (3:27), attributed to al-Firyabi, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Abi Shayba, Abu Ubayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Abu al-Shaykh. It will come later with another chain.]

13489 — Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Amr ibn Awn narrated to us, saying: Hushaym informed us, from Abu Ishaq al-Kufi, from a man, from Isa, from Hudhayfa, concerning His saying, ﴿and did not mix their belief with wrongdoing﴾, he said: "With polytheism." [Editor's note: "Abu Ishaq al-Kufi" is Abdullah ibn Maysara al-Harithi, who has passed as no. 9250.]

13490 — Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Arim Abu al-Nu'man narrated to us, saying: Hammad ibn Zayd narrated to us, from Ata' ibn al-Sa'ib, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr and others: that Ibn Abbas used to say: ﴿Those who believe and do not mix their belief with wrongdoing﴾, "with polytheism."

13491 — Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abd Allah ibn Salih narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiya narrated to me, from Ali, from Ibn Abbas, his saying: ﴿Those who believe and do not mix their belief with wrongdoing﴾, he says: "with disbelief."

13492 — Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, saying: My paternal uncle narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas: ﴿Those who believe and do not mix their belief with wrongdoing﴾, he says: "they did not mix their belief with polytheism." And he said: ﴿Indeed, polytheism is a great wrongdoing﴾.

13493 — Nasr ibn Ali al-Jahdami narrated to us, saying: My father narrated to me, saying: Jarir ibn Hazim narrated to us, from Ali ibn Zayd, from al-Musayyib: that Umar ibn al-Khattab recited, "Those who believe and do not mix their belief with wrongdoing." When he recited it he was alarmed, so he came to Ubayy ibn Ka'b and said: "O Abu al-Mundhir, I have recited a verse from the Book of God; who will be safe?" He said: "What is it?" So he recited it to him. [He said:] "Which of us does not wrong himself?" He said: "May God forgive you! Did you not hear God, may He be remembered, say: ﴿Indeed, polytheism is a great wrongdoing﴾? It is only: 'and did not mix their belief with polytheism.'" [Editor's note: "from al-Musayyib," so it appears in both the printed edition and the manuscript. I do not know who this is, but I incline to think the correct form is "from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib" or "from Ibn al-Musayyib," since Ali ibn Zayd ibn Jud'an narrates from him, and I did not find anyone named "al-Musayyib" from whom Ali ibn Zayd narrated, and who narrated himself from Umar ibn al-Khattab.]

13494 — Ibn Waki' narrated to us, saying: Yazid ibn Harun narrated to us, from Hammad ibn Salama, from Ali ibn Zayd ibn Jud'an, from Yusuf ibn Mihran, from Ibn Abbas: that Umar entered his house and read in the Mushaf (the written Qur'an). He passed by this verse, "Those who believe and do not mix their belief with wrongdoing," so he went to Ubayy and informed him. He said: "O Commander of the Faithful, it is only polytheism." [Editor's note: "Yusuf ibn Mihran al-Basri" has passed as no. 2858 and 11373.]

**Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on Surah 6, verse 82 (part 2 of 2):**

13495. Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: al-Hajjaj ibn al-Minhal narrated to us, saying: Hammad narrated to us, from Ali ibn Zayd, from Yusuf ibn Mihran, from [Ibn Mihran]: that Umar ibn al-Khattab, whenever he entered his house, would open the Mushaf (the codex of the Qur'an) and recite it. One day he entered and recited, and came to this verse: ﴿Those who believed and did not mix their belief with wrongdoing, those will have security, and they are guided.﴾ He turned away and took his cloak [[In the printed edition: "fa-ishtaghal," and in the manuscript "fa-isqal," and in al-Durr al-Manthur 3:27 "fa-intaqal," which has no meaning; the correct reading seems to be what is recorded here. One says "inftala al-rajul 'an salatihi" (the man turned away from his prayer) when he departs, and it derives from their saying "eftalahu 'an wajhihi fa-inftala," meaning he turned him away from his face and he turned away.]] Then he came to Ubayy ibn Ka'b and said: "O Abu al-Mundhir," and he recited this verse: ﴿Those who believed and did not mix their belief with wrongdoing﴾, and said: "And you see that we do wrong, and we do this and that!" He said: "O Commander of the Faithful, this is not that. Allah, may His remembrance be exalted, says: ﴿Indeed, association [with Allah] is a tremendous wrong﴾; it is only that, shirk." [[The report 13495: this is how it came in the manuscript: "from Ibn Mihran," while in the printed edition: "from Mihran." Both are, in my judgment, an error of scribal alteration. This is in fact the report of Ibn Abbas, so the correct reading, God willing, is "from Ibn Abbas," and it is the same report as the one before it. I have left it as it is in the manuscript and placed what I doubt between brackets.]]

13496. Hannad narrated to us, saying: Ibn Fudayl narrated to us, from Mutarrif, from Abu Uthman Amr ibn Salim, who said: Umar ibn al-Khattab recited this verse: ﴿Those who believed and did not mix their belief with wrongdoing﴾, and Umar said: "Successful is the one who did not mix his belief with wrongdoing!" Then Ubayy said: "O Commander of the Faithful, that is shirk!"

13497. Ibn Wakic narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from Muhammad ibn Mutarrif, from Ibn Salim, who said: Umar ibn al-Khattab recited, and he mentioned something similar. [[The reports 13496 and 13497: "Abu Uthman, Amr ibn Salim al-Ansari" is known by his kunya (teknonym), and he has passed under number 8950. His statement in the second report, "Muhammad ibn Mutarrif," is, in my judgment, an error; it is in fact "Mutarrif ibn Tarif," as in the earlier report. For that reason I placed "Muhammad ibn" between brackets.]]

13498. Muhammad ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Rahman narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from Abu Ishaq, from Abu Maysara, concerning His saying: ﴿and did not mix their belief with wrongdoing﴾, he said: "With shirk."

13499. Ibn Wakic narrated to us, saying: my father narrated to us, from Sufyan, from Abu Ishaq, from Abu Maysara, the like of it.

13500. Ibn Wakic narrated to us, saying: Husayn narrated to us, from Ali, from Za'idah, from al-Hasan ibn Ubayd Allah, from Ibrahim: ﴿and did not mix their belief with wrongdoing﴾, he said: "With shirk." [[The report 13500: "al-Hasan ibn Ubayd Allah al-Nakha'i al-Kufi," who narrated from Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, Abu al-Duha, and al-Sha'bi. Al-Thawri, Za'idah, Hafs ibn Ghiyath and others heard from him. He is trustworthy (thiqah), and he passed in the chain under number 78. He is biographed in al-Tahdhib, al-Kabir 1/2/295, and Ibn Abi Hatim 1/2/23. In the printed edition and the manuscript it was: "al-Hasan ibn Abd Allah," which is a pure error.]]

13501. Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Yazid ibn Zuray' narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, concerning His saying: ﴿Those who believed and did not mix their belief with wrongdoing﴾, that is: "with shirk."

13502. Ibn Wakic narrated to us, saying: Humayd narrated to us, from his father, from Abu Ishaq, from Abu Maysara, the like of it.

13503. Muhammad ibn Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu Asim narrated to us, saying: Isa narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: ﴿Those who believed and did not mix their belief with wrongdoing﴾, he said: "With the worship of idols."

13504. Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, the like of it.

13505. Muhammad ibn al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Ahmad ibn al-Mufaddal narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: ﴿and did not mix their belief with wrongdoing﴾, he said: "With shirk."

13506. Yunus ibn Abd al-A'la narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said concerning His saying: ﴿and did not mix their belief with wrongdoing﴾: "With shirk."

13507. Muhammad ibn Abd al-A'la narrated to me, saying: Muhammad ibn Thawr narrated to us, from Ma'mar, from al-A'mash: that Ibn Mas'ud said: "When this was revealed: ﴿and did not mix their belief with wrongdoing﴾, it weighed heavily on the Muslims, and they said: 'O Messenger of Allah, is there not one of us who wrongs himself?' The Prophet ﷺ said: 'Have you not heard the saying of Luqman: ﴿Indeed, association [with Allah] is a tremendous wrong﴾?'" [[The report 13507: this report has passed connected through the chain of al-A'mash, through several routes, from number 13476 to 13480, 13483, so refer to it there.]]

13508. Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Hakkam narrated to us, from Anbasah, from Muhammad ibn Abd al-Rahman, from al-Qasim ibn Abi Bazzah, from Mujahid concerning His saying: ﴿and did not mix their belief with wrongdoing﴾, he said: "The worship of idols."

13509. Ibn Wakic narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Bishr narrated to us, from Mis'ar, from Abu Husayn, from Abu Abd al-Rahman, who said: "With shirk." [[The report 13509: "Abu Husayn" is Uthman ibn Asim ibn Husayn al-Asadi, who has passed many times, the last of them under number 8962. "Abu Abd al-Rahman" is al-Sulami: Abd Allah ibn Habib ibn Rabi'ah, who has passed under number 82.]]

13510. Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salamah narrated to us, saying: Ibn Ishaq said: ﴿and did not mix their belief with wrongdoing﴾, he said: "With shirk."

* *

Others said: Rather, the meaning of that is: "and did not mix their belief with any of the meanings of wrongdoing," and that is: doing what Allah has forbidden doing, or abandoning what Allah has commanded doing. They said: the verse is general, because Allah did not restrict it to any one meaning of wrongdoing.

* *

They said: If someone says to us: "Is there then no security in the Hereafter except for those who have not disobeyed Allah in a minor or major matter, and except for those who meet Allah with no sin?"

We say: Allah meant by this verse a particular one among His creation, not all of them. The one He meant by it and intended by it is His intimate friend Ibrahim ﷺ. As for others, when one meets Allah without associating anything with Him, he is subject to His will, if he has committed some of the sins that do not amount to disbelief; if He wills, He does not grant him security from His punishment, and if He wills, He bestows His grace upon him and pardons him.

They said: This is the view of a group of the early predecessors (al-salaf), although they differed about who is meant by the verse.

Some of them said: Ibrahim is meant by it.

* *

Others said: The Emigrants (al-Muhajirun) among the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ are meant by it. [[In the printed edition: "al-Muhajirin," with "ini" (was meant) in the passive form; I have kept what is in the manuscript, "ini" in the passive.]]

* *

Mention of those who said: the verse is meant for Ibrahim, Khalil al-Rahman (the Intimate Friend of the Merciful) ﷺ.

13511. Ibn Wakic narrated to us, saying: Yahya ibn Yaman and Humayd ibn Abd al-Rahman narrated to us, from Qays ibn al-Rabi', from Ziyad ibn Ilaqah, from Ziyad ibn Harmalah, from Ali, who said: "This verse is for Ibrahim ﷺ specifically; this community has no share of it." [[The report 13511: "Ziyad ibn Ilaqah ibn Malik al-Tha'labi," trustworthy, from whom the main compilers narrated. He is biographed in al-Tahdhib, al-Kabir 2/1/333, and Ibn Abi Hatim 1/2/540. As for "Ziyad ibn Harmalah," I have found no mention of him in any of the books; nevertheless, he appears as such in al-Mustadrak of al-Hakim. This report was narrated by al-Hakim in al-Mustadrak 2:316, with his chain from Abu Hudhayfah, from Sufyan, from Ziyad ibn Ilaqah, from Ziyad ibn Harmalah, who said: "I heard Ali ibn Abi Talib," and he mentioned the report, and in it: "This is about Ibrahim and his companions." Then al-Hakim said: "This is a hadith with a sound chain, but the two (Bukhari and Muslim) did not record it; they agreed only on the hadith of al-A'mash, from Ibrahim, from Alqamah, from Abd Allah, that they said: 'O Messenger of Allah, which of us has not wronged himself?' the hadith in full, without this interpretation." Al-Dhahabi did not comment on it at all, and I think he left the comment in hope of finding a report about this "Ziyad ibn Harmalah." The report is weak, because of the unknown status (jahalah) of "Ziyad ibn Harmalah," until it is known who he is. Al-Suyuti attributed it in al-Durr al-Manthur 3:27 to al-Firyabi, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, al-Hakim, and Ibn Mardawayh, and he abbreviated its attribution to Ibn Jarir (al-Tabari).]]

* *

Mention of those who said: it is meant specifically for the Emigrants.

13512. Ibn Wakic narrated to us, saying: Yahya ibn Yaman and Humayd ibn Abd al-Rahman narrated to us, from Qays ibn al-Rabi', from Sammak, from Ikrimah: ﴿Those who believed and did not mix their belief with wrongdoing﴾, he said: "It is for those who emigrated to Medina."

* *

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: The more correct of the two views is that which is sound from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and it is the report which Ibn Mas'ud narrated from him, that he said: "The wrongdoing which Allah, may His remembrance be exalted, mentioned in this place is shirk." [[See the earlier reports, numbers 13476 to 13480, 13483.]]

* *

As for His saying: ﴿those will have security, and they are guided﴾, He means: these are the ones who believed and did not mix their belief with shirk; ﴿for them is security﴾ on the Day of Resurrection from the punishment of Allah; ﴿and they are guided﴾, meaning: they are those who hit upon the path of right direction and who travel the road of salvation. [[See the explanation of "guidance" (al-huda) in the preceding linguistic indexes under the root (h-d-y).]]

The commentary on the words of God: ﴿And that was Our argument which We gave Abraham against his people. We raise by degrees whom We will. Indeed, your Lord is Wise and Knowing﴾ (6:83).

Abu Ja'far said: By His words, "And that was Our argument," God, may His remembrance be exalted, means Abraham's statement to his disputing polytheist people: "Which of the two groups is more deserving of security? Is it the one that worships one God, sincerely devoting to Him the religion and the worship, or the one that worships many lords?" Their answer, saying, "Rather, the one that worships one God is more deserving of security," was their judgment against themselves. In that was the cutting off of their excuse, the severing of their argument, and the prevalence of Abraham's argument over them.

[[Praise be to God who sent down the Book with truth, and if it had been from other than God, people would have found in it much inconsistency. May God have mercy on Abu Ja'far and forgive him his errors. Abu Ja'far, despite his great standing, his memorization, his precision and his diligence, contradicted himself and produced a great inconsistency in his speech. In p. 494, he preferred that the correct reading of God's words, "those who believed and did not mix their belief with wrongdoing" (6:82), is that it is a report from God, may His remembrance be exalted, about the first of the two groups to be secure, and a decisive judgment from Him between Abraham and his people. Then he said: "That is because if it had been the statement of Abraham's people, who worshipped idols and associated them with the worship of God, they would have acknowledged monotheism and followed Abraham in what they opposed him on regarding monotheism. But it is, as you have mentioned, its interpretation from the beginning." Then he returned here after a few pages and explained this verse, claiming that it was the answer of Abraham's people to Abraham, which is the very statement he had refuted!! This is a clear contradiction, but such things occur in the books of scholars, as a proof from God upon His creation that they have no infallibility in anything, and that infallibility belongs to God alone, glorified be He.]] So this is the argument that God gave Abraham against his people, as in what was narrated:

13513 – Al-Harith narrated to me, saying: Abd al-Aziz narrated to us, saying: Sufyan al-Thawri narrated to us, from a man, from Mujahid, regarding "And that was Our argument which We gave Abraham against his people": he said, "It is 'those who believed and did not mix their belief with wrongdoing.'"

13514 – Al-Harith narrated to me, saying: Abd al-Aziz narrated to us, saying: Yahya ibn Zakariya narrated to us, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid, who said: Abraham said when he asked, "Which of the two groups is more deserving of security?" – he said: this is the argument of Abraham. As for His words, "And We gave it to Abraham against his people," it means: We guided Abraham to it, made him see it, and made him know it, "against his people. We raise by degrees whom We will."

* * *

The readers differed regarding the recitation of this.

The majority of the readers of Hijaz and Basra recited, "narfa'u darajati man nasha'" with the word "darajat" put in the genitive by annexation to "man," meaning: We raise the degrees of whom We will.

* * *

The majority of the readers of Kufa recited "narfa'u darajatin man nasha'" with tanwin on "darajat," meaning: We raise whom We will by degrees.

* * *

"Darajat" is the plural of "daraja," which means rank. Its origin is the steps of a ladder and its rungs, and then it is used for elevation of abodes and ranks. [[See the explanation of "daraja" above in 4:523–536, 7:368, 9:95, and its explanation here is clearer than what preceded.]]

* * *

Abu Ja'far said: The correct view on this, in my opinion, is to say: these are two readings, and leading readers have recited each of them, and their meanings are close. For whoever has his rank raised has been raised in degrees, and whoever is raised in degrees has had his rank raised. So whichever of the two a reader recites, he has hit the correct answer on this matter.

* * *

Thus the meaning of the speech is: "And that was Our argument which We gave Abraham against his people," so We raised his rank over them by it, and honored him over them with it in this world and the Hereafter. As for in this world, We gave him his reward in it; and as for the Hereafter, he is among the righteous. "We raise by degrees whom We will," meaning by what he did of that and other things.

* * *

As for His words, "Indeed, your Lord is Wise and Knowing," He means: indeed your Lord, O Muhammad, is "Wise" in His governance of His creation, and in His instructing His prophets with arguments against their disbelieving nations who denied monotheism toward their Lord, and in other than that of His management. "Knowing" of what the affair of His messengers and those they were sent to will lead to, whether nations remain upon their denial of them and perish upon it, or turn back in repentance by monotheism of God, may His remembrance be exalted, and by confirming His messengers, and return to His obedience. [[See the explanation of "wise" (hakim) and "knowing" (alim) above in the linguistic indexes.]]

* * *

God, may His remembrance be exalted, says to His Prophet (ﷺ): So take as a model, [["Ta'assa bihi" means he made him a model for himself in his person and conduct. In the printed edition it was "ta'assa," which has the same meaning, and I have confirmed what is in the manuscript.]] O Muhammad, in yourself and your people who deny you and the polytheists, the father of my intimate friend Abraham (ﷺ), and be patient with what befalls you from them with his patience. For I am knowing of what your affair and their affair will lead to, and Wise in managing you and them. [[In the printed edition and the manuscript it reads "bi-l-tadbir" without the conjunction waw, and the correct reading is to include it.]]

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 6, verse 84:

The interpretation of His saying: ﴿And We gave him Isaac and Jacob; each We guided, and Noah We guided before, and among his descendants David and Solomon and Job and Joseph and Moses and Aaron. Thus do We reward the good-doers﴾ (6:84).

Abu Ja'far said: He, exalted is His mention, says: We recompensed Abraham (ﷺ) for his obedience to Us, his sincerity in the Oneness of his Lord, and his separation from the religion of his polytheist people, by raising his rank in ʿIlliyyin, giving him his reward in this world, and granting him children whom We singled out for prophethood, and a descendant whom We honoured with nobility from Us and whom We preferred over the worlds. [[See the explanation of "wahb" (gift) above, 6:212.]] Among them: his son Isaac, and his grandson Jacob. ﴿Each We guided﴾: He says, We guided them all to the path of right guidance, and granted them success in the truth and the correct religion. [[See the explanation of "kull" (each) above, 9:96, note 1, and the references there.]] ﴿And Noah, We guided before﴾: He says, and We guided him to the same truth and rightness to which We guided Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and We granted him success in it, Noah, before Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.

* *

﴿And among his descendants David﴾: the pronoun in His saying "his descendants" refers to Noah. This is because Allah, exalted is His mention, mentioned in the context of the verses following this verse Lot, saying: "And Ishmael and Elisha and Jonah and Lot, and each We preferred over the worlds." It is known that Lot was not a descendant of Abraham (peace be upon them all). Since that is so, and since he was joined to the names of those we have named from his descendants, there is no doubt that if the "descendants" were meant as the descendants of Abraham, Jonah and Lot would not have been included among them. And there is no doubt that Lot is not a descendant of Abraham, but he is a descendant of Noah; therefore the pronoun in "descendants" must refer to Noah. [[See the explanation of "dhurriyyah" (descendants) above, 3:19, 73; 5:54; 6:327, 362; 8:19.]]

So the meaning of the statement is: And Noah, We granted him success in the truth and rightness before Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and We also guided from the descendants of Noah: David and Solomon.

= As for "David", he is David son of Ishai [[Written "Yasa" in the people's book; and it has passed in the tafsir (5:355) as "son of Ishi".]]. = "Solomon" is his son: Solomon son of David. = "Job" is Job son of Mus son of Razah [[In the printed and manuscript texts: "Ruh", and the correct form is from Tarikh al-Tabari 1:165.]] son of Eis son of Isaac son of Abraham. = "Joseph" is Joseph son of Jacob son of Isaac son of Abraham. = "Moses" is Moses son of Imran son of Yashhar son of Qahath son of Levi son of Jacob. = "Aaron", the brother of Moses.

* *

﴿Thus do We reward the good-doers﴾: He, exalted is His mention, says: We rewarded Noah for his patience under what he was tested with concerning Us, by guiding him and granting him success in reaching the truth from which We withheld those who disobeyed Us and opposed Our command among his people; and We guided from his descendants after him, from among the prophets He mentioned, to the same thing to which We guided him.
