Just as We rewarded these for the goodness of their obedience to Us and their patience under Our trials, so We reward every good-doer with goodness. [[See the explanation of "al-jaza'" (recompense) and "al-ihsan" (goodness) in the language indices above (root j-z-y, h-s-n).]]

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 6, verse 85:

The interpretation of His saying: ﴿And Zechariah, and John, and Jesus, and Elias; each of them was of the righteous﴾ (85)

Abu Ja'far said: He, exalted is His remembrance, says: And We also guided, to the same guidance and rectitude that We gave to Noah, from his descendants: Zechariah son of Iddo son of Berechiah, [[In the book of the people (ibn ʿIddū (in "Ezra", chapters 5 and 6. In the printed edition: "ibn Azn", and in the manuscript: "ibn Adr". The author of Qamus al-Kitab said: "Zechariah son of Berechiah ibn Iddo... he is mentioned as 'son of Iddo', and the reason for this is most likely that his father Berechiah died in the prime of youth, so he was attributed, according to custom, to his grandfather 'Iddo', who was more famous than his father." In the book of the people (Berechiah (, and in the printed edition it was "Barkiya", and in the manuscript the writing is not clear, so I have established what is in the History of al-Tabari 2: 13.]] and John son of Zechariah, and Jesus son of Mary, daughter of ʿImran son of Yashhum son of Amun son of Hezekiah, [[In the printed edition: "ʿImran son of Ashim son of Amur", an error; its correct form is from what preceded, 6: 328, 329, and from the History of al-Tabari 2: 13.]] = and Elias.

* *

They differed concerning "Elias."

Ibn Ishaq used to say: he is Elias son of Yasin [[In the History of al-Tabari 2: 13, "ibn Yasin".]] son of Phinehas son of al-ʿIzar son of Aaron son of ʿImran, the nephew of Moses, Prophet of Allah (ﷺ).

* *

Others said: he is Idris. Among those who reported this from him was ʿAbdullah ibn Mas'ud.

13515 - Muhammad ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Abu Ahmad narrated to us, saying: Israel narrated to us, from Abu Ishaq, from ʿUbaydah ibn Rabiʿah, from ʿAbdullah ibn Mas'ud, who said: "Idris" is "Elias", and "Israel" is "Jacob". [[The report 13515: "ʿUbaydah ibn Rabiʿah", a Kufan, who narrated from Ibn Mas'ud and Uthman ibn ʿAffan. Al-Sha'bi and Abu Ishaq al-Sabiʿi narrated from him. He is biographed in al-Tahdhib and Ibn Abi Hatim 3/1/91. "Abu Ishaq" is al-Sabiʿi, as passed, and in the manuscript and printed edition it was "ibn Ishaq", which is a pure error. This report was mentioned by al-Bukhari as a mu'allaq (al-Fath 6: 265), and al-Hafiz said: "As for the saying of Ibn Mas'ud, Ubayd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim connected it through a good chain from him."]]

* *

As for the genealogists, they say: "Idris" is the grandfather of Noah, son of Lamech son of Methuselah son of Enoch, and "Enoch" is "Idris son of Yard son of Mahalalel". Likewise it was narrated from Wahb ibn Munabbih.

* *

What the genealogists say is closer to the truth. That is because God, exalted is His remembrance, in this verse attributed Elias to Noah and made him from his descendants, and Noah is the son of Idris according to the people of knowledge; so it is impossible for the grandfather of his father to be described as being from his descendants.

* *

As for His saying "each of them was of the righteous," it means: those of these we have named, Zechariah, John, Jesus and Elias, peace be upon them, were "of the righteous." [[See the interpretation of "kull" in what preceded, p. 507, note 2, and the reference there.]] [[See the interpretation of "al-salih" in the language indexes of what preceded (ṣ-l-ḥ).]]

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 6, verse 86:

The interpretation of His saying: ﴿And Ishmael, and Elisha, and Jonah, and Lot—and each We preferred over the worlds﴾ (86)

Abu Ja'far said: He, may He be remembered, says: We also guided, from among the offspring of Noah, Ishmael, who is Ishmael son of Abraham; and Elisha (al-Yasa'), who is Elisha son of Akhtub son of al-Ajuz.

* *

The readers differed concerning the reading of his name.

The majority of the readers of the Hijaz and Iraq read it as ﴿wal-Yasa'a﴾ with a single lam, lightened (unstressed).

* *

Some people claimed that it is of the pattern "yaf'alu", from the speaker's saying "wasi'a yasa'u" (to be wide/ample). The Arabs hardly prefix the definite article "al-" (alif and lam) to a noun of this form, that is, "yaf'al". They do not say "ra'aytu al-Yazid" (I saw al-Yazid), nor "atani al-Yahya" (al-Yahya came to me), nor "marartu bi-al-Yashkur" (I passed by al-Yashkur), except in the necessity of poetry, and that also only when praise is intended, as one of them said:

We found al-Walid son of al-Yazid blessed, mighty at the joints of the caliphate is his shoulder.

So he prefixed the "al-" to "al-Yazid", because he had prefixed it to "al-Walid", and so he followed "al-Yazid" with a word of the same form.

* *

Some of the readers of Kufa read it as ﴿wal-Layasa'a﴾ with two lams and with doubling (stressed), and they said: when it is read thus, it resembles non-Arab names, and they rejected the lightened form. They said: we do not know in the speech of the Arabs a noun of the pattern "yaf'al" that has the definite article "al-".

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The correct reading in this matter, in my view, is the reading of whoever reads it with a single lam, lightened, because the scholars of reports agree that this is the well-known form of his name, not the doubled form, and because it is a non-Arabic name, which is pronounced as it is. The prefixing of "al-" is known only in names of Arabs of the "yaf'al" pattern. As for a name that is non-Arabic, it is pronounced as those who named with it pronounced it. If anything in it is altered when the Arabs speak it, it is altered only by straightening a letter of it, without deletion, addition or reduction. And "al-Layasa'" when doubled would acquire an addition that it did not have before doubling. Moreover, no one among the people of knowledge has been transmitted to us as saying that his name is "Layasa'", so that it would be doubled upon the prefixing of the "al-" that is used for definiteness.

* *

And Jonah is: Jonah son of Matta. ﴿And Lot and each We preferred over the worlds﴾, from the offspring of Noah and Noah, to whom We made the truth clear and guided them to it, and We preferred all of them ﴿over the worlds﴾, meaning: over the worlds of their times.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 6, verse 87:

The interpretation of His saying: ﴿And of their forefathers, their descendants, and their brothers. We chose them and guided them to a straight path.﴾

Abu Ja'far said: He, exalted is His remembrance, says: And We also guided some of the forefathers of those whom He, exalted is His remembrance, named, and their descendants and brothers, others besides them whom He did not name, to the truth and the pure religion that has no associating of partners with God, so We granted them success in it. ﴿And We chose them﴾, meaning: We selected them for Our religion and for conveying Our message to those to whom We sent them, just as We chose those We have named.

* *

It is said of this: "So-and-so chose such-and-such for himself" (ijtaba fulan li-nafsihi kadha), when he selects and favours it, "yajtabihi ijtiba'an" (he chooses it, a choosing). [[See the explanation of "ijtaba" in what has preceded, 7:427.]]

* *

Mujahid used to say concerning this:

13516 – Muhammad ibn Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, saying: 'Isa narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding the saying of God, exalted is His remembrance: "and We chose them," he said: We purified them.

13517 – Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfa narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, the same.

* *

﴿And We guided them to a straight path﴾, meaning: We made them firm and directed them to a path that is not crooked, and that is the religion of God which has no crookedness in it, namely Islam, which our Lord, God, approved for His prophets and commanded His servants to follow. [[See the explanation of "al-sirat al-mustaqim" in what has preceded, 10:146, note 2, and the references there.]]

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 6, verse 88:

The interpretation of His words: ﴿That is the guidance of Allah; He guides with it whom He wills of His servants. And if they had associated others with Him, what they used to do would have been lost from them.﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By His words, "That is the guidance of Allah," may He be exalted and remembered, He means: this guidance by which I guided those whom I have named among the prophets and messengers, granting them success through it in reaching the true religion, through reaching which they attained the good pleasure of their Lord, the nobility of this world, and the honour of the Hereafter, is "the guidance of Allah." He says: it is the success and kindness of Allah, by which He grants success to whomever He wills, and shows kindness to whomever He loves of His creatures, until he turns in repentance to obedience to Allah, sincerely directs his deeds to Him, affirms His oneness, and renounces idols and images [see the explanation of "al-huda" (guidance) in the earlier indexes of language, root h-d-y]. "And if they had associated others with Him, what they used to do would have been lost from them," He says: if these prophets whom We have named had associated others with their Lord, may He be exalted and remembered, and worshipped others alongside Him, "it would have been lost from them," He says: it would have been nullified and gone from them, the reward of their deeds which they used to do [see the explanation of "habita" (to be nullified) in the earlier volumes: 4: 317; 6: 287; 9: 592; 10: 409], because Allah does not accept any deed together with associating others with Him.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 6, verse 89:

The interpretation of His saying: ﴿Those are the ones to whom We gave the Book and the judgment and prophethood﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By His saying, may He be exalted, "those" (ulā'ika), He means those whom We have named from among His prophets and messengers: Noah and his descendants, whom He guided to the religion of Islam and chose for His message to His creation. They are "the ones to whom We gave the Book," meaning by that the scrolls of Abraham and Moses, the Psalms of David, and the Gospel of Jesus, may the blessings of God be upon them all. "And the judgment" means understanding of the Book and knowledge of the rulings contained in it. It has been related from Mujahid concerning this:

13518 - Al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Muslim ibn Ibrahim related to us, saying: Aban related to us, saying: Malik ibn Shaddad related to us, from Mujahid: "And the judgment and the prophethood," he said: "The judgment" is the lubb (intellect).

[[The report: 13518 - "Muslim ibn Ibrahim al-Azdi al-Farahidi," who has passed many times, the last at no. 7487.

And "Aban" is "Aban ibn Yazid al-Attar," who has passed at nos. 3832, 9656.

"Malik ibn Shaddad" is thus in the printed edition and the manuscript, and I have not found mention of him in the books available to me; perhaps it is a corruption of something I do not know.]] Mujahid, God willing, meant what I have said, because "lubb" is "reason," so it is as if he meant that God gave them reason through the Book, which has the same meaning as what we said, that it is understanding through it.

* *

We have already explained the meaning of "prophethood" and "judgment" earlier, with their evidences, so that suffices and there is no need to repeat it. [[See the explanation of "prophethood" earlier: 2:140–142; 6:284, 380.

And the explanation of "judgment" earlier: 3:86–88; 6:211, 538.]]

* *

The interpretation of His saying: ﴿If these disbelieve in them, then We have entrusted them to a people who are not disbelievers in them﴾

Abu Ja'far said: He, may He be exalted, says: "If he disbelieves": O Muhammad, in the signs of My Book which I have sent down to you, so these polytheists who equate others with their Lord deny them, as in what was related:

13519 - Ali ibn Dawud related to me, saying: Abu Salih related to us, saying: Mu'awiya ibn Salih related to me, from Ali ibn Abi Talha, from Ibn Abbas: "If these disbelieve in them," means: if they disbelieve in the Qur'an.

* *

Then the people of interpretation differed concerning who is meant by "these."

Some of them said: By them are meant the disbelievers of Quraysh, and by His saying, "then We have entrusted them to a people who are not disbelievers in them," the Ansar are meant.

Those who said this:

13520 - Muhammad ibn Bashshar related to us, saying: Sulayman related to us, saying: Abu Hilal related to us, from Qatada, concerning the saying of God, may He be exalted: "If these disbelieve in them," he said: the people of Mecca. "Then We have entrusted them": the people of Medina.

13521 - Ibn WakI' related to us, saying: Ubayda ibn Sulayman related to us, from Juwaybir, from al-Dahhak: "Then We have entrusted them to a people who are not disbelievers in them," he said: the Ansar.

13522 - Al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Ishaq related to us, saying: Abd al-Rahman ibn Mughra' related to us, from Juwaybir, from al-Dahhak: "If these disbelieve in them," he said: if the people of Mecca disbelieve in them. "Then We have entrusted them": the people of Medina, the Ansar. "Who are not disbelievers in them."

13523 - Muhammad ibn al-Husayn related to us, saying: Ahmad ibn al-Mufaddal related to us, saying: Asbat related to us, from al-Suddi: "If these disbelieve in them," he says: if Quraysh disbelieve in them. "Then We have entrusted them": the Ansar.

13524 - Al-Qasim related to us, saying: Al-Husayn related to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, from Ibn Juraij: "If these disbelieve in them," the people of Mecca. "Then We have entrusted them to a people who are not disbelievers in them," the people of Medina.

13525 - Muhammad ibn Sa'd related to me, saying: My father related to me, saying: My paternal uncle related to me, saying: My father related to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas, his saying: "If these disbelieve in them, then We have entrusted them to a people who are not disbelievers in them," he said: The people of Medina had already settled the abode and the faith before the Messenger of God (ﷺ) came to them. When God sent down the signs to them, the people of Mecca denied them. So God, may He be exalted, said: "If these disbelieve in them, then We have entrusted them to a people who are not disbelievers in them." Ata said: I did not hear this from Ibn Abbas, but I heard it from someone else. [[The report: 13525 - "Ata" is "Ata ibn Sa'd al-Awfi," the grandfather of "Muhammad ibn Sa'd" on the upper side, and he has been explained in the commentary of this chain at no. 305.]]

13526 - Al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Abu Salih related to us, saying: Mu'awiya related to me, from Ali ibn Abi Talha, from Ibn Abbas: "If these disbelieve in them," meaning the people of Mecca. He says: if they disbelieve in the Qur'an. "Then We have entrusted them to a people who are not disbelievers in them," meaning the people of Medina and the Ansar.

* *

Others said: The meaning is: If the people of Mecca disbelieve in them, then We have entrusted them to the angels.

Those who said this:

13527 - Ibn WakI' related to us, saying: Abu Usama related to us, from Awf, from Abu Raja': "If these disbelieve in them, then We have entrusted them to a people who are not disbelievers in them," he said: They are the angels.

13528 - Ibn Bashshar related to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ja'far, Ibn Abi Adi and Abd al-Wahhab related to us, from Awf, from Abu Raja', the like of it.

* *

Others said: By His saying, "If these disbelieve in them," He means Quraysh; and by His saying, "then We have entrusted them to a people," He means the prophets whom He named in the verses that preceded this verse.

Those who said this:

13529 - Bishr ibn Mu'adh related to us, saying: Yazid ibn Zurai' related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatada, his saying: "If these disbelieve in them," meaning the people of Mecca, "then We have entrusted them to a people who are not disbelievers in them," and they are the eighteen prophets whom God said of: "Those are the ones whom God guided, so follow their guidance."

13530 - Muhammad ibn Abd al-A'la related to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Thawr related to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatada: "If these disbelieve in them," he said: meaning the people of Muhammad. Then he said: "Then We have entrusted them to a people who are not disbelievers in them," meaning the prophets whose stories were recounted before this verse. Then he said: "Those are the ones whom God guided, so follow their guidance."

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The most correct of these opinions in the interpretation of this is the saying of the one who said: By His saying, "If these disbelieve in them," the disbelievers of Quraysh are meant, and by "then We have entrusted them to a people who are not disbelievers in them," He means the eighteen prophets whom God, may He be exalted, named in the verses before this verse. That is because the report about them in the verses before it has passed, and in those after it they are mentioned, so what lies between them being a report about them is more fitting and more worthy than being a report about others.

* *

So the interpretation of the speech, since it is so, is: If your people of Quraysh, O Muhammad, disbelieve in Our signs, and deny and reject their reality, then We have entrusted their preservation and charged with upholding them Our messengers and prophets before you, who do not reject their reality nor deny them, but rather affirm them and believe in their truth.

* *

Some of them said: The meaning of His saying, "then We have entrusted them to a people," is: We have provided them to a people.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 6, verse 90:

The interpretation of His words: ﴿Those are the ones whom God guided, so follow their guidance﴾

Abu Ja'far said: God, may His remembrance be exalted, says: "Those" — these people, whom We entrusted with Our signs and who are not disbelievers in them — are the ones whom God guided to His true religion, and who preserved what they were entrusted to preserve of the verses of His Book, and upheld its limits, followed its lawful and unlawful, and acted upon what it contains of God's commands and refrained from what it contains of His prohibitions. He, whose praise is great, granted them success in that. ﴿So follow their guidance﴾: God, may His remembrance be exalted, says: So by the deed they performed, the path they travelled, and the guidance We guided them to, and the success We granted them, ﴿follow﴾, O Muhammad. That is: act, take hold of it, and travel it, for it is a deed in which God is pleased, and a path whoever follows it is guided.

* *

This interpretation is in accordance with the view of those who interpreted His words, "For We have entrusted with them a people who are not disbelievers in them," as meaning the prophets named in the preceding verses. This is the view we have chosen in interpreting it.

* *

As for the interpretation of those who held that the people entrusted with them were the people of Medina, or that they were the angels, they made His words, "If these disbelieve in them, We have indeed entrusted with them a people who are not disbelievers in them," a parenthetical clause between the two statements, and then they linked His words, "Those are the ones whom God guided, so follow their guidance," back to His words, "Those are the ones to whom We gave the Book, the judgment and prophethood."

Mention of those who said that:

13531 - Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, regarding His words: "And We gave him Isaac and Jacob" up to His words: "Those are the ones whom God guided, so follow their guidance," O Muhammad.

13532 - Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said regarding His words: "Those are the ones whom God guided," O Muhammad, "so follow their guidance," and do not follow these people.

13533 - Muhammad ibn al-Husayn narrated to me, saying: Ahmad ibn al-Mufaddal narrated to me, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, who said: Then he turned back to the Prophet ﷺ and said: "Those are the ones whom God guided, so follow their guidance."

13534 - Ali ibn Dawud narrated to us, saying: Abd Allah ibn Salih narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiya ibn Salih narrated to me, from Ali ibn Abi Talha, from Ibn Abbas, who said: Then He said, concerning the prophets He named in this verse: "so follow their guidance."

* *

The meaning of "al-iqtida'" (following someone's example) in the speech of the Arabs, regarding a man, is to follow his trail and take hold of his guidance. It is said: "So-and-so yaqdu so-and-so" when he heads toward him and follows his trail; "qidah, qudwah, qidwah, and qidyah" [[In the printed edition: "kutb makan 'qadiyah' and 'qudwah'," which is a clear error, contrary to what is in the manuscript, which is correct.]].

* *

The interpretation of His words: ﴿Say: I do not ask you any wage for it; it is only a reminder to the worlds﴾

Abu Ja'far said: God, may His remembrance be exalted, says to His Prophet Muhammad ﷺ: "Say" to these people to whom I have commanded you to give reminders of My signs, lest a soul be given up for what it has earned, from among the polytheists of your people, O Muhammad: "I do not ask you" for my reminding you, and for the guidance to which I call you, and the Qur'an which I have brought you, any compensation that I might exchange from you for it, or any wage that I take from you. This is nothing from me but a reminder to you, and to everyone who is like you and remains upon falsehood, of God's might lest it descend upon you, and His wrath lest it come down upon you for your polytheism toward Him and your disbelief, and a warning to all of you before a severe punishment, so that you may remember and refrain.

**On the interpretation of His saying: ﴿They did not measure God with His true measure when they said, "God has not revealed anything to a human being."﴾**

Abu Ja'far said: Exalted is He, says: "They did not measure God with His true measure," meaning they did not glorify God as He should be glorified, nor did they exalt Him as He should be exalted. "When they said, 'God has not revealed anything to a human being,'" meaning when they said: God did not send down a Book or any revelation to a human being. [[See the explanation of "basharun" (human being) in what has preceded: 6:538 / 10:152.]]

* *

The interpreters (ahl al-ta'wil) differed concerning who was meant by His saying, "When they said, 'God has not revealed anything to a human being,'" and concerning the interpretation of this.

Some of them said: The one who said this was a man from the Jews.

* *

Then they differed concerning the name of that man.

Some of them said: His name was Malik ibn al-Sayf.

* *

Others said: His name was Fanhas.

* *

They also differed concerning the occasion on which he said this.

* *

Mention of those who said that the one who said this was Malik ibn al-Sayf:

13535 – Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Ya'qub al-Qummi narrated to us, from Ja'far ibn Abi al-Mughira, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: A man from the Jews, called Malik ibn al-Sayf, came disputing with the Prophet (ﷺ). The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "I adjure you by Him who sent down the Torah to Moses: do you not find in the Torah that God hates the fat rabbi?" He was a fat rabbi. He became angry and said: "By God, God has not revealed anything to a human being!" His companions who were with him said to him: "Woe to you! Nor to Moses?" He said: "By God, God has not revealed anything to a human being!" So God revealed: ﴿They did not measure God with His true measure when they said, "God has not revealed anything to a human being." Say: "Who revealed the Book that Moses brought?"﴾, to the end of the verse.

13536 – Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: Al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Juraij, from Ikrima, concerning His saying: ﴿They did not measure God with His true measure when they said, "God has not revealed anything to a human being."﴾ He said: It was revealed concerning Malik ibn al-Sayf, who was from Qurayza, one of the rabbis of the Jews. ﴿Say﴾, O Muhammad, ﴿"Who revealed the Book that Moses brought, as light and guidance for mankind?"﴾, to the end of the verse.

* *

Mention of those who said it was revealed concerning Fanhas the Jew:

13537 – Musa ibn Harun narrated to me, saying: Amr ibn Hammad narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, concerning ﴿They did not measure God with His true measure when they said, "God has not revealed anything to a human being."﴾ He said: Fanhas the Jew said: "God has not revealed anything to Muhammad!"

* *

Others said: Rather, it refers to a group of Jews who asked the Prophet (ﷺ) for signs like the signs of Moses.

Mention of those who said this:

13538 – Hannad narrated to us, saying: Yunus narrated to us, saying: Abu Ma'shar al-Madani narrated to us, from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi, who said: Some people from the Jews came to the Prophet (ﷺ) while he was sitting with his knees raised [muhtabin], and they said: "O Abu al-Qasim, will you not bring us a Book from heaven, as Moses brought tablets carried from God?" So God revealed: ﴿The People of the Book ask you to bring down for them a Book from heaven. Indeed, they asked Moses for something greater than that, when they said, "Show us God openly."﴾ [Qur'an 4:153], to the end of the verse. Then a man from the Jews knelt down and said: "God has not revealed anything to you, nor to Moses, nor to Jesus, nor to anyone!" So God revealed: ﴿They did not measure God with His true measure.﴾ Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: They did not know how God [should be described]. [[In the printed and manuscript editions: "ma 'alimu kayfa Allah", as it stands, and it is a very strange expression which I almost reject, and I fear it may be a distortion; it is an explanation of the verse, i.e., "qadaru Allah" (they measured God).]] ﴿when they said, "God has not revealed anything to a human being." Say: "Who revealed the Book that Moses brought as light?"﴾ Then the Messenger of God (ﷺ) loosened his sitting posture and began to say: "Nor to anyone!" [[The report 13538: this report was not mentioned in the interpretation of the verse in Surat al-Nisa' (9:356–358), and this is one of the ways in which Abu Ja'far abridged his exegesis.]]

13539 – Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatada, concerning ﴿They did not measure God with His true measure when they said, "God has not revealed anything to a human being,"﴾ up to His saying ﴿playing in their discourse﴾: They are the Jews and the Christians, a people to whom God gave knowledge, but they did not follow it, did not act upon it, and did not practise it, so God censured them for that conduct. It was reported to us that Abu al-Darda' used to say: "Among the things I am most likely to be disputed with tomorrow is being asked: 'O Abu al-Darda', you have known; so what did you do with what you knew?'" [[In the printed edition: "fa-lam yahtadu" (they were not guided), and I have kept what is in the manuscript.]]

13540 – Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abdullah ibn Salih narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiya narrated to me, from Ali ibn Abi Talha, from Ibn Abbas, concerning His saying: ﴿They did not measure God with His true measure when they said, "God has not revealed anything to a human being,"﴾ meaning: from the Children of Israel. The Jews said: "O Muhammad, has God revealed a Book to you?" He said: "Yes!" They said: "By God, God has not sent down any Book from heaven!" He said: So God revealed: ﴿Say, O Muhammad: "Who revealed the Book that Moses brought, as light and guidance for mankind,"﴾ to His saying ﴿nor your fathers﴾. He said: God revealed it.

* *

Others said: This is a report from God, exalted is His praise, concerning the polytheists of Quraysh, that they said: ﴿"God has not revealed anything to a human being."﴾

Mention of those who said this:

13541 – Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: Al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, saying: Ibn Juraij said: Abdullah ibn Kathir said that he heard Mujahid say: ﴿They did not measure God with His true measure when they said, "God has not revealed anything to a human being,"﴾ — it was said by the polytheists of Quraysh. He said: As for His saying: ﴿"Say: Who revealed the Book that Moses brought as light and guidance for mankind? You make it into scrolls, showing some and concealing much,"﴾ [[This is one of the two readings of the verse, with the yā' in all of them: "yaj'aluna-hu", "yubdunaha", "yukhfuna", and it differs from our reading in our Mushaf; Abu Ja'far will mention it below.]] he said: They are the Jews who show it and conceal much. He said: As for His saying: ﴿"You were taught what neither you nor your fathers knew,"﴾ he said: This is addressed to the Muslims.

13542 – Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abdullah ibn Salih narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiya narrated to me, from Ali ibn Abi Talha, from Ibn Abbas, concerning His saying: ﴿They did not measure God with His true measure,﴾ he said: They are the disbelievers, who did not believe in God's power over them. Whoever believes that God is over all things powerful has measured God with His true measure, and whoever does not believe this has not measured God with His true measure.

13543 – Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfa narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, concerning ﴿They did not measure God with His true measure﴾: he says: the polytheists of Quraysh.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The most correct of these opinions in the interpretation of this is the view of the one who said that the intended meaning of His saying ﴿They did not measure God with His true measure﴾ is the polytheists of Quraysh. That is because it is in the context of a report about them from the beginning, so that this should also be a report about them is more fitting than that it should be a report about the Jews, when no mention of them has preceded that would connect this with them. Moreover, what is said about the one whom God describes in this verse, that he denied that God had revealed any of the Books to a human being, is not something the Jews profess; rather, the well-known belief of the Jews is the acknowledgement of the scrolls of Abraham and Moses and the Psalms of David. And since [the narration that the speaker was a man from the Jews] has not come [to us] with a sound, connected chain of narration, [[In the printed and manuscript editions: "wa-idha lam yakun bi-ma rawa hadha al-khabar", which is not a correct expression; its correct form is what I have written, God willing, i.e., "wa-idha lam ya'ti bi-ma rawa . . . khabar sahih" (and if there has not come with what was narrated . . . a sound report).]] stating that the one who said it was a man from the Jews; and there is no consensus (ijma') among the interpreters that it was so; and the report from the beginning of the sūra to this point is a report about the polytheists who worship idols; and His saying ﴿They did not measure God with His true measure﴾ is connected to that, not separated from it [[The context: "wa-idha lam ya'ti bi-ma rawa . . . khabar sahih . . . wa-la kana . . . wa-kana al-khabar . . . wa-kana qawluhu," all of these are coordinated successive clauses; the answer to "wa-idha lam ya'ti" is "lam yajuz" (it is not permissible).]] it is not permissible for us to claim that this has been diverted from what it is connected to, except by a proof that must be accepted, either from a report or from reason.

But I think that those who interpreted this as a report about the Jews found His saying: ﴿"Say: Who revealed the Book that Moses brought as light and guidance for mankind, which you make into scrolls, showing some and concealing much, and you were taught what neither you nor your fathers knew"﴾, and they directed the interpretation of it toward the people of the Torah, reading it in the form of direct address to them: ﴿you make it into scrolls, showing some and concealing much, and you were taught what neither you nor your fathers knew.﴾ [[This is the second reading of the verse, and it is the reading in our Mushaf today.]] So they made the beginning of the verse a report about them, since its ending was, in their view, an address to them. Yet other interpretation and reading are more fitting to the revelation, for the reason I described earlier: that His saying ﴿They did not measure God with His true measure﴾ is in the context of a report about the polytheists of the Arabs and idol-worshippers, and it is connected to it. Therefore it is more proper that this should be a report about them.

The more correct reading of His saying ﴿you make it into scrolls, showing some and concealing much﴾ is with the yā' (they make it), not with the tā' (you make it), in the sense that the Jews make it into scrolls, showing some and concealing much; and the address in His saying ﴿Say: Who revealed the Book?﴾ is to the polytheists of Quraysh. This is the meaning that Mujahid intended, God willing, in the interpretation of this, and thus he used to recite it.

13544 – Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Al-Hajjaj ibn al-Minhal narrated to us, saying: Hammad narrated to us, from Ayyub, from Mujahid, that he used to recite this word: ﴿they make it into scrolls, showing some and concealing much.﴾

* *

On the interpretation of His saying: ﴿Say: Who revealed the Book that Moses brought as light and guidance for mankind, which you make into scrolls, showing some and concealing much?﴾

[[I have written the verse in the reading of our Mushaf, although Abu Ja'far's exegesis afterwards follows the other reading. Let the reader of the tafsir be attentive to the point of disagreement as Abu Ja'far set it out: pp. 524, 525.]] God, exalted is His remembrance, says to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ): "Say", O Muhammad, to the polytheists of your people who say to you: "God has not revealed anything to a human being." Say: "Who revealed the Book that Moses brought as light?", meaning: clarification and illumination out of the darkness of error [[See the explanation of "al-nur" (light) in what has preceded: 10:338, note 2, and the references there.]], "and guidance for mankind", meaning: a clear explanation for mankind, by which they distinguish truth from falsehood in what has become unclear to them of the matters of their religion [[See the explanation of "al-huda" (guidance) in what has preceded, in the lexical indexes under h-d-y.]], "which you make into scrolls, showing them".

* *

As for him who reads it as ﴿taj'aluna-hu﴾ (you make it), he takes it as addressed to the Jews, according to the interpretation I have explained from those who interpreted it in that way.

* *

As for him who reads it with the yā' ﴿yaj'aluna-hu﴾ (they make it), its interpretation in his reading is: its people make it into scrolls. The speech about "yubdunaha" (they show them) follows the mention of "al-qararis" (the scrolls), and what is meant is what is written in the scrolls: they show much of what they write in the scrolls, displaying it to the people, and they conceal much of what they record in the scrolls, keeping it secret and hiding it from the people. [[See the explanation of "al-qirtas" (scroll) in what has preceded, pp. 365, 366.]]

* *

Among what they concealed from them was what was in it concerning Muhammad (ﷺ) and his prophethood, as in the following:

13545 – Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfa narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: "scrolls, showing them and concealing much": the Jews.

13546 – Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: Al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Juraij, from Ikrima: "Say, O Muhammad: 'Who revealed the Book that Moses brought as light and guidance for mankind? You make it into scrolls, showing them,'" meaning the Jews, because of what they displayed of the Torah, "and concealing much", of what they hid concerning the mention of Muhammad (ﷺ) and what was revealed to him. Ibn Juraij said: Abdullah ibn Kathir said that he heard Mujahid say: "They make it into scrolls, showing them and concealing much": he said: They are the Jews, who show them and conceal much.

* *

On the interpretation of His saying: ﴿And you were taught what neither you nor your fathers knew. Say: "God." Then leave them in their idle discourse, playing.﴾ (6:91)

Abu Ja'far said: Exalted is His remembrance, says: God taught you, by the Book He sent down to you, what you did not know of the reports of those before you, and the tidings of those after you, and what is to occur at your return on the Day of Resurrection. "Nor did your fathers know", meaning: your fathers did not know it, O believers in God from among the Arabs and in His Messenger (ﷺ), as in the following:

13547 – Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Al-Hajjaj ibn al-Minhal narrated to us, saying: Hammad narrated to us, from Ayyub, from Mujahid: "And you were taught", O company of the Arabs, "what neither you nor your fathers knew."

13548 – Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: Al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Juraij, who said: Abdullah ibn Kathir said that he heard Mujahid say concerning His saying: "And you were taught what neither you nor your fathers knew": he said: This is for the Muslims.

* *

As for His saying: "Say: God", it is a command from God, exalted is His praise, to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) to answer the question he asked of these polytheists, about which he was commanded to ask them: "Say: Who revealed the Book that Moses brought as light and guidance for mankind, which you make into scrolls, showing them and concealing much?" [[This is the other reading, which Abu Ja'far chose; I have left his explanation as it is, so that the speech is not confused for its reader.]] by the saying "God." [[His saying "bi-qili Allah" (by the saying "God") is connected to "an yujib" (that he answer).]] This is like His command to him in another place in this sūra, in His saying: ﴿Say: "Who rescues you from the darknesses of land and sea, when you call upon Him humbly and in secret, saying, 'If He rescues us from this, we will surely be among the grateful.'"﴾ [Qur'an 6:63]. [[I have also left this verse as in Abu Ja'far's reading which he chose, "la-in anjaytana", as passed on p. 414; but our reading in our Mushaf is "la-in anjana". See what passed of Abu Ja'far's preference for one of the two readings over the other.]] So He commanded him to ask the polytheists about that, just as He commanded him to ask them when they said: "God has not revealed anything to a human being": "Who revealed the Book that Moses brought as light and guidance for mankind?" Then He commanded him to answer that there, by His saying: ﴿Say: "God rescues you from them and from every distress, yet you associate others with Him."﴾ [Qur'an 6:64], just as He commanded him to answer here about that by His saying: "God revealed it to Moses," as in the following:

13549 – Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Salih narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiya narrated to me, from Ali ibn Abi Talha, from Ibn Abbas: "Say: Who revealed the Book that Moses brought as light and guidance for mankind?" He said: God revealed it. [[The report 13549: this is an abridgement of the earlier report, no. 13540.]]

* *

Had it been said that its meaning is: "Say: He is God," as a command from God to him to report that, and not as an answer, since His saying "Say: Who revealed the Book?" was not a question from the polytheists to Muhammad (ﷺ), so that His saying "Say: God" would be an answer to their question; rather it is a command from God to Muhammad to ask the people: "Who revealed the Book?", then the answer from them would have to be other than what Ibn Abbas said in his interpretation. It would have been permissible, because it is a question, and a question has no answer requiring a response — and this is what we have chosen in the explanation of that, for the reasons we have given.

* *

As for His saying, "Then leave them in their discourse, playing," He is saying to His Prophet Muhammad ﷺ: "Then leave these polytheists, who equate their Lord with idols and images," [[See the explanation of "leave" (dhar) above, p. 441, footnote 1, and the references there.]] after your argument against them in their saying, "Allah has not sent down anything upon a human being," by your saying, "Who sent down the Book that Moses brought, as a light and guidance for the people," and your reply to that: that the One who sent it down is Allah, who sent down His Book to you. "In their discourse" means in what they engage in of their falsehood, their disbelief in Allah, and His signs. [[See the explanation of "discourse" (khawd) above, vol. 9, p. 320; vol. 11, p. 436.]] "Playing" means they mock and ridicule. [[See the explanation of "playing" (la'b) above, p. 441, footnote 2, and the references there.]]
* *
This is a threat from Allah to these polytheists and a warning to them. Allah, may His praise be exalted, says: "Then leave them playing, O Muhammad. Indeed, I am watching over them from beyond what they are engaged in of their mockery of My signs (bi-l-marsad), and I will make them taste My might, and I will bring down upon them My wrath if they persist in their error." [[In the printed edition: "wa-tahdid lahum" (and a warning to them). I have adopted what is in the manuscript, which is entirely correct; but the editor changed it to "tahdid" in all the previous instances, and I do not know why.]]

**The interpretation of His words: ﴿And this is a Book We have sent down, blessed, confirming what was before it, that you may warn the Mother of Cities and those around it﴾**

Abu Ja'far said: Exalted is He, says: "And this Qur'an, O Muhammad, is a *Kitab* (Book)."

This is one of the names of the Qur'an. I have explained it, and its meaning, in what preceded, in a way that makes repeating it unnecessary. Its meaning is "written" (*maktub*), so *kitab* is placed in the position of *maktub*. [[See the explanation of *kitab* above, vol. 1, pp. 97, 99.]]

"*Anzalnahu*" (We have sent it down) means: We revealed it to you. "*Mubarak*" (blessed) is on the pattern of *mufa'al*, derived from *barakah* (blessing). [[See the explanation of *mubarak* above, vol. 7, p. 25.]] "*Musaddiq alladhi bayna yadayhi*" (confirming what was before it) means: this Book confirms what preceded it of the Books of God that He sent down to His prophets before you, and does not contradict them [in proof and meaning] [[In the printed edition: "did not contradict them nor report [anything], and it is the meaning of light and guidance," which is a sentence that does not stand. In the manuscript: "did not contradict them nor report and the meaning of light and guidance," which is undotted, and also garbled. I preferred what I have written between the brackets, to fit the context of the meaning.]] "*nuran wa hudan lil-nas*" (a light and guidance for mankind). That is, it is He who sent down to you, O Muhammad, this blessed Book, confirming the Book of Moses, the Book of Jesus, and the other Books of God. But He, exalted is His praise, began the report about it, since a report had already preceded that indicated that it is [from Him and] connected to Him, [[In the printed edition: "what indicates that it is with Him connected," and in the manuscript: "what indicates that it is from origin." I preferred what I have recorded, and added "from" and "to Him" between the brackets, for this is the true meaning, God willing.]] so He said: "And this is a Book We have sent down to you, blessed." Its meaning is: Likewise, We have sent down to you this Book of Mine, blessed, just as We sent down the Torah to Moses as guidance and light.

As for His words "*wa li-tundhira Umm al-Qura wa man hawlaha*" (that you may warn the Mother of Cities and those around it), He says: We have sent down to you, O Muhammad, this Book confirming what came before it of the Books, and that by it you may warn of God's punishment and His might those in Umm al-Qura, which is Mecca, "and those around it," to the east and to the west, of those who ascribe equals to their Lord, taking other gods and rivals, and who deny His messengers, and other kinds of disbelievers.

The people of *ta'wil* (interpretation) have said the like of what we have said about this.

**Mention of those who said that:**

13550. Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Salih narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiyah ibn Salih narrated to me, from Ali ibn Abi Talhah, from Ibn Abbas regarding His words "that you may warn the Mother of Cities and those around it": By "the Mother of Cities" is meant Mecca, "and those around it" are the towns to the east and the west.

13551. Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, saying: My uncle narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas regarding His words "that you may warn the Mother of Cities and those around it": "the Mother of Cities" is Mecca, "and those around it" is the whole earth.

13552. Muhammad ibn Abd al-A'la narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Thawr narrated to us, saying: Ma'mar narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding "that you may warn the Mother of Cities": He said: It is Mecca. And with the same chain, from Ma'mar, from Qatadah, who said: It reached me that the earth was spread out (*duhiyat*) from Mecca.

13553. Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah regarding His words "that you may warn the Mother of Cities and those around it": We used to hear that the Mother of Cities is Mecca, and we used to hear that the earth was spread out from it.

13554. Muhammad ibn al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Ahmad ibn al-Mufaddal narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: "that you may warn the Mother of Cities and those around it." As for "the Mother of Cities," it is Mecca, and it was only called "the Mother of Cities" because it is the first house that was set up there.

We have already explained in what preceded the reason for which Mecca was called "the Mother of Cities," in a way that makes repeating it in this place unnecessary. [[See the explanation of "Umm al-Qura" above, vol. 1, p. 108, and also see the report no. 6589.]]

**The interpretation of His words: ﴿And those who believe in the Hereafter believe in it, and they are over their prayers ever-vigilant﴾**

Abu Ja'far said: Exalted is He, says: Whoever believes in the arising of the Hour and the return to God in the Hereafter, and confirms reward and punishment, then he believes in this Book which We have sent down to you, O Muhammad, and confirms it, and acknowledges that God sent it down, and he guards the prescribed prayers which God has commanded him to establish, [[See the explanation of "guarding the prayers" above, vol. 5, pp. 167, 168.]] because he is one who warns whoever has received God's threat for disbelieving in it and for His acts of disobedience. Those who deny it and what is in it, and reject it, are only the people who deny the Return and reject the arising of the Hour, because such a person does not hope from God any reward if he acts upon what is in it, nor fear any punishment if he does not refrain from what it commands him to refrain from.

**The interpretation of His words: ﴿And who is more wrong than one who fabricates a lie against God, or says, "It has been revealed to me," when nothing has been revealed to him, or who says, "I will send down the like of what God has sent down"﴾**

Abu Ja'far said: By His words, exalted is His mention, "And who is more wrong than one who fabricates a lie against God," He means: whoever is most mistaken in speech and most ignorant in deed, "than one who fabricates a lie against God", that is: one who invents a falsehood against God, and claims that He sent him as a prophet and dispatched him as a warner, while in his claim he is false, and in his saying he is a liar. [[See the explanation of "fabrication" (*iftira'*) above, p. 296, note 2, and the references there.]]

This is a rebuke from God to the polytheists of the Arabs, and an ascription of ignorance to them, regarding their opposition to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), with the claim of one of them, Abdullah ibn Sa'd ibn Abi Sarh, and the Hanafite Musaylimah, that they had the prophethood, and the claim of the other that he had brought the like of what the Messenger of God (ﷺ) brought. And it is a negation by Him of the fabrication of lies and the claim of falsehood against His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ).

The people of *ta'wil* have differed regarding this.

Some of them said something like what we have said about it.

**Mention of those who said that:**

13555. Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: Al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Ikrimah regarding His words "And who is more wrong than one who fabricates a lie against God, or says, 'It has been revealed to me,' when nothing has been revealed to him": He said: It was revealed about Musaylimah, the brother of the Banu Adi ibn Hanifah, concerning what he used to rhyme-prose and soothsay. "And who says, 'I will send down the like of what God has sent down'" was revealed about Abdullah ibn Sa'd ibn Abi Sarh, the brother of the Banu Amir ibn Lu'ayy. He had been writing for the Prophet (ﷺ), and what he used to dictate was "Mighty, Wise," and he would write "Forgiving, Merciful," and change it. Then he would read to him what he had written, and he would say, "Yes, it is the same." So he turned back from Islam and joined the Quraysh, and said to them: "He used to receive 'Mighty, Wise,' and I would change it, then I would read what I had written," and he would say, "Yes, it is the same!" Then he returned to Islam before the conquest of Mecca, when the Prophet (ﷺ) alighted at Marr. [["Marr" is Marr al-Zahran.]]

Others said: Rather, that was revealed about Abdullah ibn Sa'd specifically.

**Mention of those who said that:**

13556. Muhammad ibn al-Husayn narrated to me, saying: Ahmad ibn al-Mufaddal narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: "And who is more wrong than one who fabricates a lie against God, or says, 'It has been revealed to me,' when nothing has been revealed to him," up to His words "you will be recompensed with the punishment of humiliation." He said: It was revealed about Abdullah ibn Sa'd ibn Abi Sarh. He embraced Islam and used to write for the Prophet (ﷺ). When he dictated to him "Hearing, Knowing," he would write "Knowing, Wise," and when he said "Knowing, Wise," he would write "Hearing, Knowing." He doubted and disbelieved, and said: "If Muhammad is revealed to, then it has been revealed to me, and if God sends it down, then I have sent down the like of what God sent down!" Muhammad said "Hearing, Knowing," and I said "Knowing, Wise"! So he joined the polytheists, and informed on Ammar and Jubayr to Ibn al-Hadrami, or to the Banu Abd al-Dar. They seized them and tortured them until they disbelieved, and Ammar's ear was cut off that day. [["His ear was cut off" means it was severed, and he was called "the one with the cut ear" (*al-Ajda'*). See Ibn Sa'd, vol. 3, p. 181.

In the printed edition and the manuscript it reads: "and Ammar's ear was cut off," taking the word "ear" as masculine, whereas the correct form is feminine; I know of no instance of its being treated as masculine. This is a strange report. Ibn Sa'd in the Tabaqat (vol. 3, p. 181) narrated from Ibn Umar: "I saw Ammar ibn Yasir on the day of Yamamah, upon a rock, having climbed up, calling out: 'O company of Muslims! Are you fleeing from Paradise? I am Ammar ibn Yasir, come to me!' And I was looking at his ear, which had been cut off, and it was swinging, while he fought the fiercest fighting."

Then he said: "Shu'bah said: We did not know that it was struck at Yamamah." So this is a different report, and the well-known version of his report is that it was struck with the Prophet (ﷺ). It seems that this occurred during one of the campaigns.]] Ammar then went to the Prophet (ﷺ) and informed him of what had befallen him, and of the disbelief he had given them. The Prophet (ﷺ) refused to take his side. So God revealed concerning Ibn Abi Sarh, and Ammar and his companions: ﴿Whoever disbelieves in God after his faith, except one who is compelled while his heart is at rest with faith, but whoever opens his breast to disbelief﴾ [Surah al-Nahl, 16:106]. So the one who was compelled is Ammar and his companions, and the one who opened his breast to disbelief is Ibn Abi Sarh. [[The report no. 13556: the right place for this report would have been in the commentary on the verse of Surah al-Nahl, to show that it was also revealed concerning "Abdullah ibn Sa'd ibn Abi Sarh." But Abu Ja'far did not do so, and that is another decisive proof of his abridgement of his commentary.]]

Others said: Rather, the one who said "It has been revealed to me, when nothing has been revealed to him" is Musaylimah the Liar.

**Mention of those who said that:**

13557. Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Yazid ibn Zurayi narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah regarding His words "or says, 'It has been revealed to me,' when nothing has been revealed to him, and who says, 'I will send down the like of what God has sent down'": It was mentioned to us that this verse was revealed concerning Musaylimah. It was mentioned to us that the Prophet of God (ﷺ) said: "I saw in a dream as if there were two gold bracelets on my hands, and they weighed heavily upon me and troubled me. Then it was revealed to me: 'Blow on them.' So I blew on them, and they flew away. So I interpreted them in my dream as the two liars between whom I am: the liar of Yamamah, Musaylimah, and the liar of Sana'a, al-Ansi." And he used to be called "al-Aswad" (the Black). [[The report no. 13557: the report of the dream is narrated by al-Bukhari (al-Fath, 8:69, 70) and Muslim in his Sahih, 15:34.]]

13558. Muhammad ibn Abd al-A'la narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Thawr narrated to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatadah, who said: "It has been revealed to me, when nothing has been revealed to him": He said: It was revealed concerning Musaylimah.

13559. Al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah, and he added in it: And al-Zuhri informed me that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "While I was sleeping, I saw two gold bracelets on my hands, and that weighed heavily upon me, and then it was revealed to me that I should blow on them, so I blew on them and they flew away. So I interpreted that as the liar of Yamamah and the liar of Sana'a, al-Ansi." [[The report no. 13559: see the note on no. 13557.]]

**Abu Ja'far said:** The most correct of the sayings in my view regarding this is that it should be said: God said, "And who is more wrong than one who fabricates a lie against God, or says, 'It has been revealed to me,' when nothing has been revealed to him." There is no disagreement among the scholars of the Ummah that Ibn Abi Sarh was among those who said, "I have said the like of what Muhammad said," and that he apostatized from his Islam and joined the polytheists, so there is no doubt that by that saying he was a fabricator of lies. Likewise there is no disagreement among all that Musaylimah and al-Ansi, the two liars, claimed against God a lie: that He had sent them as prophets, and each of them said that God had revealed to him, and he was lying in his saying. Since this is so, everyone who invented a lie against God, and said in that time or in others, "God has revealed to me," while he was lying in his saying, and God had not revealed anything to him, has entered into this verse. As for the revelation of the verse, it is possible that it was sent down because of some of them, and it is possible that it was sent down because of all of them, and it is possible that by it all the polytheists of the Arabs are meant, since those who said such things were among them and they did not change it. So God reproached them for that, and threatened them with punishment for their leaving off denouncing it; and with their leaving off denouncing it, they were denying His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ), rejecting his prophethood, and repudiating the verses of the Book of God and its revelation. So He, exalted is His praise, said to them: "And who is more wrong than one who claims against Me the prophethood falsely," and said "It has been revealed to me," when nothing had been revealed to him, and yet he says, "God has not sent down anything upon any human being," so his saying contradicts his statement, and he denies what he affirms, and negates what he establishes. Whoever considers this with discernment and intelligence will know that the one who does it lacks reason.

**It has been related from Ibn Abbas that he used to say regarding His words "and who says, 'I will send down the like of what God has sent down'":**

13560. Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, saying: My uncle narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas regarding His words "and who says, 'I will send down the like of what God has sent down'": He said: He claimed that if he willed, he could say the like of it, meaning poetry.

So it seems that Ibn Abbas, in this interpretation of his, along with what al-Suddi interpreted, directs the meaning of the words of the speaker "I will send down the like of what God has sent down" to: "I will send down the like of what God said of poetry." And al-Suddi interpreted it likewise. We have mentioned the report from him earlier in what preceded. [[The report from al-Suddi above, no. 13556, does not mention "poetry," and perhaps Abu Ja'far forgot to write it, or perhaps he meant that this is related in the report of al-Suddi above, even though he did not mention it there.]]

The Interpretation of His Words: ﴿If only you could see when the wrongdoers are in the agonies of death, and the angels are stretching out their hands, saying, "Release your souls!"﴾

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: Exalted is He, says to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ): If only you could see, O Muhammad, when death overwhelms with its pangs those wrongdoers who ascribe equals to their Lord, gods and rivals, who say, "God has not sent down anything upon any human," who fabricate lies against God, claiming that God has revealed to them when nothing has been revealed to them, and who say, "I will send down the like of what God has sent down." [[The manuscript also has the plural here, "wa-l-muftarīn... al-zā'imīn... wa-l-qā'ilīn," while the context requires the singular. But I have left it as it is, because its meaning is clear, although I am inclined to think the correct reading is: "wa-l-muftarī 'alā Allāh kadhiban al-zā'im anna Allāh awḥā ilayhi wa-lam yūḥa ilayhi shay'un, wa-l-qā'il: sa-unzilu mithla mā anzal Allāh."]] You would see them when the agonies of death have overtaken them, the decree of God has come down upon them, and the end of their terms has arrived, while the angels are stretching out their hands, striking their faces and their backs, as He, glorified is His praise, said: ﴿So how will it be when the angels take them, striking their faces and their backs? That is because they followed what angered God and disliked His pleasure﴾ [Muhammad: 27–28]. They say to them: "Release your souls."

The word "al-ghamarāt" is the plural of "ghamra." The "ghamrat" of everything is its abundance and its greater part, and its origin is a thing that overwhelms things and covers them. From this is the saying of the poet: [[He is Bishr ibn Abi Hazim.]]

"Is there anything that saves from the overwhelming ordeals except steadfastness in battle or flight?" [[Sharh al-Mufaddaliyyat: 677; al-Naqa'id: 423; al-Aghani 13: 137; Diwan al-Khansa': 216; al-Lisan (b-r-k); and others. This verse is the last verse of a poem in al-Mufaddaliyyat, and its transmitted reading is "wa-la yunji." "Al-barākā'" (with a fatha or damma on the ba') means standing firm on the battlefield and exertion in fighting; it derives from "al-burūk," for the fighter kneels in his place, meaning he holds firm. In the printed edition it reads "tarāk li-l-qitāl," which is a clear error. In the manuscript it reads "barākā li-l-qitāl," which is also an error.]]

* *

It has been related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning this:

13561 – Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: Ibn 'Abbas said regarding His words, "If only you could see when the wrongdoers are in the agonies of death," that it means the pangs of death.

13562 – I was told by al-Husayn ibn al-Faraj, who said: I heard Abu Mu'adh say: 'Ubayd ibn Sulayman narrated to us, saying: I heard al-Dahhak say regarding His words, "in the agonies of death," that it means the pangs of death.

* *

As for "the angels stretching out their hands" [[In the printed edition: "aydīhim" (their hands); I have adopted what is in the manuscript, which is entirely correct.]], it means extending them. [[See the interpretation of "basṭ al-aydī" in what has preceded, 10: 100, 213.]]

* *

Then the people of interpretation differed concerning the reason for the angels stretching out their hands at that time.

Some of them said in line with what we have said.

Those who said this:

13563 – Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: 'Abd Allah ibn Salih narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiya ibn Salih narrated to me, from 'Ali ibn Abi Talha, from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words: "If only you could see when the wrongdoers are in the agonies of death and the angels are stretching out their hands," he said: This is at the time of death, and "the stretching out" is striking; they strike their faces and their backs.

13564 – Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, saying: My paternal uncle narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words: "If only you could see when the wrongdoers are in the agonies of death and the angels are stretching out their hands," he said: "The angels are stretching out their hands," striking their faces and their backs, while the wrongdoers are in the agonies of death and the Angel of Death is taking them.

13565 – Muhammad ibn al-Husayn narrated to me, saying: Ahmad ibn al-Mufaddal narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: "and the angels are stretching out their hands," striking them.

* *

Others said: Rather, their stretching out of their hands was with punishment.

Those who said this:

13566 – Ibn Wakī' narrated to us, saying: Abu Khalid al-Ahmar narrated to us, from Juwaybir, from al-Dahhak: "and the angels are stretching out their hands," he said: with punishment.

13567 – Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr narrated to us, from Ibn 'Uyayna, from Isma'il ibn Abi Khalid, from Abu Salih: "and the angels are stretching out their hands," with punishment.

* *

Some of the Kufan grammarians interpreted it to mean: "stretching out their hands by releasing their souls." [[This is al-Farra' in Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1: 345.]]

* *

If someone says: What is the meaning of His words "Release your souls," when the souls of the children of Adam are only taken out of the bodies of their owners by the Lord of the worlds? How then are these disbelievers addressed, and commanded at the time of death to release their own souls? If that is so, then it must be that the children of Adam themselves seize the souls of their bodies!

It is said: The meaning of that is different from what you have understood. Rather, it is a command from God, through the tongues of His messengers, who seize the spirits of these people from their bodies, by delivering up to Him the spirits that their Lord had placed in them, and handing them over to His messengers who take them.

* *

The Interpretation of His Words: ﴿Today you will be recompensed with the punishment of humiliation, for what you used to say about God other than the truth, and for being arrogant toward His signs﴾ [6:93].

Abu Ja'far said: This is a report from God, exalted is His praise, about what the messengers of God, who take the souls of these disbelievers, say to them. He informs that they say to their bodies and their companions: "Release your souls" toward the wrath and curse of God, for today you are being repaid for your disbelief in God, for your false speech about Him, for your claim that God revealed to you when He had revealed nothing to you, for your denial that God sent down anything to any human [[In the printed edition and the manuscript: "wa-indhārukum an yakūn Allāh anzal 'alā bashar shay'an," which has no meaning; it is merely a scribal distortion, and the correct reading is what I have adopted.]], and for your arrogance in refusing to submit to the command of God and the command of His Messenger and to obey Him. "The punishment of humiliation" is the punishment of Hell, which humiliates them and abases them, until they recognize the lowliness and degradation of their own souls, as:

13568 – Muhammad ibn al-Husayn narrated to me, saying: Ahmad ibn al-Mufaddal narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: As for "the punishment of humiliation," it is that which humiliates them.

13569 – Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj: "Today you will be recompensed with the punishment of humiliation," he said: the punishment of humiliation, in the Hereafter, "for what you used to do."

* *

When the Arabs intend by "al-hawn" the meaning of "al-hawan" (humiliation), they put a damma on the "ha'," and when they intend by it gentleness, ease, and lightness of burden, they put a fatha on the "ha'." [[See Majaz al-Qur'an by Abu 'Ubayda 1: 200.]] So they say: "He has little hawn of burden," and from it is God's saying: ﴿And the servants of the Most Merciful are those who walk upon the earth in humility (hawnan)﴾ [25:63], meaning: with gentleness, tranquility, and dignity. From it is the saying of Jundal ibn al-Muthanna al-Tuhawi: [[In the printed edition and the manuscript: "al-Muthanna ibn Jundal al-Tuhawi," which is a clear error; it is "Jundal ibn al-Muthanna al-Tuhawi," a Muslim-era rajiz poet who used to satirize al-Ra'i. See Simt al-La'ali p. 644, and others.]]

"And the passing of days has loosened his strength, gently, and every old man has cast away his pride." [[I have not found this rajaz, although I recall it. "Al-asr" means strength. His saying "every old man has cast away his pride" is a metaphor for the old man's incapacity when he reaches old age.]]

From it is the saying of another: [[He is Dhu Jadan al-Himyari; it is also said to be 'Alqama ibn Shurahil ibn Murthad al-Himyari.]]

"Gently, the two of you! Time does not return what has passed; do not perish in grief after those who have died." [[Sirat Ibn Hisham 1: 39; Tarikh al-Tabari 2: 107; al-Aghani 16: 70; Mu'jam ma Ista'jam: 1398; Mu'jam al-Buldan (Baynun) and (Salhun), and al-Lisan (h-w-n); and after the verse: "Where are Baynun, with no eye and no trace, and after Salhun, where people build houses; and after Himyar, when their ostrich was raised, the sands of this age have scattered them into fragments." "Baynun," "Salhun," and "Ghumdan" are among the fortresses of Yemen that were destroyed by Aryat the Abyssinian in the campaign against Yemen; Dhu Jadan mentions them, grieving over what the people of Himyar suffered of humiliation and abasement.]] He means: "Take it easy" (arwidā). [[In the printed edition: "rawdā," which is an error; the correct form is from the manuscript. "Al-irwad" means giving respite, gentleness, and deliberation; from it is said "ruwaydaka," meaning: take your time, be patient, and be gentle.]] It has been transmitted that the fatha on the "ha'" is used in this sense of "humiliation" as well, and they cited as evidence the verse of 'Amir ibn Juwayn: [[Abu Ja'far said this, but it is well known that it belongs to al-Khansa', and it is in her poetry; some verses of al-Khansa's poem are transmitted to 'Amir ibn Juwayn al-Ta'i, so perhaps this is among what is transmitted to him from her poetry. Or perhaps it is from the poetry of 'Amir ibn Juwayn, and was transmitted to al-Khansa'.]]

"He humiliates souls, and the hawn of souls at the time of harshness is more precious to them." [[Diwan al-Khansa' 215; al-Aghani 13: 136; al-Naqa'id 423; al-Lisan (h-w-n). All of them transmit it as "yawm al-karīha abqā lahā" (on the day of the calamity, it is more enduring for them). In the printed edition: "a'lā," and the correct form is from the manuscript.]]

The well-known usage in their speech is to put a damma on the "ha'" when it means humiliation and abasement, as Dhu al-Isba' al-'Adwani said:

"Go away to yourself; my mother is no shepherdess pasturing the she-camels, nor do I close my eyes to humiliation (al-hawn)." [[Sharh al-Mufaddaliyyat: 323 and following; al-Amali 1: 256; al-Lisan (h-w-n); and many others. Abu Ja'far has brought a version mentioned only in al-Lisan, from Ibn Burri; but the transmitters' version is:
"Anni ilayka fa-ummi laysat bi-ra'iya, tar'a al-makhad wa-la ra'yi bi-maghbun.
Inni abiyyun dhu muhafaza, wa-bnu abiyyin abiyyin min abiyyayn.
La yukhriju al-qasr minni ghayra ma biya, wa-la ali-nu li-man la yabtaghi linyi.
'Affun nadud, idha ma khiftu min baladin, hunan, fa-lastu bi-waqqafin 'ala al-hun."
The evidence is in the last verse.]]

That is, "in humiliation." And when it means gentleness, it is with a fatha.

The interpretation of His saying: ﴿And you have certainly come to Us alone, as We created you the first time, and you have left behind you what We bestowed upon you﴾

Abu Ja'far said: This is a report from Allah, may His praise be exalted, about what He will say on the Day of Resurrection to those who ascribe to Him gods and equals. He informs His servants that He will say to them when they come before Him: "You have certainly come to Us alone."

By His saying "alone" (furada), He means solitary, with no wealth with them, no females, no slaves [In the printed edition: "no furniture and no companion," but the correct reading is what is in the manuscript, meaning their wives and their servants. See the following report no. 13571, and see the Tafsir of al-Baghawi (in the margin of Ibn Kathir 3: 361), where he says: "Alone, with no wealth with you, no spouse, no child, and no servant." This is the correct reading, praise be to Allah.] and nothing of what Allah bestowed upon them in the world, "as We created you the first time," naked, uncircumcised, barefoot, just as their mothers bore them, [“Ghulf” is the plural of “aghlaf,” meaning one who has not been circumcised. “Ghurl” is the plural of “aghral,” which likewise means one who has not been circumcised. This is the hadith of Muslim in his Sahih from the hadith of ʿĀʾishah: “People will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection barefoot, naked, and uncircumcised” (17: 192, 193).] and as He created them in their mothers' wombs, with nothing upon them and nothing with them of what they used to boast of in the world.

* *

"Furada" is a plural; its singular is said to be "fard," as the Nabigha of Banu Dhubyan said:

From the wild cows of Wajra, spotted in its legs... lean in its belly, like the polished sword, solitary

[His Diwan: 26, and Lisan (f-r-d), and many others. From his famous ode in which he apologized to al-Nu'man ibn al-Mundhir, saying before it in describing the bull: As if my saddle, when the day passed with us... on the day of al-Jalil, on a single lone wild one.

"Wajra" is a dwelling between Mecca and Basra, a pasture for wild animals and gazelles. "Mawshi akarihu" means its legs have black dots. "Tawi al-masir" means lean in the belly; "masir" is the plural of "masran." It describes the whiteness of the bull and its gleam, as if it were a polished sword freshly burnished.]
"Fard" and "farid" are used just as "wahad," "wahid," and "wahid" are used for the singular of "awhad." The "fard" may also be pluralized as "furad," just as "wahad" is pluralized as "wuhad," and from this is the saying of the poet: [He is Tamim ibn Ubayy ibn Muqbil.]

You see the blue spearheads upon his chest... alone and in pairs, struck down by his neighing

[The verse has already been cited and explained at 7: 543, with a different narration, so refer to it there.]

Yunus al-Jurmi, [This was discussed at 10: 120, note 1, where the mention of "Yunus [al-Harmari]" was made. His case has been problematic, as I mentioned there, and it is established with this that he is "al-Jurmi." I have not found among the early grammarians anyone called "Yunus al-Jurmi," and I mentioned there that "Yunus ibn Habib" was from Dabbah, not Jurm. So perhaps someone who reads this will guide me to the correct view on it, graciously and thankfully.] as reported from him, says: "Furad" is the plural of "fard," as it is said: "Tu'm" and "Tu'am" for the plural. From it are "al-furada," "al-rudafa," and "al-qurana." [In the printed edition: "wal-ghawani," and in the manuscript: "wal-awayi" without dots; the correct reading is what has been established. It is said: "They came qurana," meaning in pairs. Dhu al-Rumma said: "Qurana and ashtatan, and a driver drives them to the water from the far reaches of the wasteland, loosed."] It is said: "a man is fard" and "a woman is fard," if she has no brother. "And the man has become fard, so he is fard, yafrud, furudan," meaning he has become solitary, and he is "fard."

* *

1357​0 - Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: [Ibn Zayd said:] ʿAmr informed me that Ibn Abi Hilal narrated to him that he heard al-Qurazi say: ʿĀʾishah, the wife of the Prophet (ﷺ), recited the saying of Allah: "And you have certainly come to Us alone, as We created you the first time," and she said: "Woe to me! Men and women will be gathered together, looking at each other's private parts!" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "For every person among them on that Day there is a matter that will occupy him." Men will not look at women, nor women at men, for they will be preoccupied with one another. [Report 13570: "ʿAmr ibn al-Harith ibn Yaʿqub al-Ansari al-Misri," trustworthy, mentioned under nos. 1387, 5973, 6889, 10330. As for "Ibn Abi Hilal," he is "Saʿid ibn Abi Hilal al-Laythi al-Misri," trustworthy, mentioned under nos. 1495, 5465.

As for "al-Qurazi," al-Hakim specified him in the chain in al-Mustadrak as "Uthman ibn ʿAbd al-Rahman al-Qurazi," but even with this specification he remains unknown, for I have not found a biography of him or any mention of him in any of the books. In the printed and manuscript editions it was "al-Qurtubi," which is an error. This report was recorded by al-Hakim in al-Mustadrak 4: 565, through the route of "ʿAbd Allah ibn Wahb, from ʿAmr ibn al-Harith," without "Ibn Zayd said," and al-Hakim said: "This is a hadith with a sound chain, though they did not record it," and al-Dhahabi commented: "Sound, but with a break in it." What appears in al-Tabari's chain, "Ibn Zayd said," in my view is an addition by the copyist, because Ibn Wahb narrates directly from ʿAmr ibn al-Harith, as he narrates from ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam, and since Abu Ja'far's chain "Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said" was long, the copyist's pen hastily inserted "Ibn Zayd" in this chain, as the chain of al-Hakim indicates. The break in this chain, as al-Dhahabi pointed out, is, in my preponderant view, that "Uthman ibn ʿAbd al-Rahman al-Qurazi" did not hear from ʿĀʾishah.]

* *

As for His saying: "And you have left behind you what We bestowed upon you," He says: You have left behind, O people, what We gave you power over in the world, which you used to boast of in it, leaving it behind you in the world and not carrying it with you.

This is a rebuke from Allah, may His praise be exalted, to these polytheists for their boasting, with which they used to take pride in their wealth in the world.

* *

Whatever one possesses and gives to another is "khawwaltuhu" [In the printed and manuscript editions: "and whoever possesses other than you…," which is a pure error; the correct reading is what has been established.] It is said of it: "khala al-rajul yakhalu, ash-shadid al-khiyal," with a kasra on the kha, "and he is khail," and from it is the saying of Abu al-Najm:

He gave and did not withhold, and was not made to withhold... a heap of humps from the property of the Giver

[From the Lamiyya of Abu al-Najm in the book al-Taraʾif, and the references there, and it will come in the tafsir at 23: 127 (Bulaq). It is the opening of his rajaz, and before it: "Praise be to Allah, the Bestower, the Generous..." And His saying "heap of humps" means large-humped camels; "kawm" is the plural of "kawma'," a she-camel with a large hump. And "al-mukhawwil," with a kasra on the waw, is Allah, the Provider, the Possessor of strength, the Firm. See my note on the verse in Tabaqat Fuhul al-Shu'ara': 576, note 4.]
It has been mentioned that Abu ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlaʾ used to recite the verse of Zuhayr:

There, if they are asked for wealth, they grant it... and if they are asked, they give, and if they cast lots, they bring forth the best

[His Diwan: 112, and Lisan (kh-b-l) (kh-w-l), and it will come in the tafsir at 23: 127 (Bulaq), and there are many others. From his famous ode in praise of Harim ibn Sinan ibn Abi Haritha and al-Harith ibn ʿAwf ibn Abi Haritha al-Murri, mentioning the generosity of their people in a time of drought, and before it: "When the white year afflicted the people and the eating of noble wealth reached the year of hunger... I saw those in need around their houses, a crowd of them, until the herbs grew..."

"There, if they are made to lend wealth..." (the rest of the line is missing)

The narration other than that of Abu ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlaʾ is: "If they seek to lend wealth, they lend," it is said: "The man asked for a she-camel as a loan, and he was lent one," when he asked to borrow a she-camel so as to benefit from its milk and wool, and he was lent one. "Istikhwal" is like it. Al-Asmaʿi related from Abu ʿAmr that he said: "If I recited it, I would recite: 'If they seek to lend wealth, they lend,'" and said: "Ikhtibal is a loaned she-camel, and I do not know istikhbal; I think it is istikhwal. Istikhwal means that they make them own it."

As for His saying "yaysiru," it is from the "maysir," in which the portions are divided. As for His saying "yughlu," it means they choose the fat portions for slaughter, so they only slaughter the most precious.]

The scholars of interpretation have said things similar to what we have said on this.

Those who said so:

13571 - Muhammad ibn al-Husayn narrated to me, saying: Ahmad ibn al-Mufaddal narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: "And you have left behind you what We bestowed upon you," from wealth and servants, "behind your backs," in the world.

* *
